abstract: We have constructed a recurrent network that stabilizes images of a moving object on the retina of a simulated eye. The structure of the network was motivated by the organization of the primate visual target tracking system. The basic components of a complete target tracking system were simulated, including visual processing, sensory-motor interface, and motor control. Our model is simpler in structure, function and performance than the primate system, but many of the complexities inherent in a complete system are present.

paragraphs: The paper presents a recurrent neural network that controls a simulated eye so that the image of a moving object remains stable on its retina. Its structure is motivated by the organization of the primate visual tracking system. The task links perception and movement because tracking requires visual information to guide changes in eye position.

The simulation includes the major components of a complete target-tracking system: visual processing, the interface between sensory information and movement, and motor control. Bringing these components together matters because successful tracking depends on their coordinated operation. A visual motion representation must ultimately support commands that stabilize the target's retinal image.

The authors explicitly describe the model as simpler than the primate system in structure, function, and performance. Even so, it includes many complexities inherent in an integrated tracking system. Its value is therefore as a working recurrent model of the complete perception-to-action task, demonstrating image stabilization while retaining a clear distinction between the simulation and biological tracking.
summary.tldr: A recurrent network integrates visual processing and motor control to stabilize a moving target's image on a simulated retina.

title: Recurrent Eye Tracking Network Using a Distributed Representation of Image Motion

abstract: This study explores the extent to which a network that learns the temporal relationships within and between the component features of Western tonal music can account for music theoretic and psychological phenomena such as the tonal hierarchy and rhythmic expectancies. Predicted and generated sequences were recorded as the representation of a 153-note waltz melody was learnt by a predictive, recurrent network. The network learned transitions and relations between and within pitch and timing components: accent and duration values interacted in the development of rhythmic and metric structures and, with training, the network developed chordal expectancies in response to the activation of individual tones. Analysis of the hidden unit representation revealed that musical sequences are represented as transitions between states in hidden unit space.

paragraphs: This paper explores whether learning relationships among musical components can account for aspects of tonal and rhythmic expectation. A predictive recurrent network learns a representation of a 153-note waltz melody. The authors record its predictions and generated sequences as training proceeds, examining how expectations develop from temporal relationships in the music.

The network learns transitions both within pitch and timing components and between them. Accent and duration interact as rhythmic and metric structures develop. With training, activating individual tones also produces expectations about chords, linking the response to a single pitch with broader tonal relationships learned from the sequence.

Analysis of the hidden units shows musical sequences represented as transitions between states in the network's internal representation. This connects the observed predictions to a changing internal context rather than only to isolated notes. Within the studied melody, the results demonstrate how a component-based predictive representation can develop interacting pitch and timing expectations, offering a computational approach to the musical and psychological phenomena motivating the study.
summary.tldr: A recurrent network learning a waltz develops interacting pitch, rhythm, and chord expectations through temporal prediction.

title: Tonal Music as a Componential Code: Learning Temporal Relationships Between and Within Pitch and Timing Components

abstract: This paper describes a small, compact circuit that captures the temporal and adaptation properties both of the photoreceptor and of the laminar layers of the fly. This circuit uses only six transis(cid:173) tors and two capacitors. It is operated in the subthreshold domain. The circuit maintains a high transient gain by using adaptation to the background intensity as a form of gain control. The adapta(cid:173) tion time constant of the circuit can be controlled via an external bias. Its temporal filtering properties change with the background intensity or signal-to-noise conditions. The frequency response of the circuit shows that in the frequency range of 1 to 100 Hz, the circuit response goes from highpass filtering under high light levels to lowpass filtering under low light levels (Le., when the signal-to(cid:173) noise ratio is low). A chip with 20x20 pixels has been fabricated in 1.2J.Lm ORBIT CMOS nwell technology.

paragraphs: This paper presents a compact circuit that reproduces temporal response and adaptation properties of the fly's photoreceptors and laminar layers. The circuit uses six transistors and two capacitors and operates in the subthreshold domain. A fabricated chip contains a 20-by-20 array of these pixels.

Adaptation to background intensity acts as gain control, allowing the circuit to maintain a strong response to transient changes. An external bias controls the adaptation time constant, meaning the timescale over which this adjustment occurs can be set. The design therefore combines sensitivity to change with an adjustable response to the prevailing light level.

Its temporal filtering also varies with illumination and signal-to-noise conditions. Across the reported range of 1 to 100 Hz, it behaves as a high-pass filter under bright light and as a low-pass filter under dim light, when signal-to-noise is low. This demonstrates a visual sensing circuit whose treatment of temporal changes adapts to the conditions under which it operates.
summary.tldr: A compact silicon-retina circuit adapts its gain and temporal filtering to background illumination.

title: Silicon Retina with Adaptive Filtering Properties

abstract: It is known that decision tree learning can be viewed as a form of boosting. However, existing boosting theorems for decision tree learning allow only binary-branching trees and the generalization to multi-branching trees is not immediate. Practical decision tree al(cid:173) gorithms, such as CART and C4.5, implement a trade-off between the number of branches and the improvement in tree quality as measured by an index function. Here we give a boosting justifica(cid:173) tion for a particular quantitative trade-off curve. Our main theorem states, in essence, that if we require an improvement proportional to the log of the number of branches then top-down greedy con(cid:173) struction of decision trees remains an effective boosting algorithm.

However, existing boosting theorems for decision tree learning allow only binary-branching trees and the generalization to multi-branching trees is not immediate. paragraphs: The paper extends the theoretical connection between decision-tree learning and boosting to trees with more than two branches at a split. Existing boosting results covered binary branching, but allowing additional branches changes the trade-off involved in growing a tree. A split can improve the tree's quality while also making its structure more elaborate.

Practical algorithms such as CART and C4.5 already balance the number of branches against improvement measured by a tree-quality index. The authors provide a boosting justification for a particular mathematical form of that balance. The required improvement grows in proportion to the logarithm of the number of branches.

The main theorem states, in essence, that top-down greedy tree construction remains an effective boosting algorithm when this improvement requirement is met. This is a conditional guarantee: the quality gain must satisfy the stated relationship to branching. Its significance is to give a theoretical basis for evaluating multi-way splits, connecting a local choice during tree construction to the broader boosting interpretation.
summary.tldr: Multi-way decision-tree growth retains a boosting guarantee when split improvement scales with the logarithm of the branch count.

title: Boosting with Multi-Way Branching in Decision Trees

abstract: We have designed and fabricated a VLSI synapse that can learn a conditional probability or correlation between spike-based inputs and feedback signals. The synapse is low power, compact, provides nonvolatile weight storage, and can perform simultaneous multiplication and adaptation. We can calibrate arrays of synapses to ensure uniform adaptation characteristics. Finally, adaptation in our synapse does not necessarily depend on the signals used for computation. Consequently, our synapse can implement learning rules that correlate past and present synaptic activity. We provide analysis and experimental chip results demonstrating the operation in learning and calibration mode, and show how to use our synapse to implement various learning rules in silicon.

paragraphs: The paper presents a fabricated silicon synapse that learns a conditional probability or correlation between spike-based inputs and feedback signals. The device combines learning and computation in one circuit: it can multiply signals while adapting its stored weight. The authors describe it as compact and low power, with weight storage that persists without continuous power.

Arrays of these synapses can be calibrated to have uniform adaptation characteristics. Another feature is that the signals driving adaptation need not be the same ones used for computation. This flexibility allows learning rules that relate earlier synaptic activity to present activity, broadening the temporal relationships the hardware can learn.

The paper supplies circuit analysis and experimental chip results for both learning and calibration modes. It also explains how the synapse can implement several learning rules in silicon. The evidence therefore concerns an operating physical device, while the architectural contribution is a synapse whose computation, persistent storage, and adaptation can be used together.
summary.tldr: A fabricated low-power synapse learns spike-based probabilities or correlations while supporting persistent weights, simultaneous computation, and calibrated adaptation.

title: Learning Spike-Based Correlations and Conditional Probabilities in Silicon

abstract: Mesoscopical, mathematical descriptions of dynamics of populations of spiking neurons are getting increasingly important for the understanding of large-scale processes in the brain using simulations. In our previous work, integral equation formulations for population dynamics have been derived for a special type of spiking neurons. For Integrate- and- Fire type neurons , these formulations were only approximately correct. Here, we derive a mathematically compact, exact population dynamics formulation for Integrate- and- Fire type neurons. It can be shown quantitatively in simulations that the numerical correspondence with microscopically modeled neuronal populations is excellent.

paragraphs: The paper develops a mathematical description of how populations of integrate-and-fire neurons evolve. Its motivation is the growing importance of population-level models for simulating large-scale brain processes. Such descriptions operate between the behavior of individual spiking neurons and the larger systems formed by many neurons, making the relationship between those levels a central concern.

The authors' earlier work had produced integral-equation descriptions for a particular type of spiking neuron. When applied to integrate-and-fire neurons, those formulations were only approximately correct. Here, the authors derive a compact formulation that is mathematically exact for integrate-and-fire population dynamics, directly addressing that approximation in the earlier treatment.

They also assess the formulation numerically by comparing it with populations modeled at the individual-neuron level. Simulations show excellent quantitative agreement between the two descriptions. The contribution thus has two linked parts: an exact mathematical population formulation and numerical evidence that its computed behavior closely matches microscopic neuronal simulations. This supports its use in understanding population dynamics within the stated neuron model.
summary.tldr: A compact, exact formulation describes integrate-and-fire neuron populations and closely matches individual-neuron simulations.

title: Exact differential equation population dynamics for integrate-and-fire neurons

abstract: We present a modiﬁed version of the perceptron learning algorithm (PLA) which solves semideﬁnite programs (SDPs) in polynomial time. The algorithm is based on the following three observations: (i) Semideﬁnite programs are linear programs with inﬁnitely many (linear) constraints; (ii) every linear program can be solved by a sequence of constraint satisfaction problems with linear constraints; (iii) in general, the perceptron learning algorithm solves a constraint satisfaction problem with linear constraints in ﬁnitely many updates. Combining the PLA with a probabilistic rescaling algorithm (which, on average, increases the size of the feasable region) results in a prob- abilistic algorithm for solving SDPs that runs in polynomial time. We present preliminary results which demonstrate that the algo- rithm works, but is not competitive with state-of-the-art interior point methods.

The algorithm is based on the following three observations: (i) Semideﬁnite programs are linear programs with inﬁnitely many (linear) constraints; (ii) every linear program can be solved by a sequence of constraint satisfaction problems with linear constraints; (iii) in general, the perceptron learning algorithm solves a constraint satisfaction problem with linear constraints in ﬁnitely many updates. Combining the PLA with a probabilistic rescaling algorithm (which, on average, increases the size of the feasable region) results in a prob- abilistic algorithm for solving SDPs that runs in polynomial time. We present preliminary results which demonstrate that the algo- rithm works, but is not competitive with state-of-the-art interior point methods.

paragraphs: This paper develops a probabilistic polynomial-time method for semidefinite programming using a modified perceptron learning algorithm. Its starting point is a connection between optimization and constraint satisfaction. Semidefinite programs can be viewed as linear programs with infinitely many linear constraints, while linear programs can be approached through sequences of linear constraint-satisfaction problems.

The perceptron supplies a procedure for satisfying linear constraints through updates. To obtain the stated polynomial-time algorithm, the authors combine it with probabilistic rescaling. This rescaling increases the size of the feasible region on average, changing the geometry of the constraint problem in a way that supports the overall method.

Preliminary experiments show that the algorithm works, but it is not competitive with state-of-the-art interior-point methods. The paper’s significance is therefore the demonstrated algorithmic connection and its complexity guarantee, alongside a candid early performance result. It shows how a learning procedure, augmented by rescaling, can be used to solve this class of optimization problems.
summary.tldr: Perceptron updates plus probabilistic rescaling yield a polynomial-time SDP solver, though preliminary performance trails interior-point methods.

title: Semi-Definite Programming by Perceptron Learning

abstract: Existing algorithms for discrete partially observable Markov decision processes can at best solve problems of a few thousand states due to two important sources of intractability: the curse of dimensionality and the policy space complexity. This paper describes a new algorithm (VDCBPI) that mitigates both sources of intractability by combining the Value Directed Compression (VDC) technique [13] with Bounded Policy Iteration (BPI) [14]. The scalability of VDCBPI is demonstrated on synthetic network management problems with up to 33 million states.
originalAbstract: Existing algorithms for discrete partially observable Markov decision processes can at best solve problems of a few thousand states due to two important sources of intractability: the curse of dimensionality and the policy space complexity. This paper describes a new algorithm (VDCBPI) that mitigates both sources of intractability by combining the Value Directed Compression (VDC) technique [13] with Bounded Policy Iteration (BPI) [14]. The scalability of VDCBPI is demonstrated on synthetic network management problems with up to 33 million states.

paragraphs: The paper addresses scaling in discrete partially observable Markov decision processes, where decisions must be made without directly observing the full state. It identifies two sources of computational difficulty: the curse of dimensionality and the complexity of the policy space. Together, these make representing the problem and searching for a decision policy expensive.

The proposed algorithm, VDCBPI, combines Value Directed Compression with Bounded Policy Iteration. The authors describe this combination as mitigating both sources of intractability. Bringing compression and policy iteration into the same approximate algorithm addresses the size of the decision problem alongside the complexity of finding a policy.

The scalability demonstration uses synthetic network-management problems containing up to 33 million states. This is the paper's concrete evidence that the combined method can operate at a much larger state scale than the few-thousand-state reach attributed to existing algorithms in the abstract. The result supports the scalability of this approximate approach on the demonstrated problem family, with the combination of techniques as the central contribution.
summary.tldr: VDCBPI combines value-directed compression and bounded policy iteration, demonstrating scalability on synthetic POMDPs with up to 33 million states.

title: VDCBPI: an Approximate Scalable Algorithm for Large POMDPs

abstract: While kernel canonical correlation analysis (kernel CCA) has been applied in many problems, the asymptotic convergence of the functions estimated from a finite sample to the true functions has not yet been established. This paper gives a rigorous proof of the statistical convergence of kernel CCA and a related method (NOCCO), which provides a theoretical justification for these methods. The result also gives a sufficient condition on the decay of the regularization coefficient in the methods to ensure convergence.
originalAbstract: While kernel canonical correlation analysis (kernel CCA) has been applied in many problems, the asymptotic convergence of the functions estimated from a finite sample to the true functions has not yet been established. This paper gives a rigorous proof of the statistical convergence of kernel CCA and a related method (NOCCO), which provides a theoretical justification for these methods. The result also gives a sufficient condition on the decay of the regularization coefficient in the methods to ensure convergence.

paragraphs: This paper addresses a theoretical question about kernel canonical correlation analysis: whether functions estimated from a finite sample approach the true functions as more data become available. The method had already been applied to many problems, but the abstract identifies this asymptotic convergence question as an unresolved part of its statistical foundation.

The authors provide a rigorous convergence proof for kernel CCA and for a related method called NOCCO. This gives theoretical support for the estimation procedures by connecting what they learn from samples with their underlying target functions. The contribution concerns statistical convergence, rather than simply whether a numerical optimization procedure finishes.

The analysis also gives a sufficient condition governing how the regularization coefficient decreases as the sample grows. Following that condition ensures convergence within the result's scope. A sufficient condition supplies a valid route to the guarantee; it does not establish that every other schedule must fail. The paper therefore contributes both a foundational proof and guidance about regularization in the asymptotic setting.
summary.tldr: The paper proves statistical convergence of kernel CCA and NOCCO and gives a sufficient condition on regularization decay.

title: Statistical Convergence of Kernel CCA

abstract: In real-world planning problems, we must reason not only about our own goals, but about the goals of other agents with which we may interact. Often these agents' goals are neither completely aligned with our own nor directly opposed to them. Instead there are opportunities for cooperation: by joining forces, the agents can all achieve higher utility than they could separately. But, in order to cooperate, the agents must negotiate a mutually acceptable plan from among the many possible ones, and each agent must trust that the others will follow their parts of the deal. Research in multi-agent planning has often avoided the problem of making sure that all agents have an incentive to follow a proposed joint plan. On the other hand, while game theoretic algorithms handle incentives correctly, they often don't scale to large planning problems. In this paper we attempt to bridge the gap between these two lines of research: we present an efficient game-theoretic approximate planning algorithm, along with a negotiation protocol which encourages agents to compute and agree on joint plans that are fair and optimal in a sense defined below. We demonstrate our algorithm and protocol on two simple robotic planning problems.1

In this paper we attempt to bridge the gap between these two lines of research: we present an efficient game-theoretic approximate planning algorithm, along with a negotiation protocol which encourages agents to compute and agree on joint plans that are fair and optimal in a sense defined below. We demonstrate our algorithm and protocol on two simple robotic planning problems.1

paragraphs: Robots planning together may have goals that partly overlap without being identical. Cooperation can benefit all participants, but they still need to select a mutually acceptable plan and have reasons to follow it. The paper addresses this combination of planning, negotiation, and incentives in general-sum stochastic games.

The authors identify a gap between two research traditions. Multi-agent planning often leaves aside whether every participant has an incentive to carry out a proposed agreement. Game-theoretic algorithms address incentives but can struggle with large planning problems. The paper proposes an efficient approximate game-theoretic planning algorithm to help connect these concerns.

A negotiation protocol accompanies the algorithm and encourages agents to compute and agree on joint plans that are fair and optimal according to the paper's definitions. The method concerns approximating subgame-perfect equilibria, bringing continued incentives into the planning problem. Demonstrations use two simple robotic planning tasks. These illustrate the combined algorithm and protocol; the abstract's efficiency claim and demonstrations should not be read as evidence of deployment across arbitrary large robotic systems.
summary.tldr: An approximate game-theoretic planner and negotiation protocol help robots agree on cooperative plans with incentives to follow them.

title: Multi-Robot Negotiation: Approximating the Set of Subgame Perfect Equilibria in General-Sum Stochastic Games

abstract: We propose an active learning algorithm that learns a continuous valuation model from discrete preferences. The algorithm automatically decides what items are best presented to an individual in order to find the item that they value highly in as few trials as possible, and exploits quirks of human psychology to minimize time and cognitive burden. To do this, our algorithm maximizes the expected improvement at each query without accurately modelling the entire valuation surface, which would be needlessly expensive. The problem is particularly difficult because the space of choices is infinite. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the new algorithm compared to related active learning methods. We also embed the algorithm within a decision making tool for assisting digital artists in rendering materials. The tool finds the best parameters while minimizing the number of queries.

The algorithm automatically decides what items are best presented to an individual in order to find the item that they value highly in as few trials as possible, and exploits quirks of human psychology to minimize time and cognitive burden. To do this, our algorithm maximizes the expected improvement at each query without accurately modelling the entire valuation surface, which would be needlessly expensive. paragraphs: People can express preferences by choosing among presented items, even when the possible items vary continuously. This paper develops an active learning algorithm that uses these discrete choices to learn a continuous valuation model. The practical objective is to find something an individual values highly while keeping the number of interactions small.

The algorithm chooses each query by maximizing expected improvement. This focuses its effort on finding better items without requiring an accurate model of preferences across the entire choice space. That distinction matters because there are infinitely many possible choices, making comprehensive modeling needlessly expensive for the stated objective. The design also uses characteristics of human psychology to reduce time and cognitive burden.

The authors demonstrate effectiveness relative to related active learning methods and integrate the algorithm into a tool for digital artists choosing material-rendering parameters. In that application, preference queries guide the search for desirable settings. The work connects an adaptive statistical search strategy to an interactive task where the cost of asking a person another question is part of the problem.
summary.tldr: An active preference learner selects choices by expected improvement to find highly valued items with fewer interactions.

title: Active Preference Learning with Discrete Choice Data

abstract: We propose a compact, low power VLSI network of spiking neurons which can learn to classify complex patterns of mean ﬁring rates on–line and in real–time. The network of integrate-and-ﬁre neurons is connected by bistable synapses that can change their weight using a local spike–based plasticity mechanism. Learning is supervised by a teacher which provides an extra input to the output neurons during training. The synaptic weights are updated only if the current generated by the plastic synapses does not match the output desired by the teacher (as in the perceptron learning rule). We present experimental results that demonstrate how this VLSI network is able to robustly classify uncorrelated linearly separable spatial patterns of mean ﬁring rates.
originalAbstract: We propose a compact, low power VLSI network of spiking neurons which can learn to classify complex patterns of mean ﬁring rates on–line and in real–time. The network of integrate-and-ﬁre neurons is connected by bistable synapses that can change their weight using a local spike–based plasticity mechanism. Learning is supervised by a teacher which provides an extra input to the output neurons during training. The synaptic weights are updated only if the current generated by the plastic synapses does not match the output desired by the teacher (as in the perceptron learning rule). We present experimental results that demonstrate how this VLSI network is able to robustly classify uncorrelated linearly separable spatial patterns of mean ﬁring rates.

paragraphs: The paper presents a compact, low-power hardware network that learns to classify patterns represented by mean neural firing rates. Learning occurs online and in real time, making adaptation part of the network’s operation. The implementation uses integrate-and-fire neurons connected through synapses with two stable weight states.

Synaptic changes follow a local mechanism driven by spikes. During training, a teacher supplies additional input to the output neurons to indicate the desired response. Weights change only when the current produced by the plastic synapses fails to match that desired output. This error-dependent update resembles the perceptron learning rule within a spiking hardware implementation.

Experiments demonstrate robust classification of uncorrelated, linearly separable spatial patterns of mean firing rates. Those properties describe the demonstrated class of patterns and should remain attached to the result. The contribution is a working hardware learning scheme that combines local synaptic adaptation, teacher supervision, and real-time operation, with experimental evidence for the specified classification setting.
summary.tldr: A compact spiking-neuron chip learns online through local, teacher-guided synaptic updates and robustly classifies the tested linearly separable patterns.

title: Learning to classify complex patterns using a VLSI network of spiking neurons

abstract: We develop an algorithm for efficient range search when the notion of dissimilarity is given by a Bregman divergence. The range search task is to return all points in a potentially large database that are within some specified distance of a query. It arises in many learning algorithms such as locally-weighted regression, kernel density estimation, neighborhood graph-based algorithms, and in tasks like outlier detection and information retrieval. In metric spaces, efficient range search-like algorithms based on spatial data structures have been deployed on a variety of statistical tasks. Here we describe the first algorithm for range search for an arbitrary Bregman divergence. This broad class of dissimilarity measures includes the relative entropy, Mahalanobis distance, Itakura-Saito divergence, and a variety of matrix divergences. Metric methods cannot be directly applied since Bregman divergences do not in general satisfy the triangle inequality. We derive geometric properties of Bregman divergences that yield an efficient algorithm for range search based on a recently proposed space decomposition for Bregman divergences.

The range search task is to return all points in a potentially large database that are within some specified distance of a query. It arises in many learning algorithms such as locally-weighted regression, kernel density estimation, neighborhood graph-based algorithms, and in tasks like outlier detection and information retrieval. In metric spaces, efficient range search-like algorithms based on spatial data structures have been deployed on a variety of statistical tasks. Here we describe the first algorithm for range search for an arbitrary Bregman divergence. This broad class of dissimilarity measures includes the relative entropy, Mahalanobis distance, Itakura-Saito divergence, and a variety of matrix divergences. Metric methods cannot be directly applied since Bregman divergences do not in general satisfy the triangle inequality. We derive geometric properties of Bregman divergences that yield an efficient algorithm for range search based on a recently proposed space decomposition for Bregman divergences.

paragraphs: Range search asks for every database point whose dissimilarity to a query falls within a specified threshold. This operation supports methods such as local regression, density estimation, neighborhood graphs, and outlier detection. The paper develops an efficient search algorithm for situations where dissimilarity is measured by a Bregman divergence.

The difficulty is geometric. Many established search methods rely on the triangle inequality to reason about distances and organize spatial searches. Bregman divergences generally do not satisfy that inequality, so those methods cannot simply be carried over. The relevant family includes relative entropy, Mahalanobis distance, Itakura-Saito divergence, and several divergences between matrices.

The authors derive geometric properties that support search without depending on the usual metric argument. They combine these properties with a recently proposed decomposition of space for Bregman divergences. The abstract identifies this as the first range-search algorithm covering an arbitrary Bregman divergence. Its significance is to make efficient neighborhood retrieval available across a broad family of dissimilarity measures used in learning.
summary.tldr: New geometric results enable efficient range search for arbitrary Bregman divergences despite their general lack of a triangle inequality.

title: Efficient Bregman Range Search

abstract: We consider the problem of Bayesian inference for continuous time multi-stable stochastic systems which can change both their diffusion and drift parameters at discrete times. We propose exact inference and sampling methodologies for two specific cases where the discontinuous dynamics is given by a Poisson process and a two-state Markovian switch. We test the methodology on simulated data, and apply it to two real data sets in finance and systems biology. Our experimental results show that the approach leads to valid inferences and non-trivial insights.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of Bayesian inference for continuous time multi-stable stochastic systems which can change both their diffusion and drift parameters at discrete times. We propose exact inference and sampling methodologies for two specific cases where the discontinuous dynamics is given by a Poisson process and a two-state Markovian switch. We test the methodology on simulated data, and apply it to two real data sets in finance and systems biology. Our experimental results show that the approach leads to valid inferences and non-trivial insights.

paragraphs: Some stochastic systems evolve continuously while changing their behavior at distinct moments. This paper considers Bayesian inference for multistable systems in which both drift and diffusion parameters can change at discrete times. The modeling task must therefore account for continuous evolution together with abrupt changes in the parameters governing that evolution.

The authors develop exact inference and sampling methods for two specified forms of switching dynamics: one governed by a Poisson process and another by a two-state Markovian switch. These cases give concrete mathematical settings in which uncertainty about a changing system can be handled exactly. The exactness claim applies to those particular cases.

The methods are tested on simulated data and applied to two real datasets drawn from finance and systems biology. The authors report valid inferences and substantive insights from these experiments. The contribution links a precise treatment of discontinuous parameter changes with applications involving continuously evolving observations, showing that the proposed inference framework can produce useful interpretations in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Exact Bayesian inference and sampling methods handle two specified kinds of parameter switching in continuous-time stochastic systems.

title: Inference in continuous-time change-point models

abstract: In this work we study how the stimulus distribution influences the optimal coding of an individual neuron. Closed-form solutions to the optimal sigmoidal tuning curve are provided for a neuron obeying Poisson statistics under a given stimulus distribution. We consider a variety of optimality criteria, including maximizing discriminability, maximizing mutual information and minimizing estimation error under a general $L_p$ norm. We generalize the Cramer-Rao lower bound and show how the $L_p$ loss can be written as a functional of the Fisher Information in the asymptotic limit, by proving the moment convergence of certain functions of Poisson random variables. In this manner, we show how the optimal tuning curve depends upon the loss function, and the equivalence of maximizing mutual information with minimizing $L_p$ loss in the limit as $p$ goes to zero.

They then express that loss in terms of Fisher information in an asymptotic limit, supported by a moment-convergence result for functions of Poisson variables.

summary.tldr: For Poisson neurons, optimal sigmoidal tuning depends on stimulus statistics and coding objectives, with an information–loss equivalence as p approaches zero.

title: Optimal Neural Tuning Curves for Arbitrary Stimulus Distributions: Discrimax, Infomax and Minimum $L_p$ Loss

abstract: The problem of multiple change point estimation is considered for sequences with unknown number of change points. A consistency framework is suggested that is suitable for highly dependent time-series, and an asymptotically consistent algorithm is proposed. In order for the consistency to be established the only assumption required is that the data is generated by stationary ergodic time-series distributions. No modeling, independence or parametric assumptions are made; the data are allowed to be dependent and the dependence can be of arbitrary form. The theoretical results are complemented with experimental evaluations.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to locate multiple changes in a sequence when the number of changes is unknown. Its focus is time-series data with potentially strong dependence between observations. In this setting, treating successive measurements as independent would exclude the kinds of sequences the authors want to handle.

The authors propose a consistency framework and an algorithm that is asymptotically consistent within it. The stated distributional assumption is stationary ergodicity: the generating time-series distributions have stable statistical behavior and support long-run regularity. They impose no independence or parametric assumptions, and permit dependence to take an arbitrary form.

This matters because the guarantee is formulated around broad properties of the generating processes rather than a particular model of their dependence. The asymptotic qualification places the result in the limit of increasing data, rather than promising exact answers for every finite sequence. Experimental evaluations complement the theory, supplying an empirical examination of an approach designed for highly dependent observations.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes asymptotically consistent change-point estimation for stationary ergodic time series with arbitrary dependence and an unknown number of changes.

title: Locating Changes in Highly Dependent Data with Unknown Number of Change Points

abstract: Crowdsourcing has become a popular paradigm for labeling large datasets. However, it has given rise to the computational task of aggregating the crowdsourced labels provided by a collection of unreliable annotators. We approach this problem by transforming it into a standard inference problem in graphical models, and applying approximate variational methods, including belief propagation (BP) and mean field (MF). We show that our BP algorithm generalizes both majority voting and a recent algorithm by Karger et al, while our MF method is closely related to a commonly used EM algorithm. In both cases, we find that the performance of the algorithms critically depends on the choice of a prior distribution on the workers' reliability; by choosing the prior properly, both BP and MF (and EM) perform surprisingly well on both simulated and real-world datasets, competitive with state-of-the-art algorithms based on more complicated modeling assumptions.

paragraphs: Crowdsourced datasets often contain conflicting labels from annotators whose reliability is uncertain. This paper treats aggregation of those labels as an inference problem in a graphical model. It applies approximate methods, including belief propagation and mean field, to turn a collection of unreliable judgments into inferred labels.

The formulation also connects several existing approaches. The proposed belief propagation algorithm generalizes both majority voting and an earlier aggregation algorithm, while the mean-field method is closely related to a commonly used expectation-maximization algorithm. These relationships place familiar methods within a shared inference perspective and help expose choices that affect their behavior.

The authors find that performance depends critically on the prior distribution over worker reliability. With a suitable prior, belief propagation, mean field, and expectation maximization perform strongly on simulated and real-world datasets, remaining competitive with state-of-the-art algorithms using more complicated assumptions. The finding emphasizes that the reliability prior is a consequential modeling choice: good results arise from the combination of inference method and appropriately chosen prior.
summary.tldr: Graphical-model inference aggregates crowdsourced labels competitively, with performance critically dependent on the prior over worker reliability.

title: Variational Inference for Crowdsourcing

abstract: Conditional random fields, which model the distribution of a multivariate response conditioned on a set of covariates using undirected graphs, are widely used in a variety of multivariate prediction applications. Popular instances of this class of models such as categorical-discrete CRFs, Ising CRFs, and conditional Gaussian based CRFs, are not however best suited to the varied types of response variables in many applications, including count-valued responses. We thus introduce a “novel subclass of CRFs”, derived by imposing node-wise conditional distributions of response variables conditioned on the rest of the responses and the covariates as arising from univariate exponential families. This allows us to derive novel multivariate CRFs given any univariate exponential distribution, including the Poisson, negative binomial, and exponential distributions. Also in particular, it addresses the common CRF problem of specifying feature'' functions determining the interactions between response variables and covariates. We develop a class of tractable penalized $M$-estimators to learn these CRF distributions from data, as well as a unified sparsistency analysis for this general class of CRFs showing exact structure recovery can be achieved with high probability."

paragraphs: Conditional random fields predict several related response variables together, using an undirected graph to represent their dependencies given input covariates. Familiar versions accommodate some response types well, but are less suited to others, including counts. The paper develops a broader construction that starts from distributions appropriate for individual response variables.

Each response's conditional distribution, given the other responses and the covariates, is required to belong to a univariate exponential family. This leads to multivariate conditional models based on distributions such as Poisson, negative binomial, and exponential. The construction also addresses how to specify the feature functions that express interactions between responses and covariates.

For learning, the authors develop tractable penalized estimators and a unified analysis of sparse structure recovery. They show that exact recovery of the graph can be achieved with high probability. The contribution links model construction and estimation: the same framework expands the available response distributions and supplies a theoretical basis for learning which dependencies are present.
summary.tldr: Building CRFs from univariate exponential-family conditionals expands supported response types and enables high-probability structure-recovery guarantees.

title: Conditional Random Fields via Univariate Exponential Families

abstract: Optimal transportation distances are a fundamental family of parameterized distances for histograms in the probability simplex. Despite their appealing theoretical properties, excellent performance and intuitive formulation, their computation involves the resolution of a linear program whose cost is prohibitive whenever the histograms' dimension exceeds a few hundreds. We propose in this work a new family of optimal transportation distances that look at transportation problems from a maximum-entropy perspective. We smooth the classical optimal transportation problem with an entropic regularization term, and show that the resulting optimum is also a distance which can be computed through Sinkhorn's matrix scaling algorithm at a speed that is several orders of magnitude faster than that of transportation solvers. We also report improved performance on the MNIST benchmark problem over competing distances.

paragraphs: Optimal transport compares probability histograms through a transportation problem: how their mass can be moved between locations. Although this formulation has appealing properties, computing it requires solving a linear program. The paper identifies that computation as prohibitively expensive once histogram dimensions extend beyond a few hundred.

The proposed approach introduces an entropy regularization term into the classical transportation problem. This smooths the optimization and gives it a maximum-entropy interpretation. The resulting formulation can be computed using Sinkhorn's matrix scaling algorithm, providing a different computational route to transport-based comparisons.

The authors present a new family of transportation distances and report computation several orders of magnitude faster than transportation solvers. They also report better performance than competing distances on the MNIST benchmark. These findings concern both the cost of computing comparisons and their usefulness in the evaluated task. The paper's central contribution is to connect an entropy-modified transport objective with an efficient matrix-scaling procedure, making transport-based histogram comparison substantially more practical in the reported setting.
summary.tldr: Entropy regularization enables Sinkhorn matrix scaling to compute transport-based histogram distances far faster, with improved reported MNIST performance.

title: Sinkhorn Distances: Lightspeed Computation of Optimal Transport

abstract: A large number of algorithms in machine learning, from principal component analysis (PCA), and its non-linear (kernel) extensions, to more recent spectral embedding and support estimation methods, rely on estimating a linear subspace from samples. In this paper we introduce a general formulation of this problem and derive novel learning error estimates. Our results rely on natural assumptions on the spectral properties of the covariance operator associated to the data distribution, and hold for a wide class of metrics between subspaces. As special cases, we discuss sharp error estimates for the reconstruction properties of PCA and spectral support estimation. Key to our analysis is an operator theoretic approach that has broad applicability to spectral learning methods.

Key to our analysis is an operator theoretic approach that has broad applicability to spectral learning methods.

paragraphs: Many learning methods estimate a linear subspace from observed samples. This paper places that shared task into a general formulation, covering connections to principal component analysis, kernel extensions, spectral embeddings, and support estimation. The central question is how accurately the learned subspace represents the target when only sample data are available.

The authors derive learning-error estimates using an operator-theoretic analysis. Their results depend on assumptions about the spectral properties of the data distribution's covariance operator. Those properties describe structure relevant to subspace estimation, and the resulting guarantees hold for a broad collection of ways to measure differences between subspaces.

The paper develops sharp error estimates for PCA reconstruction and spectral support estimation as special cases. This makes the general theory useful for assessing concrete properties of established learning methods. Its significance is a common analytical approach that can support multiple spectral-learning tasks and multiple error measures, with the stated guarantees tied to assumptions about the covariance spectrum.
summary.tldr: A general operator-theoretic analysis gives subspace-learning error estimates under assumptions on the data's covariance spectrum.

title: On the Sample Complexity of Subspace Learning

abstract: We present two related contributions of independent interest: (1) high-probability finite sample rates for k-NN density estimation, and (2) practical mode estimators – based on k-NN – which attain minimax-optimal rates under surprisingly general distributional conditions.
originalAbstract: We present two related contributions of independent interest: (1) high-probability finite sample rates for k-NN density estimation, and (2) practical mode estimators – based on k-NN – which attain minimax-optimal rates under surprisingly general distributional conditions.
title: Optimal rates for k-NN density and mode estimation

abstract: Determinantal point processes (DPPs) are point process models thatnaturally encode diversity between the points of agiven realization, through a positive definite kernel $K$. DPPs possess desirable properties, such as exactsampling or analyticity of the moments, but learning the parameters ofkernel $K$ through likelihood-based inference is notstraightforward. First, the kernel that appears in thelikelihood is not $K$, but another kernel $L$ related to $K$ throughan often intractable spectral decomposition. This issue is typically bypassed in machine learning bydirectly parametrizing the kernel $L$, at the price of someinterpretability of the model parameters. We follow this approachhere. Second, the likelihood has an intractable normalizingconstant, which takes the form of large determinant in the case of aDPP over a finite set of objects, and the form of a Fredholm determinant in thecase of a DPP over a continuous domain. Our main contribution is to derive bounds on the likelihood ofa DPP, both for finite and continuous domains. Unlike previous work, our bounds arecheap to evaluate since they do not rely on approximating the spectrumof a large matrix or an operator. Through usual arguments, these bounds thus yield cheap variationalinference and moderately expensive exact Markov chain Monte Carlo inference methods for DPPs.

paragraphs: Determinantal point processes model collections whose elements tend to be diverse. Their useful mathematical properties do not make likelihood-based parameter learning straightforward. The likelihood involves a kernel L related to the model's kernel K through a potentially intractable spectral decomposition, and its normalizing constant introduces another substantial computational obstacle.

The paper directly parameterizes L, following an existing approach that sacrifices some parameter interpretability. Its main contribution addresses the normalization problem by deriving likelihood bounds for both finite and continuous domains. In the finite case the normalizer involves a large determinant; in the continuous case it involves a Fredholm determinant. The bounds can be evaluated cheaply without approximating the relevant matrix or operator spectrum.

These bounds support inexpensive variational inference and moderately expensive exact Markov chain Monte Carlo inference. The practical significance is a way to perform likelihood-based learning without the spectral calculations that otherwise make it difficult. The method retains the stated interpretability tradeoff of parameterizing L, while opening inference routes for both discrete collections and continuous point-process domains.
summary.tldr: Cheap likelihood bounds enable DPP inference on finite and continuous domains without approximating matrix or operator spectra.

title: Inference for determinantal point processes without spectral knowledge

abstract: Large labeled training sets are the critical building blocks of supervised learning methods and are key enablers of deep learning techniques. For some applications, creating labeled training sets is the most time-consuming and expensive part of applying machine learning. We therefore propose a paradigm for the programmatic creation of training sets called data programming in which users provide a set of labeling functions, which are programs that heuristically label subsets of the data, but that are noisy and may conflict. By viewing these labeling functions as implicitly describing a generative model for this noise, we show that we can recover the parameters of this model to "denoise" the generated training set, and establish theoretically that we can recover the parameters of these generative models in a handful of settings. We then show how to modify a discriminative loss function to make it noise-aware, and demonstrate our method over a range of discriminative models including logistic regression and LSTMs. Experimentally, on the 2014 TAC-KBP Slot Filling challenge, we show that data programming would have led to a new winning score, and also show that applying data programming to an LSTM model leads to a TAC-KBP score almost 6 F1 points over a state-of-the-art LSTM baseline (and into second place in the competition). Additionally, in initial user studies we observed that data programming may be an easier way for non-experts to create machine learning models when training data is limited or unavailable.

paragraphs: Data programming addresses the expense of manually labeling large training sets. Users write labeling functions: programs that assign heuristic labels to portions of the data. These programs can be inaccurate and disagree with one another, so their outputs need a way to account for noise before they become useful supervision.

The paper treats the labeling functions as implicitly specifying a generative model of labeling noise. It shows how recovering that model’s parameters can help denoise the resulting training set, with theoretical recovery guarantees established in several settings. It also modifies discriminative training losses to account for noise and demonstrates the approach with models including logistic regression and LSTMs.

On the 2014 TAC-KBP Slot Filling challenge, the authors report a result that would have won the competition. Applying data programming to an LSTM also improves its score by almost six F1 points over a state-of-the-art LSTM baseline. Initial user studies suggest that programming labeling rules may make model creation easier for non-experts when labeled data is scarce or absent.
summary.tldr: Data programming turns noisy labeling programs into training supervision by modeling their errors and adapting downstream learning to label uncertainty.

title: Data Programming: Creating Large Training Sets, Quickly

abstract: We study the estimation of the latent variable Gaussian graphical model (LVGGM), where the precision matrix is the superposition of a sparse matrix and a low-rank matrix. In order to speed up the estimation of the sparse plus low-rank components, we propose a sparsity constrained maximum likelihood estimator based on matrix factorization and an efficient alternating gradient descent algorithm with hard thresholding to solve it. Our algorithm is orders of magnitude faster than the convex relaxation based methods for LVGGM. In addition, we prove that our algorithm is guaranteed to linearly converge to the unknown sparse and low-rank components up to the optimal statistical precision. Experiments on both synthetic and genomic data demonstrate the superiority of our algorithm over the state-of-the-art algorithms and corroborate our theory.

paragraphs: The paper studies latent-variable Gaussian graphical models whose precision matrix combines sparse and low-rank components. Estimation requires recovering both components from data. The authors focus on speeding up this process, proposing an alternative to approaches based on convex relaxation while retaining theoretical guarantees about the resulting estimates.

Their method uses a sparsity-constrained maximum likelihood estimator and represents the low-rank component through matrix factorization. An alternating gradient descent algorithm updates the components, with hard thresholding enforcing sparsity. This formulation gives an efficient way to work with the two structures during optimization. The paper reports that the algorithm is orders of magnitude faster than convex-relaxation methods for this problem.

The theoretical analysis proves linear convergence toward the unknown components up to optimal statistical precision. That qualification ties the recovery claim to the precision supported by the data. Experiments on synthetic and genomic data demonstrate advantages over the compared state-of-the-art algorithms and support the theory. The contribution combines computational speed with an analysis of estimation accuracy.
summary.tldr: Factorization and thresholded alternating gradient descent accelerate sparse-plus-low-rank Gaussian model estimation with convergence guarantees.

title: Speeding Up Latent Variable Gaussian Graphical Model Estimation via Nonconvex Optimization

abstract: Several algorithms for solving constraint satisfaction problems are based on survey propagation, a variational inference scheme used to obtain approximate marginal probability estimates for variable assignments. These marginals correspond to how frequently each variable is set to true among satisfying assignments, and are used to inform branching decisions during search; however, marginal estimates obtained via survey propagation are approximate and can be self-contradictory. We introduce a more general branching strategy based on streamlining constraints, which sidestep hard assignments to variables. We show that streamlined solvers consistently outperform decimation-based solvers on random k-SAT instances for several problem sizes, shrinking the gap between empirical performance and theoretical limits of satisfiability by 16.3% on average for k = 3, 4, 5, 6.

paragraphs: Survey propagation estimates how frequently variables take particular values among satisfying assignments. Solvers use these estimates to guide search, but the approximate marginals can contradict one another. Hard decisions based on them may therefore commit the search to an unhelpful branch.

The authors propose a more general branching strategy using streamlining constraints. These constraints avoid immediately fixing individual variables, providing another way to incorporate approximate inference into a constraint-satisfaction solver. The comparison is with decimation-based methods that make hard assignments.

On random k-SAT instances across several problem sizes, streamlined solvers consistently outperform the decimation-based alternatives. For k equal to 3, 4, 5, and 6, the average reduction in the gap between empirical performance and theoretical satisfiability limits is 16.3%. This figure describes that gap, not a universal runtime reduction or an improvement on every family of constraint-satisfaction problems.
summary.tldr: Streamlining constraints improve satisfiability search without committing immediately to individual variable values.

title: Streamlining Variational Inference for Constraint Satisfaction Problems

abstract: Deep Neural Networks are powerful models that attained remarkable results on a variety of tasks. These models are shown to be extremely efficient when training and test data are drawn from the same distribution. However, it is not clear how a network will act when it is fed with an out-of-distribution example. In this work, we consider the problem of out-of-distribution detection in neural networks. We propose to use multiple semantic dense representations instead of sparse representation as the target label. Specifically, we propose to use several word representations obtained from different corpora or architectures as target labels. We evaluated the proposed model on computer vision, and speech commands detection tasks and compared it to previous methods. Results suggest that our method compares favorably with previous work. Besides, we present the efficiency of our approach for detecting wrongly classified and adversarial examples.

paragraphs: A neural network's success on familiar data does not establish how it behaves on inputs from another distribution. This paper addresses detecting those unfamiliar examples by changing the representation of the labels used as training targets. The central idea is to provide several dense semantic descriptions of each label instead of a sparse representation.

These target descriptions come from word representations learned using different corpora or architectures. Using several representations gives the model multiple semantic versions of the same target label. The proposed approach therefore makes the label space itself part of the detection method, connecting predictions to meaning-bearing vectors rather than relying on only a sparse class identifier.

The authors evaluate the method on computer-vision and speech-command detection tasks. Their results suggest favorable performance compared with previous methods, a qualified empirical claim rather than a universal advantage. They also present its effectiveness for identifying incorrectly classified examples and adversarial examples. Together, the evaluations examine whether the changed targets help recognize several kinds of problematic inputs or predictions.
summary.tldr: Multiple semantic label representations show promise for detecting out-of-distribution, misclassified, and adversarial examples.

title: Out-of-Distribution Detection using Multiple Semantic Label Representations

abstract: Suppose an n x d design matrix in a linear regression problem is given, but the response for each point is hidden unless explicitly requested. The goal is to sample only a small number k << n of the responses, and then produce a weight vector whose sum of squares loss over all points is at most 1+epsilon times the minimum. When k is very small (e.g., k=d), jointly sampling diverse subsets of points is crucial. One such method called "volume sampling" has a unique and desirable property that the weight vector it produces is an unbiased estimate of the optimum. It is therefore natural to ask if this method offers the optimal unbiased estimate in terms of the number of responses k needed to achieve a 1+epsilon loss approximation. Surprisingly we show that volume sampling can have poor behavior when we require a very accurate approximation -- indeed worse than some i.i.d. sampling techniques whose estimates are biased, such as leverage score sampling. We then develop a new rescaled variant of volume sampling that produces an unbiased estimate which avoids this bad behavior and has at least as good a tail bound as leverage score sampling: sample size k=O(d log d + d/epsilon) suffices to guarantee total loss at most 1+epsilon times the minimum with high probability. Thus, we improve on the best previously known sample size for an unbiased estimator, k=O(d^2/epsilon). Our rescaling procedure leads to a new efficient algorithm for volume sampling which is based on a "determinantal rejection sampling" technique with potentially broader applications to determinantal point processes. Other contributions include introducing the combinatorics needed for rescaled volume sampling and developing tail bounds for sums of dependent random matrices which arise in the process.

paragraphs: The paper studies linear regression when all input vectors are known but responses must be requested individually. The objective is to query few responses and still obtain nearly the smallest possible squared loss across the entire dataset. Selecting diverse groups of points is particularly valuable when the response budget is very small.

Volume sampling produces an unbiased estimate of the optimal regression weights, but the authors show that it can perform poorly when a highly accurate loss approximation is required. They introduce a rescaled version that preserves unbiasedness while avoiding this behavior. With high probability, O(d log d + d/epsilon) responses suffice for loss within a factor of 1+epsilon of the minimum.

This improves the previously known O(d²/epsilon) sample requirement for an unbiased estimator. The rescaling also leads to an efficient volume-sampling algorithm based on determinantal rejection sampling. Supporting contributions include combinatorial results and bounds for dependent random matrices, connecting the response-efficiency guarantee to a concrete sampling procedure.
summary.tldr: Rescaled volume sampling preserves unbiased regression estimates while reducing the responses sufficient for a high-probability near-optimal loss guarantee.

title: Leveraged volume sampling for linear regression

abstract: We develop two new non-ergodic alternating proximal augmented Lagrangian algorithms (NEAPAL) to solve a class of nonsmooth constrained convex optimization problems. Our approach relies on a novel combination of the augmented Lagrangian framework, alternating/linearization scheme, Nesterov's acceleration techniques, and adaptive strategy for parameters. Our algorithms have several new features compared to existing methods. Firstly, they have a Nesterov's acceleration step on the primal variables compared to the dual one in several methods in the literature. Secondly, they achieve non-ergodic optimal convergence rates under standard assumptions, i.e. an $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{k}\right)$ rate without any smoothness or strong convexity-type assumption, or an $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{k^2}\right)$ rate under only semi-strong convexity, where $k$ is the iteration counter. Thirdly, they preserve or have better per-iteration complexity compared to existing algorithms. Fourthly, they can be implemented in a parallel fashion. Finally, all the parameters are adaptively updated without heuristic tuning. We verify our algorithms on different numerical examples and compare them with some state-of-the-art methods.

title: Non-Ergodic Alternating Proximal Augmented Lagrangian Algorithms with Optimal Rates

abstract: Valid causal inference in observational studies often requires controlling for confounders. However, in practice measurements of confounders may be noisy, and can lead to biased estimates of causal effects. We show that we can reduce bias induced by measurement noise using a large number of noisy measurements of the underlying confounders. We propose the use of matrix factorization to infer the confounders from noisy covariates. This flexible and principled framework adapts to missing values, accommodates a wide variety of data types, and can enhance a wide variety of causal inference methods. We bound the error for the induced average treatment effect estimator and show it is consistent in a linear regression setting, using Exponential Family Matrix Completion preprocessing. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed procedure in numerical experiments with both synthetic data and real clinical data.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed procedure in numerical experiments with both synthetic data and real clinical data.

paragraphs: Observational causal analysis often depends on controlling for confounders, but the measurements available for those confounders can be noisy. Adjusting for imperfect measurements can leave causal-effect estimates biased. This paper studies how a large collection of noisy measurements can help recover the underlying confounders and reduce measurement-induced bias.

The proposed framework uses matrix factorization to infer confounders from observed covariates before applying causal inference methods. It accommodates missing entries and different data types, making the preprocessing useful across a variety of causal estimators. The approach draws on the information shared across many measurements rather than treating each recorded covariate as an accurate confounder measurement.

The authors bound the error of the resulting average treatment effect estimator. In a linear regression setting, they prove consistency when preprocessing uses Exponential Family Matrix Completion. Numerical experiments with synthetic and real clinical data demonstrate the procedure’s effectiveness. These results support combining measurement recovery with causal estimation, while locating the stated consistency guarantee in the specific linear setting analyzed.
summary.tldr: Matrix factorization can recover confounder information from many noisy measurements and reduce bias in causal-effect estimation.

title: Causal Inference with Noisy and Missing Covariates via Matrix Factorization

abstract: We consider the problem of learning optimal reserve price in repeated auctions against non-myopic bidders, who may bid strategically in order to gain in future rounds even if the single-round auctions are truthful. Previous algorithms, e.g., empirical pricing, do not provide non-trivial regret rounds in this setting in general. We introduce algorithms that obtain small regret against non-myopic bidders either when the market is large, i.e., no bidder appears in a constant fraction of the rounds, or when the bidders are impatient, i.e., they discount future utility by some factor mildly bounded away from one. Our approach carefully controls what information is revealed to each bidder, and builds on techniques from differentially private online learning as well as the recent line of works on jointly differentially private algorithms.

paragraphs: In repeated auctions, a bidder may sacrifice an immediate benefit to influence what happens in later rounds. This creates a challenge for learning a reserve price: even if each individual auction encourages truthful bidding, bidders who care about the future may act strategically across auctions. The paper studies reserve-price learning under that behavior.

The authors introduce algorithms with small regret under either of two conditions. One is a large market, defined so that no bidder appears in a constant fraction of the rounds. The other is bidder impatience, expressed by discounting future utility by a factor mildly bounded away from one. These are alternative conditions supporting the guarantees.

The approach carefully manages the information revealed to each bidder. It draws on differentially private online learning and jointly differentially private algorithms. This information control is the central mechanism for handling strategic participation. The result establishes that useful learning guarantees remain possible in the stated settings, where previous approaches such as empirical pricing do not generally provide nontrivial regret guarantees.
summary.tldr: Information-controlled auction algorithms achieve small regret against forward-looking bidders when markets are large or bidders are sufficiently impatient.

title: Learning Optimal Reserve Price against Non-myopic Bidders

abstract: Training convolutional neural network models is memory intensive since back-propagation requires storing activations of all intermediate layers. This presents a practical concern when seeking to deploy very deep architectures in production, especially when models need to be frequently re-trained on updated datasets. In this paper, we propose a new implementation for back-propagation that significantly reduces memory usage, by enabling the use of approximations with negligible computational cost and minimal effect on training performance. The algorithm reuses common buffers to temporarily store full activations and compute the forward pass exactly. It also stores approximate per-layer copies of activations, at significant memory savings, that are used in the backward pass. Compared to simply approximating activations within standard back-propagation, our method limits accumulation of errors across layers. This allows the use of much lower-precision approximations without affecting training accuracy. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet show that our method yields performance close to exact training, while storing activations compactly with as low as 4-bit precision.

paragraphs: Training convolutional networks consumes substantial memory because backpropagation needs intermediate activations from the forward computation. Keeping all of those values becomes a practical burden for deep models, especially when updated data requires frequent retraining. This paper changes how activations are stored and reused so that training requires less memory.

The method computes the forward pass exactly, using shared buffers to hold full activations temporarily. It also saves compact, approximate copies for each layer, which are then used during the backward pass. This separation matters because it limits the accumulation of errors across layers compared with simply approximating activations throughout standard backpropagation. The authors report negligible additional computational cost and minimal effects on training performance.

Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet obtain performance close to exact training while storing activations at precision as low as four bits. The result demonstrates that the values retained for backward computation can be substantially compressed without requiring the forward computation itself to use the same approximations.
summary.tldr: Exact forward computation paired with compressed activations for backpropagation reduces training memory while retaining performance close to exact training.

title: Backprop with Approximate Activations for Memory-efficient Network Training

abstract: Learning with auxiliary tasks can improve the ability of a primary task to generalise. However, this comes at the cost of manually labelling auxiliary data. We propose a new method which automatically learns appropriate labels for an auxiliary task, such that any supervised learning task can be improved without requiring access to any further data. The approach is to train two neural networks: a label-generation network to predict the auxiliary labels, and a multi-task network to train the primary task alongside the auxiliary task. The loss for the label-generation network incorporates the loss of the multi-task network, and so this interaction between the two networks can be seen as a form of meta learning with a double gradient. We show that our proposed method, Meta AuXiliary Learning (MAXL), outperforms single-task learning on 7 image datasets, without requiring any additional data. We also show that MAXL outperforms several other baselines for generating auxiliary labels, and is even competitive when compared with human-defined auxiliary labels. The self-supervised nature of our method leads to a promising new direction towards automated generalisation. Source code can be found at \url{https://github.com/lorenmt/maxl}.

paragraphs: An auxiliary task can help a model learn features that improve its main task, but creating auxiliary labels often requires additional human effort. Meta AuXiliary Learning, or MAXL, learns those labels automatically from the available data. Its aim is to make auxiliary supervision useful without collecting further examples or annotations.

The method trains two interacting networks. A label-generation network produces auxiliary labels, while a multitask network learns the primary task together with the generated task. The label generator's loss incorporates the multitask network's loss. This creates a meta-learning interaction involving a double gradient, so auxiliary label generation is trained in relation to the learning process it supports.

Across seven image datasets, MAXL outperforms single-task learning without additional data. It also surpasses several alternative methods for generating auxiliary labels and is competitive with human-defined auxiliary labels. These findings support automatically learned auxiliary tasks as a way to improve generalization in the evaluated settings. The broader proposal is to automate part of task design that would otherwise require manual labeling decisions.
summary.tldr: MAXL learns auxiliary labels through meta-learning and improves image-task generalization without additional training data.

title: Self-Supervised Generalisation with Meta Auxiliary Learning

abstract: Residual networks (ResNet) and weight normalization play an important role in various deep learning applications. However, parameter initialization strategies have not been studied previously for weight normalized networks and, in practice, initialization methods designed for un-normalized networks are used as a proxy. Similarly, initialization for ResNets have also been studied for un-normalized networks and often under simplified settings ignoring the shortcut connection. To address these issues, we propose a novel parameter initialization strategy that avoids explosion/vanishment of information across layers for weight normalized networks with and without residual connections. The proposed strategy is based on a theoretical analysis using mean field approximation. We run over 2,500 experiments and evaluate our proposal on image datasets showing that the proposed initialization outperforms existing initialization methods in terms of generalization performance, robustness to hyper-parameter values and variance between seeds, especially when networks get deeper in which case existing methods fail to even start training. Finally, we show that using our initialization in conjunction with learning rate warmup is able to reduce the gap between the performance of weight normalized and batch normalized networks.
