paragraphs: Hyper-Skin is a dataset for learning to reconstruct detailed facial skin spectra from RGB images. Its measurements span visible wavelengths from 400 to 700 nanometers and near-infrared wavelengths from 700 to 1000 nanometers. The intended research direction is to make richer skin analysis accessible from the images available on consumer devices.

The dataset contains 330 hyperspectral cubes collected from 51 people with a pushbroom hyperspectral camera, covering different viewing angles and facial poses. Each cube contains 1024 by 1024 spatial positions and 448 spectral channels. The authors pair these measurements with synthetic RGB images generated using real camera responses, connecting the detailed spectral observations to ordinary three-channel image inputs.

To demonstrate the dataset's usefulness, the authors apply existing reconstruction models to 31 resampled bands spanning visible and near-infrared wavelengths. The resource supports research into spectral properties associated with quantities such as melanin and hemoglobin concentrations. Its contribution is paired data and a reconstruction demonstration that enable such investigations, with data-request instructions and benchmarking code made publicly available.
summary.tldr: Hyper-Skin pairs detailed facial hyperspectral measurements with synthetic RGB images to support skin-spectrum reconstruction research.

title: Hyper-Skin: A Hyperspectral Dataset for Reconstructing Facial Skin-Spectra from RGB Images

abstract: We introduce Three Towers (3T), a flexible method to improve the contrastive learning of vision-language models by incorporating pretrained image classifiers. While contrastive models are usually trained from scratch, LiT (Zhai et al., 2022) has recently shown performance gains from using pretrained classifier embeddings. However, LiT directly replaces the image tower with the frozen embeddings, excluding any potential benefits from training the image tower contrastively. With 3T, we propose a more flexible strategy that allows the image tower to benefit from both pretrained embeddings and contrastive training. To achieve this, we introduce a third tower that contains the frozen pretrained embeddings, and we encourage alignment between this third tower and the main image-text towers. Empirically, 3T consistently improves over LiT and the CLIP-style from-scratch baseline for retrieval tasks. For classification, 3T reliably improves over the from-scratch baseline, and while it underperforms relative to LiT for JFT-pretrained models, it outperforms LiT for ImageNet-21k and Places365 pretraining.

paragraphs: Vision-language contrastive learning aligns representations of images and text. Pretrained image classifiers offer useful visual representations, but directly substituting frozen classifier embeddings for the image branch prevents that branch from learning contrastively. Three Towers, or 3T, is designed to retain both sources of benefit.

The method keeps trainable image and text towers and adds a third tower containing frozen pretrained image embeddings. Training encourages alignment between the third tower and the main image-text towers. The pretrained representations thus guide learning while the main image tower remains able to adapt through the contrastive objective.

The empirical outcome depends on the task and pretraining source. For retrieval, 3T consistently improves over both LiT and the CLIP-style baseline trained from scratch. For classification, it reliably improves over the from-scratch baseline, but its comparison with LiT is mixed: it performs worse with JFT pretraining and better with ImageNet-21k or Places365 pretraining. These results support a flexible way to incorporate pretrained visual knowledge while showing that the classification advantage is conditional.
summary.tldr: 3T adds frozen classifier representations as a third tower, improving retrieval while yielding pretraining-dependent classification gains over LiT.

title: Three Towers: Flexible Contrastive Learning with Pretrained Image Models

abstract: In this paper, we present a novel robust framework for low-level vision tasks, including denoising, object removal, frame interpolation, and super-resolution, that does not require any external training data corpus. Our proposed approach directly learns the weights of neural modules by optimizing over the corrupted test sequence, leveraging the spatio-temporal coherence and internal statistics of videos. Furthermore, we introduce a novel spatial pyramid loss that leverages the property of spatio-temporal patch recurrence in a video across the different scales of the video. This loss enhances robustness to unstructured noise in both the spatial and temporal domains. This further results in our framework being highly robust to degradation in input frames and yields state-of-the-art results on downstream tasks such as denoising, object removal, and frame interpolation. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct qualitative and quantitative evaluations on standard video datasets such as DAVIS, UCF-101, and VIMEO90K-T.

Furthermore, we introduce a novel spatial pyramid loss that leverages the property of spatio-temporal patch recurrence in a video across the different scales of the video. This loss enhances robustness to unstructured noise in both the spatial and temporal domains. This further results in our framework being highly robust to degradation in input frames and yields state-of-the-art results on downstream tasks such as denoising, object removal, and frame interpolation. paragraphs: A video contains repeated patterns and relationships between neighboring frames that can provide evidence for repairing corrupted content. This paper builds a video-enhancement framework around those internal statistics. It learns the weights of neural modules directly from the corrupted test sequence, without requiring an external collection of training videos.

The approach uses coherence across space and time, together with a spatial pyramid loss. That loss draws on the recurrence of video patches at different scales, bringing multiscale repetition into the optimization objective. The authors find that this improves robustness to unstructured noise affecting both spatial content and temporal behavior.

The framework covers denoising, object removal, frame interpolation, and super-resolution. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations use DAVIS, UCF-101, and VIMEO90K-T, with state-of-the-art results reported for denoising, object removal, and frame interpolation. These findings support learning from the particular video being processed: its repeated structure can supply a useful prior for enhancement even when the input frames themselves are degraded.
summary.tldr: Video Dynamics Prior learns directly from a corrupted video, using multiscale repetition and temporal coherence to support robust enhancement.

title: Video Dynamics Prior: An Internal Learning Approach for Robust Video Enhancements

abstract: We give the first polynomial-time algorithm for the testable learning of halfspaces in the presence of adversarial label noise under the Gaussian distribution. In the recently introduced testable learning model, one is required to produce a tester-learner such that if the data passes the tester, then one can trust the output of the robust learner on the data. Our tester-learner runs in time $\text{poly}(d/\epsilon)$ and outputs a halfspace with misclassification error $O(\text{opt})+\epsilon$, where $\text{opt}$ is the 0-1 error of the best fitting halfspace. At a technical level, our algorithm employs an iterative soft localization technique enhanced with appropriate testers to ensure that the data distribution is sufficiently similar to a Gaussian. Finally, our algorithm can be readily adapted to yield an efficient and testable active learner requiring only $d ~ \text{polylog}(1/\epsilon)$ labeled examples.

Our tester-learner runs in time $\text{poly}(d/\epsilon)$ and outputs a halfspace with misclassification error $O(\text{opt})+\epsilon$, where $\text{opt}$ is the 0-1 error of the best fitting halfspace. paragraphs: This paper studies learning a linear decision boundary when labels may be corrupted adversarially. Its focus is testable learning: the procedure includes a test of the data, and passing that test supports a guarantee for the learner's output. This connects robust learning to an explicit check of whether the data has the distributional properties needed by the analysis.

The authors provide a polynomial-time tester-learner for the Gaussian setting. Its runtime is polynomial in d/epsilon, and its classification error is O(opt) plus epsilon, where opt is the error of the best-fitting linear boundary. The benchmark therefore allows for labels that no halfspace can classify perfectly. The guarantee is tied to the testing framework rather than being an unconditional promise for arbitrary data.

Technically, the algorithm combines iterative soft localization with tests that check sufficient similarity to a Gaussian distribution. The authors also adapt it to active learning, where the method requires only d times a polylogarithmic function of 1/epsilon labeled examples. This extends the result to a setting concerned with label efficiency.
summary.tldr: A polynomial-time tester-learner provides conditional error guarantees for halfspaces with adversarial label noise and supports label-efficient active learning.

title: Efficient Testable Learning of Halfspaces with Adversarial Label Noise

abstract: The Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) is a widely employed metric in long-tailed classification scenarios. Nevertheless, most existing methods primarily assume that training and testing examples are drawn i.i.d. from the same distribution, which is often unachievable in practice. Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) enhances model performance by optimizing it for the local worst-case scenario, but directly integrating AUC optimization with DRO results in an intractable optimization problem. To tackle this challenge, methodically we propose an instance-wise surrogate loss of Distributionally Robust AUC (DRAUC) and build our optimization framework on top of it. Moreover, we highlight that conventional DRAUC may induce label bias, hence introducing distribution-aware DRAUC as a more suitable metric for robust AUC learning. Theoretically, we affirm that the generalization gap between the training loss and testing error diminishes if the training set is sufficiently large. Empirically, experiments on corrupted benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method. Code is available at: https://github.com/EldercatSAM/DRAUC.

paragraphs: AUC is widely used to assess classifiers when class frequencies are highly uneven. However, optimizing it under the assumption that training and test examples share a distribution can leave a mismatch with practical conditions. This paper studies robust AUC learning, where optimization accounts for unfavorable distributions near the training distribution.

Directly combining AUC optimization with distributionally robust optimization produces an intractable problem. The authors introduce an instance-wise surrogate loss that makes a DRAUC optimization framework possible. They also identify a potential label bias in conventional DRAUC and propose a distribution-aware version as a more suitable metric for robust AUC learning. These are separate steps toward a workable and better-targeted objective.

The theoretical analysis shows that the gap between training loss and testing error diminishes when the training set is sufficiently large. Experiments on corrupted benchmark datasets support the method's effectiveness. Together, the results connect a tractable training objective with conditional generalization support and empirical evidence under the evaluated corruptions.
summary.tldr: DRAUC makes robust AUC optimization tractable through an instance-wise surrogate and addresses potential label bias with a distribution-aware formulation.

title: DRAUC: An Instance-wise Distributionally Robust AUC Optimization Framework

abstract: The empirical loss, commonly referred to as the average loss, is extensively utilized for training machine learning models. However, in order to address the diverse performance requirements of machine learning models, the use of the rank-based loss is prevalent, replacing the empirical loss in many cases. The rank-based loss comprises a weighted sum of sorted individual losses, encompassing both convex losses like the spectral risk, which includes the empirical risk and conditional value-at-risk, and nonconvex losses such as the human-aligned risk and the sum of the ranked range loss. In this paper, we introduce a unified framework for the optimization of the rank-based loss through the utilization of a proximal alternating direction method of multipliers. We demonstrate the convergence and convergence rate of the proposed algorithm under mild conditions. Experiments conducted on synthetic and real datasets illustrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed algorithm.

The rank-based loss comprises a weighted sum of sorted individual losses, encompassing both convex losses like the spectral risk, which includes the empirical risk and conditional value-at-risk, and nonconvex losses such as the human-aligned risk and the sum of the ranked range loss. In this paper, we introduce a unified framework for the optimization of the rank-based loss through the utilization of a proximal alternating direction method of multipliers. We demonstrate the convergence and convergence rate of the proposed algorithm under mild conditions. Experiments conducted on synthetic and real datasets illustrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed algorithm.

paragraphs: Training a machine learning model usually involves minimizing the average error across examples. Rank-based objectives offer another option: sort the individual errors and assign weights according to their positions. This makes it possible to express different performance priorities through the training objective, rather than giving every error the same contribution.

The paper develops a single optimization framework for this broad family of objectives. It covers convex examples, including spectral risk and conditional value-at-risk, as well as nonconvex examples such as human-aligned risk and ranked-range losses. Its algorithm uses a proximal alternating direction method of multipliers, bringing these different objectives into a shared optimization approach.

The authors establish convergence and a convergence rate under conditions described as mild. These are conditional guarantees, rather than a claim that every possible rank-based problem is solved without restrictions. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets also support the algorithm’s effectiveness and efficiency. Together, the results provide a common computational foundation for training with several different ways of weighting ranked errors.
summary.tldr: A unified optimization framework handles multiple rank-based training objectives, with conditional convergence guarantees and supporting experiments.

title: A Unified Framework for Rank-based Loss Minimization

abstract: Attention networks such as transformers have achieved state-of-the-art performance in many domains. These networks rely heavily on the dot product attention operator, which computes the similarity between two points by taking their inner product.However, the inner product does not explicitly model the complex structural properties of real world datasets, such as hierarchies between data points.To remedy this, we introduce cone attention, a drop-in replacement for dot product attention based on hyperbolic entailment cones.Cone attention associates two points by the depth of their lowest common ancestor in a hierarchy defined by hyperbolic cones, which intuitively measures the divergence of two points and gives a $\textit{hierarchy aware}$ similarity score.We test cone attention on a wide variety of models and tasks and show that it improves task-level performance over dot product attention and other baselines, and is able to match dot-product attention with significantly fewer parameters.Our results suggest that cone attention is an effective way to capture hierarchical relationships when calculating attention.

These networks rely heavily on the dot product attention operator, which computes the similarity between two points by taking their inner product.However, the inner product does not explicitly model the complex structural properties of real world datasets, such as hierarchies between data points.To remedy this, we introduce cone attention, a drop-in replacement for dot product attention based on hyperbolic entailment cones.Cone attention associates two points by the depth of their lowest common ancestor in a hierarchy defined by hyperbolic cones, which intuitively measures the divergence of two points and gives a $\textit{hierarchy aware}$ similarity score.We test cone attention on a wide variety of models and tasks and show that it improves task-level performance over dot product attention and other baselines, and is able to match dot-product attention with significantly fewer parameters.Our results suggest that cone attention is an effective way to capture hierarchical relationships when calculating attention.

paragraphs: Attention mechanisms decide how strongly different representations should influence one another. Transformers commonly calculate these relationships using dot products. Although effective across many tasks, this operation does not explicitly represent hierarchical relationships between data points. The paper introduces cone attention to make that structure part of the similarity calculation itself.

Cone attention uses hyperbolic entailment cones to define a hierarchy. It associates two points through the depth of their lowest common ancestor: the position in that hierarchy where their paths meet. This produces a similarity score that reflects their hierarchical relationship. The authors design the operation as a drop-in replacement for dot product attention.

Across a variety of tested models and tasks, cone attention improves task performance over dot product attention and other baselines. It also matches dot product attention’s performance with substantially fewer parameters in the reported evaluations. These results suggest that explicitly representing hierarchy can improve how attention relates data points, while also offering opportunities to reduce model size. The evidence supports this approach across the tested settings.
summary.tldr: Cone attention replaces dot-product similarity with a hierarchy-aware score and improves performance or parameter efficiency in tested settings.

title: Coneheads: Hierarchy Aware Attention

abstract: Pretraining CNN models (i.e., UNet) through self-supervision has become a powerful approach to facilitate medical image segmentation under low annotation regimes. Recent contrastive learning methods encourage similar global representations when the same image undergoes different transformations, or enforce invariance across different image/patch features that are intrinsically correlated. However, CNN-extracted global and local features are limited in capturing long-range spatial dependencies that are essential in biological anatomy. To this end, we present a keypoint-augmented fusion layer that extracts representations preserving both short- and long-range self-attention. In particular, we augment the CNN feature map at multiple scales by incorporating an additional input that learns long-range spatial self-attention among localized keypoint features. Further, we introduce both global and local self-supervised pretraining for the framework. At the global scale, we obtain global representations from both the bottleneck of the UNet, and by aggregating multiscale keypoint features. These global features are subsequently regularized through image-level contrastive objectives. At the local scale, we define a distance-based criterion to first establish correspondences among keypoints and encourage similarity between their features. Through extensive experiments on both MRI and CT segmentation tasks, we demonstrate the architectural advantages of our proposed method in comparison to both CNN and Transformer-based UNets, when all architectures are trained with randomly initialized weights. With our proposed pretraining strategy, our method further outperforms existing SSL methods by producing more robust self-attention and achieving state-of-the-art segmentation results. The code is available at https://github.com/zshyang/kaf.git.

paragraphs: Medical image segmentation often has few annotated examples, making self-supervised pretraining useful. This paper targets a representational weakness of CNN-based approaches: their global and local features can struggle to capture long-range spatial relationships in anatomy. The proposed architecture supplements a UNet with keypoint features that carry information about relationships between distant locations.

A fusion layer augments CNN feature maps at multiple scales using an additional input that learns self-attention among localized keypoints. Pretraining operates at two levels. Global contrastive objectives regularize representations from the UNet bottleneck and aggregated multiscale keypoints. Locally, a distance-based rule establishes keypoint correspondences and encourages the matched features to be similar.

MRI and CT experiments separate the architectural contribution from the pretraining contribution. With random initialization across architectures, the proposed design shows advantages over CNN- and Transformer-based UNets. Adding the proposed pretraining further improves performance over existing self-supervised methods, producing more robust self-attention and reported state-of-the-art segmentation results. These findings support combining local CNN features with longer-range keypoint relationships when annotations are limited.
summary.tldr: Multiscale keypoint attention and global-local self-supervised pretraining improve medical segmentation with limited annotations.

title: Keypoint-Augmented Self-Supervised Learning for Medical Image Segmentation with Limited Annotation

abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning (Meta-RL) has attracted attention due to its capability to enhance reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms, in terms of data efficiency and generalizability. In this paper, we develop a bilevel optimization framework for meta-RL (BO-MRL) to learn the meta-prior for task-specific policy adaptation, which implements multiple-step policy optimization on one-time data collection. Beyond existing meta-RL analyses, we provide upper bounds of the expected optimality gap over the task distribution. This metric measures the distance of the policy adaptation from the learned meta-prior to the task-specific optimum, and quantifies the model's generalizability to the task distribution. We empirically validate the correctness of the derived upper bounds and demonstrate the superior effectiveness of the proposed algorithm over benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper studies how reinforcement learning can learn a starting point that adapts effectively across tasks. The proposed BO-MRL framework uses bilevel optimization: one level learns the shared meta-prior, while another adapts a policy to a particular task. Task adaptation performs multiple policy-optimization steps using data collected on a single occasion.

The theoretical contribution is an upper bound on the expected gap between the adapted policy and each task's own optimum. Averaging this gap over the task distribution evaluates how well the learned starting point supports adaptation across that distribution. This comparison ties generalization to task-specific optimal performance rather than merely measuring improvement from the initial policy.

The authors empirically validate their derived bounds and report stronger effectiveness than benchmark methods. Together, the analysis and experiments connect a concrete adaptation procedure with a measure of how close its results come to task optima. The guarantee concerns expected performance over the task distribution, rather than an unconditional claim about every individual task.
summary.tldr: BO-MRL learns a reusable policy prior and bounds the expected gap between task-adapted policies and their task-specific optima.

title: Meta-Reinforcement Learning with Universal Policy Adaptation: Provable Near-Optimality under All-task Optimum Comparator

abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel activation function tailored specifically for graph data in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Motivated by the need for graph-adaptive and flexible activation functions, we introduce DiGRAF, leveraging Continuous Piecewise-Affine Based (CPAB) transformations, which we augment with an additional GNN to learn a graph-adaptive diffeomorphic activation function in an end-to-end manner. In addition to its graph-adaptivity and flexibility, DiGRAF also possesses properties that are widely recognized as desirable for activation functions, such as differentiability, boundness within the domain, and computational efficiency. We conduct an extensive set of experiments across diverse datasets and tasks, demonstrating a consistent and superior performance of DiGRAF compared to traditional and graph-specific activation functions, highlighting its effectiveness as an activation function for GNNs. Our code is available at https://github.com/ipsitmantri/DiGRAF.

paragraphs: An activation function shapes how a neural network transforms information as it passes through the model. This paper argues for making that transformation responsive to graph data in graph neural networks. Its proposed function, DiGRAF, learns a flexible activation that adapts to the graph instead of relying on a fixed transformation.

DiGRAF builds on Continuous Piecewise-Affine Based transformations and adds another graph neural network to learn the adaptive function. The resulting transformation is diffeomorphic: its shape can change while retaining a smooth, invertible structure. The activation and the surrounding model are learned together through end-to-end training, making adaptation part of the network’s learning process.

The authors emphasize that flexibility comes with other useful properties, including differentiability, boundedness within the domain, and computational efficiency. Across experiments spanning diverse datasets and tasks, DiGRAF consistently outperforms the traditional and graph-specific activation functions used for comparison. These findings suggest that the activation itself is a productive place to incorporate graph-dependent behavior, alongside the other learned components of a GNN.
summary.tldr: DiGRAF learns smooth, graph-adaptive activation functions and reports consistent improvements over the activation functions evaluated.

title: DiGRAF: Diffeomorphic Graph-Adaptive Activation Function

abstract: Algorithms with predictions is a recent framework for decision-making under uncertainty that leverages the power of machine-learned predictions without making any assumption about their quality. The goal in this framework is for algorithms to achieve an improved performance when the predictions are accurate while maintaining acceptable guarantees when the predictions are erroneous. A serious concern with algorithms that use predictions is that these predictions can be biased and, as a result, cause the algorithm to make decisions that are deemed unfair. We show that this concern manifests itself in the classical secretary problem in the learning-augmented setting---the state-of-the-art algorithm can have zero probability of accepting the best candidate, which we deem unfair, despite promising to accept a candidate whose expected value is at least $\max\{\Omega (1) , 1 - O(\varepsilon)\}$ times the optimal value, where $\varepsilon$ is the prediction error.We show how to preserve this promise while also guaranteeing to accept the best candidate with probability $\Omega(1)$. Our algorithm and analysis are based on a new ``pegging'' idea that diverges from existing works and simplifies/unifies some of their results. Finally, we extend to the $k$-secretary problem and complement our theoretical analysis with experiments.

paragraphs: Algorithms with predictions aim to benefit from accurate forecasts while retaining useful guarantees when forecasts are wrong. This paper examines a fairness problem in a prediction-assisted secretary algorithm. Even with a strong guarantee on the expected value of the selected candidate, the existing algorithm can give the best candidate no chance of selection.

The authors treat that exclusion as unfair and design an algorithm that preserves the value guarantee while ensuring a constant positive probability of selecting the best candidate. The retained guarantee combines a constant-factor fallback with performance approaching the optimum as prediction error decreases. Thus, protection against poor predictions and access for the best candidate are established together.

The algorithm uses a new idea called pegging, which also simplifies or unifies some earlier results. The authors extend their approach to the setting where multiple candidates may be selected and supplement the theory with experiments. The key distinction is between high expected selection value and a meaningful selection chance for the best individual; the paper shows how to guarantee both in its setting.
summary.tldr: A new secretary algorithm preserves prediction-assisted value guarantees while giving the best candidate a constant positive chance of selection.

title: Fair Secretaries with Unfair Predictions

abstract: The joint prediction of continuous fields and statistical estimation of the underlying discrete parameters is a common problem for many physical systems, governed by PDEs. Hitherto, it has been separately addressed by employing operator learning surrogates for field prediction while using simulation-based inference (and its variants) for statistical parameter determination. Here, we argue that solving both problems within the same framework can lead to consistent gains in accuracy and robustness. To this end, we propose a novel and flexible formulation of the operator learning problem that jointly predicts continuous quantities and infers distributions of discrete parameters, thereby amortizing the cost of both the inverse and the surrogate models to a joint pre-training step. We present the capabilities of the proposed methodology for predicting continuous and discrete biomarkers in full-body haemodynamics simulations under different levels of missing information. We also consider a test case for atmospheric large-eddy simulation of a two-dimensional dry cold bubble, where we infer both continuous time-series and information about the system's conditions. We present comparisons against different baselines to showcase significantly increased accuracy in both the inverse and the surrogate tasks.

paragraphs: Physical systems governed by partial differential equations often pose two connected learning problems: predicting continuous fields and estimating the parameters underlying those fields. These have commonly been handled separately, using operator-learning surrogates for prediction and simulation-based inference for parameter estimation. FUSE investigates the benefits of learning both within one framework.

The proposed formulation jointly predicts continuous quantities and infers distributions over discrete parameters. A shared pretraining step absorbs the cost of learning both the simulation surrogate and the inverse model. This makes the connection between predicting a system's behavior and estimating its underlying conditions part of the learning problem itself. The authors argue that this joint treatment can improve accuracy and robustness.

The paper demonstrates the approach on full-body blood-flow simulations, predicting continuous and discrete biomarkers under different amounts of missing information. It also studies an atmospheric simulation of a two-dimensional dry cold bubble, inferring time series and system conditions. Comparisons with multiple baselines show significantly higher accuracy for both surrogate prediction and inverse estimation in these evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: FUSE jointly learns physical-field prediction and parameter-distribution inference, improving both tasks in blood-flow and atmospheric simulation studies.

title: FUSE: Fast Unified Simulation and Estimation for PDEs

abstract: Data-driven algorithm design is a paradigm that uses statistical and machine learning techniques to select from a class of algorithms for a computational problem an algorithm that has the best expected performance with respect to some (unknown) distribution on the instances of the problem. We build upon recent work in this line of research by considering the setup where, instead of selecting a single algorithm that has the best performance, we allow the possibility of selecting an algorithm based on the instance to be solved, using neural networks. In particular, given a representative sample of instances, we learn a neural network that maps an instance of the problem to the most appropriate algorithm *for that instance*. We formalize this idea and derive rigorous sample complexity bounds for this learning problem, in the spirit of recent work in data-driven algorithm design. We then apply this approach to the problem of making good decisions in the branch-and-cut framework for mixed-integer optimization (e.g., which cut to add?). In other words, the neural network will take as input a mixed-integer optimization instance and output a decision that will result in a small branch-and-cut tree for that instance. Our computational results provide evidence that our particular way of using neural networks for cut selection can make a significant impact in reducing branch-and-cut tree sizes, compared to previous data-driven approaches.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning to choose an algorithm separately for each problem instance. Conventional data-driven algorithm design can select one algorithm with good average performance over a distribution of problems. Here, a neural network uses the instance itself to select an appropriate algorithm, allowing choices to vary across the workload.

The authors formalize this learning problem and derive sample complexity bounds. These bounds address how much representative instance data are needed to learn the selection rule. The framework therefore provides a theoretical treatment of instance-dependent algorithm choice, with the training sample serving as evidence about the unknown distribution of future problems.

The application is branch-and-cut for mixed-integer optimization, where decisions such as which cut to add can affect the resulting search tree. The network maps an optimization instance to a decision intended to produce a smaller tree. Computational results provide evidence of substantial tree-size reductions compared with previous data-driven approaches. This supports the practical value of tailoring cut selection to instances within the studied setting.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds the data needed for neural algorithm selection and shows evidence of smaller branch-and-cut trees.

title: Sample Complexity of Algorithm Selection Using Neural Networks and Its Applications to Branch-and-Cut

abstract: We study the convergence rate of first-order methods for rectangular matrix factorization, which is a canonical nonconvex optimization problem. Specifically, given a rank-$r$ matrix $\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, we prove that gradient descent (GD) can find a pair of $\epsilon$-optimal solutions $\mathbf{X}_T\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}$ and $\mathbf{Y}_T\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, where $d\geq r$, satisfying $\lVert\mathbf{X}_T\mathbf{Y}_T^\top-\mathbf{A}\rVert_F\leq\epsilon\lVert\mathbf{A}\rVert_F$ in $T=O(\kappa^2\log\frac{1}{\epsilon})$ iterations with high probability, where $\kappa$ denotes the condition number of $\mathbf{A}$. Furthermore, we prove that Nesterov's accelerated gradient (NAG) attains an iteration complexity of $O(\kappa\log\frac{1}{\epsilon})$, which is the best-known bound of first-order methods for rectangular matrix factorization. Different from small balanced random initialization in the existing literature, we adopt an unbalanced initialization, where $\mathbf{X}_0$ is large and $\mathbf{Y}_0$ is $0$. Moreover, our initialization and analysis can be further extended to linear neural networks, where we prove that NAG can also attain an accelerated linear convergence rate. In particular, we only require the width of the network to be greater than or equal to the rank of the output label matrix. In contrast, previous results achieving the same rate require excessive widths that additionally depend on the condition number and the rank of the input data matrix.

paragraphs: Rectangular matrix factorization seeks two factors whose product approximates a target matrix. Although the objective is nonconvex, this paper proves convergence rates for gradient descent and Nesterov’s accelerated gradient. The factor width must be at least the rank of the target matrix, allowing the factors to represent the required structure.

The analysis uses an unbalanced initialization: one factor starts large and the other starts at zero. With high probability, gradient descent reaches relative approximation error epsilon in O(kappa² log(1/epsilon)) iterations, where kappa is the target matrix’s condition number. Nesterov’s method improves this to O(kappa log(1/epsilon)), giving the paper’s stated best-known first-order bound for rectangular matrix factorization.

The initialization and analysis also extend to linear neural networks, yielding an accelerated linear convergence rate. There, the required width only needs to match or exceed the rank of the output-label matrix. Earlier results at the same rate required additional width depending on conditioning and input rank. The contribution therefore combines provable acceleration with less demanding width requirements in the analyzed setting.
summary.tldr: An unbalanced initialization enables provable Nesterov acceleration for rectangular matrix factorization and linear neural networks with modest width requirements.

title: Provable Acceleration of Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient for Asymmetric Matrix Factorization and Linear Neural Networks

abstract: The impressive performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) across various natural language processing tasks comes at the cost of vast computational resources and storage requirements. One-shot pruning techniques offer a way to alleviate these burdens by removing redundant weights without the need for retraining. Yet, the massive scale of LLMs often forces current pruning approaches to rely on heuristics instead of optimization-based techniques, potentially resulting in suboptimal compression. In this paper, we introduce ALPS, an optimization-based framework that tackles the pruning problem using the operator splitting technique and a preconditioned conjugate gradient-based post-processing step. Our approach incorporates novel techniques to accelerate and theoretically guarantee convergence while leveraging vectorization and GPU parallelism for efficiency. ALPS substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of the pruning objective and perplexity reduction, particularly for highly sparse models. On the LLaMA3-8B model with 70\% sparsity, ALPS achieves a 29\% reduction in test perplexity on the WikiText dataset and a 8\% improvement in zero-shot benchmark performance compared to existing methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/mazumder-lab/ALPS.

paragraphs: ALPS addresses the cost of storing and running large language models by improving one-shot pruning: removing weights without retraining the model. At language-model scale, existing approaches often use heuristics because solving the pruning optimization problem is expensive. The paper develops an optimization-based approach intended to make that more systematic treatment practical.

The framework uses operator splitting to tackle the pruning problem, followed by a post-processing step based on preconditioned conjugate gradients. It combines techniques for accelerating optimization and guaranteeing convergence with vectorization and GPU parallelism. These components connect the mathematical pruning objective to an implementation designed for the scale of large models.

The authors report improvements in both the pruning objective and perplexity, especially at high sparsity. For LLaMA3-8B with 70% sparsity, ALPS reduces WikiText test perplexity by 29% and improves zero-shot benchmark performance by 8% relative to existing methods. Those results indicate that more effective pruning optimization can preserve substantially more model performance when a large fraction of weights is removed.
summary.tldr: ALPS makes optimization-based one-shot pruning practical and reports stronger language-model performance at high sparsity.

title: ALPS: Improved Optimization for Highly Sparse One-Shot Pruning for Large Language Models

abstract: We introduce graphcodes, a novel multi-scale summary of the topological properties of a dataset that is based on the well-established theory of persistent homology. Graphcodes handle datasets that are filtered along two real-valued scale parameters. Such multi-parameter topological summaries are usually based on complicated theoretical foundations and difficult to compute; in contrast, graphcodes yield an informative and interpretable summary and can be computed as efficient as one-parameter summaries. Moreover, a graphcode is simply an embedded graph and can therefore be readily integrated in machine learning pipelines using graph neural networks. We describe such a pipeline and demonstrate that graphcodes achieve better classification accuracy than state-of-the-art approaches on various datasets.

paragraphs: A dataset's topological structure describes aspects of its shape across scales. Persistent homology provides a way to summarize such structure, but using more than one scale parameter usually creates substantial theoretical and computational difficulty. This paper introduces graphcodes for data examined along two real-valued scale parameters.

A graphcode packages the resulting multiscale information as an embedded graph. The authors describe it as informative and interpretable, with computation as efficient as that of one-parameter summaries. Its graph form also creates a direct connection to graph neural networks, allowing the topological summary to become an input to a learning system.

The paper develops this integration into a classification pipeline and reports higher accuracy than state-of-the-art alternatives on several datasets. The contribution therefore spans both representation and use: it makes two-parameter topological information more practical to compute and supplies a familiar machine-learning structure for processing it. The classification results provide empirical support that this representation preserves information useful for distinguishing examples in the evaluated datasets.
summary.tldr: Graphcodes turn two-parameter topological summaries into efficiently computed graphs that improve classification in the reported evaluations.

title: Graphcode: Learning from multiparameter persistent homology using graph neural networks

abstract: Unsupervised skill discovery is a learning paradigm that aims to acquire diverse behaviors without explicit rewards. However, it faces challenges in learning complex behaviors and often leads to learning unsafe or undesirable behaviors. For instance, in various continuous control tasks, current unsupervised skill discovery methods succeed in learning basic locomotions like standing but struggle with learning more complex movements such as walking and running. Moreover, they may acquire unsafe behaviors like tripping and rolling or navigate to undesirable locations such as pitfalls or hazardous areas. In response, we present **DoDont** (Do’s and Dont’s), an instruction-based skill discovery algorithm composed of two stages. First, in instruction learning stage, DoDont leverages action-free instruction videos to train an instruction network to distinguish desirable transitions from undesirable ones. Then, in the skill learning stage, the instruction network adjusts the reward function of the skill discovery algorithm to weight the desired behaviors. Specifically, we integrate the instruction network into a distance-maximizing skill discovery algorithm, where the instruction network serves as the distance function. Empirically, with less than 8 instruction videos, DoDont effectively learns desirable behaviors and avoids undesirable ones across complex continuous control tasks. Code and videos are available at https://mynsng.github.io/dodont/

paragraphs: Unsupervised skill discovery aims to learn varied behaviors without explicit rewards, but diversity alone does not ensure useful behavior. An agent might learn basic movements while failing to walk or run, or acquire unwanted behaviors such as tripping or entering hazardous areas. DoDont introduces video instructions to guide which skills the agent discovers.

The method has two stages. First, it trains an instruction network from videos that do not include action information. This network learns to distinguish desirable transitions from undesirable ones. Second, the network modifies the reward used during skill discovery, giving the learning process a way to favor behavior consistent with the instructions.

The authors integrate this mechanism into a skill discovery algorithm that maximizes distance, using the instruction network itself as the distance function. In experiments across complex continuous control tasks, fewer than eight instruction videos were sufficient to learn desirable behaviors and avoid undesirable ones. These findings show how a small amount of behavioral guidance can shape otherwise unsupervised skill learning in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: DoDont uses a small set of instruction videos to steer skill discovery toward desirable behaviors and away from unwanted ones.

title: Do's and Don'ts: Learning Desirable Skills with Instruction Videos

abstract: Detecting 3D keypoints with semantic consistency is widely used in many scenarios such as pose estimation, shape registration and robotics. Currently, most unsupervised 3D keypoint detection methods focus on the rigid-body objects. However, when faced with deformable objects, the keypoints they identify do not preserve semantic consistency well. In this paper, we introduce an innovative unsupervised keypoint detector Key-Grid for both the rigid-body and deformable objects, which is an autoencoder framework. paragraphs: Useful three-dimensional keypoints should identify corresponding meaningful parts across objects, even when shapes deform. abstract: The advancement of function-calling agent models requires diverse, reliable, and high-quality datasets. This paper presents APIGen, an automated data generation pipeline designed to synthesize high-quality datasets for function-calling applications. We leverage APIGen and collect 3,673 executable APIs across 21 different categories to generate diverse function-calling datasets in a scalable and structured manner. Each data in our dataset is verified through three hierarchical stages: format checking, actual function executions, and semantic verification, improving its reliability and correctness. We demonstrate that models trained with our curated datasets, even with only 7B parameters, can achieve state-of-the-art performance on the Berkeley Function-Calling Benchmark, outperforming multiple GPT-4 models. Moreover, our 1B model achieves exceptional performance, surpassing GPT-3.5-Turbo and Claude-3 Haiku. We release a dataset containing 60,000 high-quality entries, aiming to advance the field of function-calling agent domains. The dataset and models are available on the project homepage \url{https://apigen-pipeline.github.io/}.

paragraphs: Models that call software functions need examples that are both varied and correct. A plausible-looking function call is insufficient if its format is wrong, it fails when executed, or it does not match the intended request. APIGen addresses this training-data problem with an automated generation and verification pipeline.

The pipeline draws on 3,673 executable APIs spanning 21 categories. Each generated example passes through three levels of checking: its format is inspected, its functions are actually executed, and its meaning is verified. These checks address different aspects of correctness, making reliability part of dataset construction rather than relying solely on the appearance of the generated text.

The authors release 60,000 entries and report strong results from models trained on the resulting data. A model with 7 billion parameters achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Berkeley Function-Calling Benchmark, exceeding multiple GPT-4 models; a 1-billion-parameter model surpasses GPT-3.5-Turbo and Claude-3 Haiku. These benchmark results highlight the value of diverse, execution-checked training examples for function-calling capability.
summary.tldr: APIGen generates and verifies diverse function-calling data that supports strong benchmark performance even in small models.

title: APIGen: Automated PIpeline for Generating Verifiable and Diverse Function-Calling Datasets

abstract: Within distributed learning, workers typically compute gradients on their assigned dataset chunks and send them to the parameter server (PS), which aggregates them to compute either an exact or approximate version of $\nabla L$ (gradient of the loss function $L$). However, in large-scale clusters, many workers are slower than their promised speed or even failure-prone. A gradient coding solution introduces redundancy within the assignment of chunks to the workers and uses coding theoretic ideas to allow the PS to recover $\nabla L$ (exactly or approximately), even in the presence of stragglers. Unfortunately, most existing gradient coding protocols are inefficient from a computation perspective as they coarsely classify workers as operational or failed; the potentially valuable work performed by slow workers (partial stragglers) is ignored. In this work, we present novel gradient coding protocols that judiciously leverage the work performed by partial stragglers. Our protocols are efficient from a computation and communication perspective and numerically stable. For an important class of chunk assignments, we present efficient algorithms for optimizing the relative ordering of chunks within the workers; this ordering affects the overall execution time. For exact gradient reconstruction, our protocol is around $2\times$ faster than the original class of protocols and for approximate gradient reconstruction, the mean-squared-error of our reconstructed gradient is several orders of magnitude better.

paragraphs: Distributed training divides gradient computation among workers and combines their results at a parameter server. Some workers run slowly or fail, so gradient coding assigns redundant work that allows the server to reconstruct the gradient despite missing contributions. Many existing protocols treat workers as either finished or failed, discarding useful partial work from slower workers.

This paper introduces coding protocols that incorporate those partial contributions. The authors describe the protocols as computationally efficient, communication efficient, and numerically stable. They also study the order in which each worker processes its assigned data chunks. For an important class of assignments, they provide efficient algorithms for optimizing that order because it affects total execution time.

For exact gradient reconstruction, the proposed protocol is reported to run around twice as fast as the original class of protocols. For approximate reconstruction, the reconstructed gradient has mean-squared error several orders of magnitude lower. The findings show how retaining partial progress can improve either recovery speed or approximation quality, depending on the reconstruction objective.
summary.tldr: New gradient coding protocols use slow workers' partial results to accelerate exact recovery and improve approximate gradient accuracy.

title: Leveraging partial stragglers within gradient coding

abstract: Low-bit quantization has become widespread for compressing image super-resolution (SR) models for edge deployment, which allows advanced SR models to enjoy compact low-bit parameters and efficient integer/bitwise constructions for storage compression and inference acceleration, respectively. However, it is notorious that low-bit quantization degrades the accuracy of SR models compared to their full-precision (FP) counterparts. Despite several efforts to alleviate the degradation, the transformer-based SR model still suffers severe degradation due to its distinctive activation distribution. In this work, we present a dual-stage low-bit post-training quantization (PTQ) method for image super-resolution, namely 2DQuant, which achieves efficient and accurate SR under low-bit quantization. The proposed method first investigates the weight and activation and finds that the distribution is characterized by coexisting symmetry and asymmetry, long tails. Specifically, we propose Distribution-Oriented Bound Initialization (DOBI), using different searching strategies to search a coarse bound for quantizers. To obtain refined quantizer parameters, we further propose Distillation Quantization Calibration (DQC), which employs a distillation approach to make the quantized model learn from its FP counterpart. Through extensive experiments on different bits and scaling factors, the performance of DOBI can reach the state-of-the-art (SOTA) while after stage two, our method surpasses existing PTQ in both metrics and visual effects. 2DQuant gains an increase in PSNR as high as 4.52dB on Set5 (x2) compared with SOTA when quantized to 2-bit and enjoys a 3.60x compression ratio and 5.08x speedup ratio. The code and models are available at https://github.com/Kai-Liu001/2DQuant.

paragraphs: Image super-resolution models reconstruct higher-resolution images, but compressing their numerical representations can reduce reconstruction quality. Transformer-based models are particularly affected because their internal activations have distributions that are difficult to represent with few bits. This paper introduces 2DQuant, a two-stage method for quantizing an already trained model while retaining more of its accuracy.

The first stage examines weights and activations, whose distributions combine symmetric and asymmetric patterns with long tails. Distribution-Oriented Bound Initialization uses different search strategies to select initial quantization bounds. The second stage, Distillation Quantization Calibration, refines the quantizer parameters by having the compressed model learn from its full-precision counterpart. Together, these stages address both initial numerical range selection and subsequent calibration.

Experiments across bit widths and scaling factors report competitive results from initialization alone and improvements over existing post-training quantization after calibration. At two bits, the reported PSNR gain reaches 4.52 dB on Set5 at twofold enlargement. The abstract also reports 3.60-fold compression and 5.08-fold acceleration, connecting reconstruction improvements with deployment efficiency.
summary.tldr: 2DQuant combines distribution-aware initialization and teacher-guided calibration to improve low-bit image super-resolution.

title: 2DQuant: Low-bit Post-Training Quantization for Image Super-Resolution

abstract: Spatial representation learning (SRL) aims at learning general-purpose neural network representations from various types of spatial data (e.g., points, polylines, polygons, networks, images, etc.) in their native formats. Learning good spatial representations is a fundamental problem for various downstream applications such as species distribution modeling, weather forecasting, trajectory generation, geographic question answering, etc. Even though SRL has become the foundation of almost all geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI) research, we have not yet seen significant efforts to develop an extensive deep learning framework and benchmark to support SRL model development and evaluation. To fill this gap, we propose TorchSpatial, a learning framework and benchmark for location (point) encoding,which is one of the most fundamental data types of spatial representation learning. TorchSpatial contains three key components: 1) a unified location encoding framework that consolidates 15 commonly recognized location encoders, ensuring scalability and reproducibility of the implementations; 2) the LocBench benchmark tasks encompassing 7 geo-aware image classification and 10 geo-aware imageregression datasets; 3) a comprehensive suite of evaluation metrics to quantify geo-aware models’ overall performance as well as their geographic bias, with a novel Geo-Bias Score metric. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis and insights into the model performance and geographic bias of different location encoders. We believe TorchSpatial will foster future advancement of spatial representationlearning and spatial fairness in GeoAI research. The TorchSpatial model framework and LocBench benchmark are available at https://github.com/seai-lab/TorchSpatial, and the Geo-Bias Score evaluation framework is available at https://github.com/seai-lab/PyGBS.

paragraphs: Spatial representation learning turns geographic data into representations that neural networks can use. Although the broader field includes many spatial formats, TorchSpatial focuses on encoding point locations. The paper addresses the need for a common framework and benchmark that can support the development and comparison of these location representations.

TorchSpatial brings fifteen established location encoders into a unified implementation framework intended to support scalability and reproducibility. Its LocBench benchmark includes seven geographically informed image-classification datasets and ten geographically informed image-regression datasets. These tasks provide a shared setting for examining how location encodings contribute to predictive performance.

The evaluation suite considers both overall model performance and geographic bias, including a new Geo-Bias Score. The authors use it to analyze differences among location encoders along both dimensions. This matters because an aggregate performance measure alone does not describe geographic bias. The contribution supplies tools and comparative evidence for studying location representations and spatial fairness together.
summary.tldr: TorchSpatial unifies location encoders and benchmarks their predictive performance and geographic bias across geographically informed image tasks.

title: TorchSpatial: A Location Encoding Framework and Benchmark for Spatial Representation Learning

abstract: Neural networks are most often trained under the assumption that data come from a stationary distribution. However, settings in which this assumption is violated are of increasing importance; examples include supervised learning with distributional shifts, reinforcement learning, continual learning and non-stationary contextual bandits. Here, we introduce a novel learning approach that automatically models and adapts to non-stationarity by linking parameters through an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with an adaptive drift parameter. The adaptive drift draws the parameters towards the distribution used at initialisation, so the approach can be understood as a form of soft parameter reset. We show empirically that our approach performs well in non-stationary supervised, and off-policy reinforcement learning settings.

However, settings in which this assumption is violated are of increasing importance; examples include supervised learning with distributional shifts, reinforcement learning, continual learning and non-stationary contextual bandits. Here, we introduce a novel learning approach that automatically models and adapts to non-stationarity by linking parameters through an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with an adaptive drift parameter. The adaptive drift draws the parameters towards the distribution used at initialisation, so the approach can be understood as a form of soft parameter reset. paragraphs: Neural-network training often assumes that the distribution producing the data stays fixed. That assumption breaks down when supervised data shifts or when a reinforcement-learning system encounters changing learning conditions. This paper introduces a learning approach that explicitly models non-stationarity and adapts the network’s parameters as those conditions evolve.

The method links parameters through an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process with an adaptive drift parameter. The drift draws parameters toward the distribution used to initialize the network. This gives the method an interpretation as a soft reset: parameters are pulled toward their initialization distribution rather than being replaced in a single reset operation. The adaptive drift makes this restoring behavior part of the learning procedure.

The authors empirically evaluate the approach in non-stationary supervised learning and off-policy reinforcement learning, reporting good performance in both settings. The contribution is a mechanism for adapting to change directly through parameter dynamics. Although the motivation includes continual learning and non-stationary contextual bandits, the stated empirical findings concern supervised and off-policy reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: An adaptive stochastic parameter process softly pulls weights toward their initialization distribution to support learning under changing conditions.

title: Non-Stationary Learning of Neural Networks with Automatic Soft Parameter Reset

abstract: Optimizing complex and high-dimensional black-box functions is ubiquitous in science and engineering fields. Unfortunately, the online evaluation of these functions is restricted due to time and safety constraints in most cases. In offline model-based optimization (MBO), we aim to find a design that maximizes the target function using only a pre-existing offline dataset. While prior methods consider forward or inverse approaches to address the problem, these approaches are limited by conservatism and the difficulty of learning highly multi-modal mappings. Recently, there has been an emerging paradigm of learning to improve solutions with synthetic trajectories constructed from the offline dataset. In this paper, we introduce a novel conditional generative modeling approach to produce trajectories toward high-scoring regions. First, we construct synthetic trajectories toward high-scoring regions using the dataset while injecting locality bias for consistent improvement directions. Then, we train a conditional diffusion model to generate trajectories conditioned on their scores. Lastly, we sample multiple trajectories from the trained model with guidance to explore high-scoring regions beyond the dataset and select high-fidelity designs among generated trajectories with the proxy function. Extensive experiment results demonstrate that our method outperforms competitive baselines on Design-Bench and its practical variants. The code is publicly available in \url{https://github.com/dbsxodud-11/GTG}.

paragraphs: In offline model-based optimization, the goal is to find a high-scoring design using an existing dataset, without repeatedly evaluating the true objective. This matters when evaluations are constrained by time or safety. The paper develops a method that learns sequences of improving designs, building on the idea that an optimization trajectory can be a useful object to generate.

First, the authors construct synthetic trajectories from the available data. They introduce a preference for local relationships so that the trajectories have consistent improvement directions. A conditional diffusion model then learns to generate these sequences based on their scores. During generation, guidance steers multiple sampled trajectories toward high-scoring regions beyond those represented in the dataset.

A proxy function evaluates generated candidates and helps select promising designs from the trajectories. Thus, the method connects trajectory construction, score-conditioned generation, and candidate selection in one workflow. Experiments report better results than competitive baselines on Design-Bench and practical variants. The stated finding supports generating guided improvement paths as an effective approach to offline optimization, where access to new evaluations of the real function is restricted.
summary.tldr: The method trains a guided diffusion model on synthetic improvement trajectories to propose high-scoring designs from offline data.

title: Guided Trajectory Generation with Diffusion Models for Offline Model-based Optimization

abstract: The majority of language model training builds on imitation learning. It covers pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and affects the starting conditions for reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). The simplicity and scalability of maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) for next token prediction led to its role as predominant paradigm. However, the broader field of imitation learning can more effectively utilize the sequential structure underlying autoregressive generation. We focus on investigating the inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) perspective to imitation, extracting rewards and directly optimizing sequences instead of individual token likelihoods and evaluate its benefits for fine-tuning large language models. We provide a new angle, reformulating inverse soft-Q-learning as a temporal difference regularized extension of MLE. This creates a principled connection between MLE and IRL and allows trading off added complexity with increased performance and diversity of generations in the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) setting. We find clear advantages for IRL-based imitation, in particular for retaining diversity while maximizing task performance, rendering IRL a strong alternative on fixed SFT datasets even without online data generation. Our analysis of IRL-extracted reward functions further indicates benefits for more robust reward functions via tighter integration of supervised and preference-based LLM post-training.

This paper explores a broader imitation-learning approach: inverse reinforcement learning, which extracts rewards and optimizes sequences. The aim is to use the sequential structure of language generation more directly during supervised fine-tuning.

The authors reformulate inverse soft-Q-learning as maximum likelihood estimation extended with temporal-difference regularization. This establishes a principled connection between the familiar token-prediction objective and inverse reinforcement learning. It also provides a way to balance added training complexity against improvements in task performance and generation diversity.

These benefits appear with fixed supervised fine-tuning datasets, without requiring online data generation. Analysis of the extracted reward functions also indicates potential benefits for reward robustness when supervised and preference-based post-training are more tightly integrated. The contribution combines an alternative training perspective with a formulation connected to standard language model learning.
summary.tldr: A scalable inverse reinforcement learning formulation improves the performance–diversity balance of language model imitation on fixed fine-tuning datasets.

title: Imitating Language via Scalable Inverse Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Monte-Carlo tree search (MCTS) and reinforcement learning contributed crucially to the success of AlphaGo and AlphaZero, and A$^*$ is a tree search algorithm among the most well-known ones in the classical AI literature. MCTS and A$^*$ both perform heuristic search and are mutually beneficial. Efforts have been made to the renaissance of A$^*$ from three possible aspects, two of which have been confirmed by studies in recent years, while the third is about the OPEN list that consists of open nodes of A$^*$ search, but still lacks deep investigation. This paper aims at the third, i.e., developing the Sampling-exploration enhanced A$^*$ (SeeA$^*$) search by constructing a dynamic subset of OPEN through a selective sampling process, such that the node with the best heuristic value in this subset instead of in the OPEN is expanded. Nodes with the best heuristic values in OPEN are most probably picked into this subset, but sometimes may not be included, which enables SeeA$^*$ to explore other promising branches. Three sampling techniques are presented for comparative investigations. Moreover, under the assumption about the distribution of prediction errors, we have theoretically shown the superior efficiency of SeeA$^*$ over A$^*$ search, particularly when the accuracy of the guiding heuristic function is insufficient. Experimental results on retrosynthetic planning in organic chemistry, logic synthesis in integrated circuit design, and the classical Sokoban game empirically demonstrate the efficiency of SeeA$^*$, in comparison with the state-of-the-art heuristic search algorithms.

paragraphs: A* search maintains an OPEN list of candidate nodes and uses heuristic values to decide which one to expand. SeeA* changes this selection process to encourage exploration. The motivation is that a heuristic can misjudge promising branches, especially when its predictions are insufficiently accurate, making strict reliance on its top-ranked choice inefficient.

At each selection, SeeA* constructs a dynamic subset of OPEN through selective sampling and expands the best-ranked node within that subset. Nodes with the strongest heuristic values are likely to be included, but they can occasionally be omitted. This creates opportunities to explore other branches while still making substantial use of the heuristic's guidance.

The paper compares three sampling techniques. Under an assumption about the distribution of prediction errors, it proves an efficiency advantage over A*, particularly with less accurate heuristics. Experiments on chemical retrosynthesis, integrated-circuit logic synthesis, and Sokoban also demonstrate efficiency against leading heuristic-search methods. The theoretical advantage is tied to the stated error-distribution assumption, while the experiments provide evidence across distinct search applications.
summary.tldr: SeeA* samples candidate nodes before selecting an expansion, improving exploration when heuristic guidance is imperfect.

title: SeeA*: Efficient Exploration-Enhanced A* Search by Selective Sampling

abstract: A Random Utility Model (RUM) is a classical model of user behavior defined by a distribution over $\mathbb{R}^n$. A user, presented with a subset of $\\{1,\ldots,n\\}$, will select the item of the subset with the highest utility, according to a utility vector drawn from the specified distribution. In practical settings, the subset is often of small size, as in the ``ten blue links'' of web search. In this paper, we consider a learning setting with complete information on user choices from subsets of size at most $k$. We show that $k=\Theta(\sqrt{n})$ is both necessary and sufficient to predict the distribution of all user choices with an arbitrarily small, constant error.Based on the upper bound, we obtain new algorithms for approximate RUM learning and variations thereof. Furthermore, we employ our lower bound for approximate RUM learning to derive lower bounds to fractional extensions of the well-studied $k$-deck and trace reconstruction problems.
originalAbstract: A Random Utility Model (RUM) is a classical model of user behavior defined by a distribution over $\mathbb{R}^n$. A user, presented with a subset of $\\{1,\ldots,n\\}$, will select the item of the subset with the highest utility, according to a utility vector drawn from the specified distribution. In practical settings, the subset is often of small size, as in the ``ten blue links'' of web search. In this paper, we consider a learning setting with complete information on user choices from subsets of size at most $k$. We show that $k=\Theta(\sqrt{n})$ is both necessary and sufficient to predict the distribution of all user choices with an arbitrarily small, constant error.Based on the upper bound, we obtain new algorithms for approximate RUM learning and variations thereof. Furthermore, we employ our lower bound for approximate RUM learning to derive lower bounds to fractional extensions of the well-studied $k$-deck and trace reconstruction problems.

paragraphs: A Random Utility Model represents choice by drawing a vector of item utilities and selecting the highest-utility item among those offered. In practice, users often see only small subsets of all available items. This paper asks how much information about choices from small subsets is needed to predict choices over the full range of possible subsets.

The analysis assumes complete information about choice behavior for every subset containing at most k items. Under that setting, the authors show that k must scale on the order of the square root of the total number of items, and that this scale also suffices, to predict all choice distributions with arbitrarily small constant error. The result provides matching necessity and sufficiency bounds.

The upper bound leads to new algorithms for approximate learning of Random Utility Models and related variants. The lower bound also yields limits for fractional versions of k-deck and trace reconstruction problems. The central finding identifies the subset-size threshold under complete choice information, clarifying what small-slate observations can reveal about broader choice behavior.
summary.tldr: With complete choice information, subsets of size proportional to √n are necessary and sufficient for approximate prediction of all Random Utility Model choices.

title: Tight Bounds for Learning RUMs from Small Slates

abstract: Classical optimization and learning-based methods are the two reigning paradigms in deformable image registration. While optimization-based methods boast generalizability across modalities and robust performance, learning-based methods promise peak performance, incorporating weak supervision and amortized optimization. However, the exact conditions for either paradigm to perform well over the other are shrouded and not explicitly outlined in the existing literature. In this paper, we make an explicit correspondence between the mutual information of the distribution of per-pixel intensity and labels, and the performance of classical registration methods. This strong correlation hints to the fact that architectural designs in learning-based methods is unlikely to affect this correlation, and therefore, the performance of learning-based methods. This hypothesis is thoroughly validated with state-of-the-art classical and learning-based methods. However, learning-based methods with weak supervision can perform high-fidelity intensity and label registration, which is not possible with classical methods. Next, we show that this high-fidelity feature learning does not translate to invariance to domain shift, and learning-based methods are sensitive to such changes in the data distribution. We reassess and recalibrate performance expectations from classical and DLIR methods under access to label supervision, training time, and its generalization capabilities under minor domain shifts.

paragraphs: Deformable image registration aligns medical images despite differences in shape. Classical methods optimize the alignment directly, while learning-based methods learn how to perform it. This paper investigates which properties of the data, available supervision, and distribution changes help explain when either approach performs well.

The authors find a strong correspondence between classical registration performance and the mutual information between pixel intensities and labels. This suggests that changing a learned model's architecture is unlikely to remove the underlying relationship or its effect on performance. They examine that hypothesis using state-of-the-art classical and learning-based methods, grounding the comparison in the information available in the images.

Weak supervision gives learning-based methods an additional capability: high-fidelity alignment of both intensities and labels that classical methods cannot achieve in the studied comparison. However, the learned features do not make these methods invariant to domain shift; performance remains sensitive to changes in the data distribution. The paper therefore reassesses expectations around label supervision, training time, and generalization under even minor distribution shifts.
summary.tldr: The paper connects registration performance to intensity-label information and finds that weak supervision helps learned methods without ensuring robustness to domain shifts.

title: Deep Learning in Medical Image Registration: Magic or Mirage?

abstract: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) aims to learn a reward function and a corresponding policy that best fit the demonstrated trajectories of an expert. However, current IRL works cannot learn incrementally from an ongoing trajectory because they have to wait to collect at least one complete trajectory to learn. To bridge the gap, this paper considers the problem of learning a reward function and a corresponding policy while observing the initial state-action pair of an ongoing trajectory and keeping updating the learned reward and policy when new state-action pairs of the ongoing trajectory are observed. We formulate this problem as an online bi-level optimization problem where the upper level dynamically adjusts the learned reward according to the newly observed state-action pairs with the help of a meta-regularization term, and the lower level learns the corresponding policy. We propose a novel algorithm to solve this problem and guarantee that the algorithm achieves sub-linear local regret $O(\sqrt{T}+\log T+\sqrt{T}\log T)$. If the reward function is linear, we prove that the proposed algorithm achieves sub-linear regret $O(\log T)$. Experiments are used to validate the proposed algorithm.
