paragraphs: Word embeddings often learn relationships from which words occur together, while giving limited attention to ordering and word structure. This paper proposes a neural language model that includes both word order and character order in its representations. The approach brings information about sequences of words and the internal arrangement of characters into the embedding model.

The model produces several vector spaces with meaningful internal structure. The authors support this claim through word-analogy performance, reporting 85.8% on a recent task and a 58% error-margin improvement over the best published syntactic analogy scores. These findings provide task-specific evidence that the representations capture useful relationships, particularly those evaluated through syntactic analogies.

The paper also introduces parallel training methods to support very large models. Its most prominent scaling result is training a skip-gram network with 160 billion parameters overnight on three multicore CPUs, described as 14 times larger than the previous largest neural network. The work therefore combines an order-aware representation approach with methods for making large-scale training computationally feasible.
summary.tldr: Order-aware word and character representations achieve strong analogy results, alongside parallel methods for training extremely large embedding networks.

title: Modeling Order in Neural Word Embeddings at Scale

abstract: We consider the maximum likelihood parameter estimation problem for a generalized Thurstone choice model, where choices are from comparison sets of two or more items. We provide tight characterizations of the mean square error, as well as necessary and sufficient conditions for correct classification when each item belongs to one of two classes. These results provide insights into how the estimation accuracy depends on the choice of a generalized Thurstone choice model and the structure of comparison sets. We find that for a priori unbiased structures of comparisons, e.g., when comparison sets are drawn independently and uniformly at random, the number of observations needed to achieve a prescribed estimation accuracy depends on the choice of a generalized Thurstone choice model. For a broad set of generalized Thurstone choice models, which includes all popular instances used in practice, the estimation error is shown to be largely insensitive to the cardinality of comparison sets. On the other hand, we found that there exist generalized Thurstone choice models for which the estimation error decreases much faster with the cardinality of comparison sets.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes maximum-likelihood estimation for generalized Thurstone models, where an observation records a choice from a set of at least two items. The authors give tight descriptions of mean squared estimation error. They also establish necessary and sufficient conditions for correct classification when items belong to one of two classes.

The analysis examines how accuracy depends jointly on the choice model and the arrangement of comparison sets. For structures that are unbiased in advance, including independently and uniformly sampled sets, the observations needed for a target accuracy depend on the particular generalized Thurstone model. This makes model selection relevant to the statistical value of collected choices.

For a broad family containing the popular models used in practice, estimation error is largely insensitive to the number of items in each comparison set. However, other models exist for which error falls much faster as sets grow. The finding qualifies the intuition that larger comparison sets necessarily provide substantially better estimates: their benefit depends on the underlying choice model.
summary.tldr: Estimation guarantees show that the benefit of larger comparison sets depends strongly on the generalized Thurstone choice model.

title: Parameter Estimation for Generalized Thurstone Choice Models

abstract: Rejection sampling is a technique for sampling from difficult distributions. However, its use is limited due to a high rejection rate. Common adaptive rejection sampling methods either work only for very specific distributions or without performance guarantees. In this paper, we present pliable rejection sampling (PRS), a new approach to rejection sampling, where we learn the sampling proposal using a kernel estimator. Since our method builds on rejection sampling, the samples obtained are with high probability i.i.d. and distributed according to f. Moreover, PRS comes with a guarantee on the number of accepted samples.
originalAbstract: Rejection sampling is a technique for sampling from difficult distributions. However, its use is limited due to a high rejection rate. Common adaptive rejection sampling methods either work only for very specific distributions or without performance guarantees. In this paper, we present pliable rejection sampling (PRS), a new approach to rejection sampling, where we learn the sampling proposal using a kernel estimator. Since our method builds on rejection sampling, the samples obtained are with high probability i.i.d. and distributed according to f. Moreover, PRS comes with a guarantee on the number of accepted samples.

paragraphs: Rejection sampling generates samples from a difficult target distribution by proposing candidates and accepting only some of them. Its usefulness can be limited when too many proposals are rejected. The paper introduces pliable rejection sampling, or PRS, to improve the proposal through learning while retaining guarantees about the resulting sampling process.

PRS learns its sampling proposal using a kernel estimator. Adapting the proposal addresses the central efficiency issue: a proposal poorly suited to the target can waste many candidate draws. The authors position their approach against adaptive rejection methods that either apply only to very specific distributions or lack performance guarantees.

The stated results cover both sample validity and acceptance performance. With high probability, the obtained samples are independent, identically distributed, and drawn from the target distribution. PRS also provides a guarantee on the number of accepted samples. This combination matters because improving acceptance is useful only alongside control over what distribution the accepted samples represent; the validity claim retains its high-probability qualification.
summary.tldr: PRS learns a rejection-sampling proposal with a kernel estimator, providing high-probability sample validity and a guarantee on accepted sample counts.

title: Pliable Rejection Sampling

abstract: Real data tensors are usually high dimensional but their intrinsic information is preserved in low-dimensional space, which motivates to use tensor decompositions such as Tucker decomposition. Often, real data tensors are not only low dimensional, but also smooth, meaning that the adjacent elements are similar or continuously changing, which typically appear as spatial or temporal data. To incorporate the smoothness property, we propose the smoothed Tucker decomposition (STD). STD leverages the smoothness by the sum of a few basis functions, which reduces the number of parameters. The objective function is formulated as a convex problem and, to solve that, an algorithm based on the alternating direction method of multipliers is derived. We theoretically show that, under the smoothness assumption, STD achieves a better error bound. The theoretical result and performances of STD are numerically verified.

paragraphs: Tensor decomposition represents a high-dimensional array using lower-dimensional structure. The paper observes that spatial and temporal data can have another useful property: adjacent entries often vary smoothly. Its smoothed Tucker decomposition, or STD, incorporates this smoothness alongside the low-dimensional structure that motivates Tucker decomposition.

STD expresses smooth structure using a sum of a few basis functions, reducing the number of parameters needed for the representation. The authors formulate the objective as a convex problem and derive an optimization algorithm based on the alternating direction method of multipliers. The modeling choice and solver are therefore developed together.

The theoretical result is a better error bound under the smoothness assumption. That condition is central: the improvement is justified for data satisfying the assumed smooth structure. Numerical results verify the theoretical finding and the performance of STD. The contribution shows how neighboring-entry relationships can supply additional information beyond low dimensionality, and how that information can be incorporated into a tensor model with a corresponding estimation guarantee.
summary.tldr: Smoothed Tucker decomposition uses basis functions to reduce parameters and achieves a better error bound under a smoothness assumption.

title: Tensor Decomposition with Smoothness

abstract: We develop a framework for augmenting online algorithms with a machine learned oracle to achieve competitive ratios that provably improve upon unconditional worst case lower bounds when the oracle has low error. Our approach treats the oracle as a complete black box, and is not dependent on its inner workings, or the exact distribution of its errors. We apply this framework to the traditional caching problem {—} creating an eviction strategy for a cache of size k. We demonstrate that naively following the oracle’s recommendations may lead to very poor performance, even when the average error is quite low. Instead we show how to modify the Marker algorithm to take into account the oracle’s predictions, and prove that this combined approach achieves a competitive ratio that both (i) decreases as the oracle’s error decreases, and (ii) is always capped by O(log k), which can be achieved without any oracle input. We complement our results with an empirical evaluation of our algorithm on real world datasets, and show that it performs well empirically even using simple off the shelf predictions.

We apply this framework to the traditional caching problem {—} creating an eviction strategy for a cache of size k. We demonstrate that naively following the oracle’s recommendations may lead to very poor performance, even when the average error is quite low. Instead we show how to modify the Marker algorithm to take into account the oracle’s predictions, and prove that this combined approach achieves a competitive ratio that both (i) decreases as the oracle’s error decreases, and (ii) is always capped by O(log k), which can be achieved without any oracle input. We complement our results with an empirical evaluation of our algorithm on real world datasets, and show that it performs well empirically even using simple off the shelf predictions.

paragraphs: Caching requires deciding which items to evict before future requests are known. Learned predictions may help, but following them directly can perform badly even when their average error is small. This paper develops a framework for incorporating a learned oracle into online algorithms while preserving protection against unreliable advice.

For a cache of size k, the authors modify the Marker algorithm to use oracle predictions. The resulting competitive ratio improves as prediction error decreases and remains bounded by O(log k), the guarantee available without predictions. A competitive ratio measures performance relative to an optimal benchmark, so the result connects the benefit of accurate advice with a fallback guarantee when advice is poor.

The framework treats the oracle as a black box and does not depend on its internal implementation or the precise distribution of its errors. Experiments on real-world datasets show good performance even with simple off-the-shelf predictors. The central contribution is a way to benefit from learned information without allowing prediction mistakes to remove the algorithm’s stated worst-case protection.
summary.tldr: A prediction-aware caching algorithm improves with accurate advice while retaining an O(log k) competitive guarantee when predictions are unreliable.

title: Competitive Caching with Machine Learned Advice

abstract: We propose a new statistical model for ranking data, i.e., a new family of probability distributions on permutations. Our model is inspired by the idea of a data-generating process in the form of a noisy sorting procedure, in which deterministic comparisons between pairs of items are replaced by Bernoulli trials. The probability of producing a certain ranking as a result then essentially depends on the Bernoulli parameters, which can be interpreted as pairwise preferences. We show that our model can be written in closed form if insertion or quick sort are used as sorting algorithms, and propose a maximum likelihood approach for parameter estimation. We also introduce a generalization of the model, in which the constraints on pairwise preferences are relaxed, and for which maximum likelihood estimation can be carried out based on a variation of the generalized iterative scaling algorithm. Experimentally, we show that the models perform very well in terms of goodness of fit, compared to existing models for ranking data.

The probability of producing a certain ranking as a result then essentially depends on the Bernoulli parameters, which can be interpreted as pairwise preferences. We show that our model can be written in closed form if insertion or quick sort are used as sorting algorithms, and propose a maximum likelihood approach for parameter estimation. We also introduce a generalization of the model, in which the constraints on pairwise preferences are relaxed, and for which maximum likelihood estimation can be carried out based on a variation of the generalized iterative scaling algorithm. paragraphs: The paper introduces probability models for rankings by imagining that rankings are generated through a noisy sorting procedure. Each comparison between two items becomes a Bernoulli trial instead of a deterministic decision. The comparison probabilities can be interpreted as pairwise preferences, connecting local choices between items to probabilities over complete rankings.

When the sorting procedure is insertion sort or quicksort, the authors show that the resulting model has a closed-form expression. They propose maximum likelihood estimation to learn its parameters from observed ranking data. This gives the sorting-based construction both a probabilistic interpretation and a concrete route for fitting the model.

A generalized version relaxes constraints on the pairwise preferences and uses a variation of generalized iterative scaling for maximum likelihood estimation. Experiments report strong goodness of fit compared with existing ranking models. The findings support noisy sorting as a useful statistical construction: a familiar algorithmic process becomes a mechanism for describing variation across observed orderings.
summary.tldr: Noisy sorting procedures define learnable probability distributions over rankings, with strong reported fit compared with existing models.

title: Ranking Distributions based on Noisy Sorting

abstract: Low-dimensional discriminative representations enhance machine learning methods in both performance and complexity, motivating supervised dimensionality reduction (DR) that transforms high-dimensional data to a discriminative subspace. Most DR methods require data to be i.i.d., however, in some domains, data naturally come in sequences, where the observations are temporally correlated. We propose a DR method called LT-LDA to learn low-dimensional temporal representations. We construct the separability among sequence classes by lifting the holistic temporal structures, which are established based on temporal alignments and may change in different subspaces. We jointly learn the subspace and the associated alignments by optimizing an objective which favors easily-separable temporal structures, and show that this objective is connected to the inference of alignments, thus allows an iterative solution. We provide both theoretical insight and empirical evaluation on real-world sequence datasets to show the interest of our method.

Most DR methods require data to be i.i.d., however, in some domains, data naturally come in sequences, where the observations are temporally correlated. We propose a DR method called LT-LDA to learn low-dimensional temporal representations. We construct the separability among sequence classes by lifting the holistic temporal structures, which are established based on temporal alignments and may change in different subspaces. We jointly learn the subspace and the associated alignments by optimizing an objective which favors easily-separable temporal structures, and show that this objective is connected to the inference of alignments, thus allows an iterative solution. We provide both theoretical insight and empirical evaluation on real-world sequence datasets to show the interest of our method.

paragraphs: Supervised dimensionality reduction seeks compact representations that preserve information useful for distinguishing classes. Many methods assume independent observations, but sequence data contain temporal relationships. LT-LDA addresses this mismatch by learning low-dimensional representations that account for the structure of entire sequences rather than treating their observations as independent examples.

The method uses temporal alignments to establish sequence structure and builds class separability around those structures. Crucially, an alignment may change when the representation changes. The authors therefore learn the subspace and its associated alignments together, optimizing an objective that favors temporal structures that are easy to distinguish across classes. This joint treatment makes the representation and the sequence comparisons part of the same learning problem.

The paper connects the objective to alignment inference, which enables an iterative solution. It provides theoretical insight and evaluations on real-world sequence datasets to support the approach. The stated contribution is a way to make dimensionality reduction sensitive to temporal organization, while allowing that organization to adapt as the lower-dimensional representation is learned.
summary.tldr: LT-LDA jointly learns a compact representation and temporal alignments to make sequence classes easier to distinguish.

title: Learning Low-Dimensional Temporal Representations

abstract: While it’s always possible to compute a variational approximation to a posterior distribution, it can be difficult to discover problems with this approximation. We propose two diagnostic algorithms to alleviate this problem. The Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (PSIS) diagnostic gives a goodness of fit measurement for joint distributions, while simultaneously improving the error in the estimate. The variational simulation-based calibration (VSBC) assesses the average performance of point estimates.
originalAbstract: While it’s always possible to compute a variational approximation to a posterior distribution, it can be difficult to discover problems with this approximation. We propose two diagnostic algorithms to alleviate this problem. The Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (PSIS) diagnostic gives a goodness of fit measurement for joint distributions, while simultaneously improving the error in the estimate. The variational simulation-based calibration (VSBC) assesses the average performance of point estimates.

paragraphs: Variational inference produces an approximation to a posterior distribution, but obtaining that approximation does not by itself reveal whether it has important problems. The paper addresses this evaluation step with two diagnostic algorithms. They examine different aspects of approximation quality, separating the fit of a joint distribution from the average performance of point estimates.

The Pareto-smoothed importance sampling diagnostic, or PSIS, provides a goodness-of-fit measurement for joint distributions. It also improves the error in the estimate while carrying out that assessment. Its role therefore includes both checking the approximation and improving estimation, connecting diagnosis with a corrective contribution to the resulting estimate.

Variational simulation-based calibration, or VSBC, assesses the average performance of point estimates. This asks a different question from whether the joint distribution fits well: it focuses on the estimates extracted from the approximation. Together, the proposed diagnostics give users two distinct ways to evaluate a variational result, according to whether their concern is distributional fit or average point-estimation performance.
summary.tldr: Two diagnostics assess variational inference through joint-distribution fit and average point-estimate performance.

title: Yes, but Did It Work?: Evaluating Variational Inference

abstract: We study the use of predictions by multiple experts (such as machine learning algorithms) to improve the performance of online algorithms. In particular, we consider the classical rent-or-buy problem (also called ski rental), and obtain algorithms that provably improve their performance over the adversarial scenario by using these predictions. We also prove matching lower bounds to show that our algorithms are the best possible, and perform experiments to empirically validate their performance in practice
originalAbstract: We study the use of predictions by multiple experts (such as machine learning algorithms) to improve the performance of online algorithms. In particular, we consider the classical rent-or-buy problem (also called ski rental), and obtain algorithms that provably improve their performance over the adversarial scenario by using these predictions. We also prove matching lower bounds to show that our algorithms are the best possible, and perform experiments to empirically validate their performance in practice

paragraphs: Online algorithms must make decisions as information arrives, before the full future is available. This paper studies how predictions from multiple experts, including machine learning algorithms, can improve those decisions. It focuses on the classical rent-or-buy problem, also known as ski rental, where an algorithm must choose between continuing to rent and committing to a purchase.

The authors develop algorithms that use the expert predictions and prove performance improvements over the adversarial scenario. This makes advice a formal part of the online decision problem: the analysis asks what improvement is achievable when predictions are available, rather than evaluating a forecasting system independently of the decisions it supports.

The paper also proves matching lower bounds. Within the studied setting, these establish that the algorithms attain the best possible performance described by the bounds. Experiments provide an empirical check of their practical behavior. The contribution therefore combines a way to use multiple experts with both achievable guarantees and limits on how much an algorithm can improve.
summary.tldr: Expert-assisted rent-or-buy algorithms achieve provable improvements over the adversarial setting, with matching lower bounds.

title: Online Algorithms for Rent-Or-Buy with Expert Advice

abstract: We present differentially private efficient algorithms for learning union of polygons in the plane (which are not necessarily convex). Our algorithms achieve $(\alpha,\beta)$-PAC learning and $(\epsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy using a sample of size $\tilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{\alpha\epsilon}k\log d\right)$, where the domain is $[d]\times[d]$ and $k$ is the number of edges in the union of polygons.
originalAbstract: We present differentially private efficient algorithms for learning union of polygons in the plane (which are not necessarily convex). Our algorithms achieve $(\alpha,\beta)$-PAC learning and $(\epsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy using a sample of size $\tilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{\alpha\epsilon}k\log d\right)$, where the domain is $[d]\times[d]$ and $k$ is the number of edges in the union of polygons.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning a geometric region made from a union of polygons in a two-dimensional discrete domain. The polygons need not be convex, so the target class includes regions with inward bends. Its contribution is an efficient learning approach that combines a statistical accuracy guarantee with differential privacy.

The statistical guarantee uses the PAC framework: alpha controls the tolerated prediction error, while beta controls the probability of failing to meet that accuracy target. The privacy guarantee uses epsilon and delta to constrain how much the learning procedure's output can change when an individual's example changes. Both guarantees apply to the same learning algorithms.

The stated sample requirement is approximately k log d divided by alpha epsilon, with additional logarithmic factors suppressed. Here, k counts edges in the polygon union, and the domain is a d-by-d grid. This expresses how the amount of data depends on geometric complexity, domain size, accuracy, and privacy. In particular, the displayed dependence is linear in the number of edges and logarithmic in the grid's side length.
summary.tldr: Efficient private algorithms learn unions of possibly nonconvex polygons with sample bounds tied to their edge count and grid size.

title: Differentially Private Learning of Geometric Concepts

abstract: By building upon the recent theory that established the connection between implicit generative modeling (IGM) and optimal transport, in this study, we propose a novel parameter-free algorithm for learning the underlying distributions of complicated datasets and sampling from them. The proposed algorithm is based on a functional optimization problem, which aims at finding a measure that is close to the data distribution as much as possible and also expressive enough for generative modeling purposes. We formulate the problem as a gradient flow in the space of probability measures. The connections between gradient flows and stochastic differential equations let us develop a computationally efficient algorithm for solving the optimization problem. We provide formal theoretical analysis where we prove finite-time error guarantees for the proposed algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, the proposed algorithm is the first nonparametric IGM algorithm with explicit theoretical guarantees. Our experimental results support our theory and show that our algorithm is able to successfully capture the structure of different types of data distributions.

Our experimental results support our theory and show that our algorithm is able to successfully capture the structure of different types of data distributions.

paragraphs: Generative modeling aims to learn a data distribution and produce new samples from it. This paper proposes a parameter-free, nonparametric algorithm built on connections between implicit generative modeling and optimal transport. Its starting point is an optimization problem over probability distributions, seeking a distribution that both matches the data and remains expressive enough for generation.

The authors formulate that optimization as a gradient flow in the space of probability measures. This describes how an entire distribution evolves toward the objective. Connections between these flows and stochastic differential equations then provide a computationally efficient algorithm for carrying out the evolution and obtaining samples.

The paper proves finite-time error guarantees, giving explicit theoretical control over the proposed algorithm's approximation. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first nonparametric implicit generative modeling method with such guarantees. Experiments support the analysis and show that the algorithm captures structure across different types of data distributions, connecting the mathematical formulation to demonstrated generative behavior.
summary.tldr: A nonparametric generative algorithm evolves probability distributions through gradient flows and stochastic differential equations, with finite-time error guarantees.

title: Sliced-Wasserstein Flows: Nonparametric Generative Modeling via Optimal Transport and Diffusions

abstract: We consider probabilistic PCA and related factor models from a Bayesian perspective. These models are in general not identifiable as the likelihood has a rotational symmetry. This gives rise to complicated posterior distributions with continuous subspaces of equal density and thus hinders efficiency of inference as well as interpretation of obtained parameters. In particular, posterior averages over factor loadings become meaningless and only model predictions are unambiguous. Here, we propose a parameterization based on Householder transformations, which remove the rotational symmetry of the posterior. Furthermore, by relying on results from random matrix theory, we establish the parameter distribution which leaves the model unchanged compared to the original rotationally symmetric formulation. In particular, we avoid the need to compute the Jacobian determinant of the parameter transformation. This allows us to efficiently implement probabilistic PCA in a rotation invariant fashion in any state of the art toolbox. Here, we implemented our model in the probabilistic programming language Stan and illustrate it on several examples.

paragraphs: Bayesian probabilistic PCA and related factor models can have multiple parameter descriptions with the same likelihood because rotating the factors leaves the model unchanged. This symmetry creates continuous regions of equal posterior density. It complicates inference and makes averages of factor loadings meaningless even though the model’s predictions remain unambiguous.

The paper proposes a parameterization based on Householder transformations that removes this rotational symmetry from the posterior. The authors also use random matrix theory to establish the parameter distribution needed to preserve the original model. This preservation matters because changing how parameters are represented should not inadvertently change the probabilistic model being fitted.

Their construction avoids computing the Jacobian determinant of the parameter transformation, simplifying implementation. The authors implement the model in Stan and illustrate it with several examples. The contribution addresses a source of ambiguity in Bayesian factor models while retaining their original probabilistic meaning, allowing inference and interpretation to work with a representation that no longer contains the same rotational redundancy.
summary.tldr: A Householder-based parameterization removes rotational ambiguity in Bayesian PCA while preserving the original probabilistic model.

title: Rotation Invariant Householder Parameterization for Bayesian PCA

abstract: In this paper, we formulate a novel problem of learning to select a set of items maximizing the quality of their ordered list, where the order is predefined by some explicit rule. Unlike the classic information retrieval problem, in our setting, the predefined order of items in the list may not correspond to their quality in general. For example, this is a dominant scenario in personalized news and social media feeds, where items are ordered by publication time in a user interface. We propose new theoretically grounded algorithms based on direct optimization of the resulting list quality. Our offline and online experiments with a large-scale product search engine demonstrate the overwhelming advantage of our methods over the baselines in terms of all key quality metrics.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to choose items when their eventual display order is fixed by an explicit rule. Selecting a good set is different from simply finding individually strong items, because the final ordered list is the object being evaluated. The predefined order may have little relationship to item quality.

A motivating example is a personalized feed that displays items by publication time. The system can choose which items appear, but the display rule determines their positions. The authors formulate this as a learning problem and propose theoretically grounded algorithms that directly optimize the quality of the list produced after the ordering rule is applied.

Offline and online experiments with a large-scale product search engine report substantial advantages over the baselines across all key quality metrics evaluated. The findings support treating selection and its resulting order together. For systems with a fixed ordering convention, the relevant optimization target is the quality of the displayed sequence, rather than a ranking the interface will never actually use.
summary.tldr: The paper learns which items to select by optimizing list quality under a predefined display order.

title: Learning to select for a predefined ranking

abstract: We consider the problem of privacy-amplification by under the Renyi Differential Privacy framework. This is the main technique underlying the moments accountants (Abadi et al., 2016) for differentially private deep learning. Unlike previous attempts on this problem which deals with Sampling with Replacement, we consider the Poisson subsampling scheme which selects each data point independently with a coin toss. This allows us to significantly simplify and tighten the bounds for the RDP of subsampled mechanisms and derive numerically stable approximation schemes. In particular, for subsampled Gaussian mechanism and subsampled Laplace mechanism, we prove an analytical formula of their RDP that exactly matches the lower bound. The result is the first of its kind and we numerically demonstrate an order of magnitude improvement in the privacy-utility tradeoff.

The sampling rule is therefore part of the mathematical problem.

For this independent-selection scheme, they derive simpler and tighter bounds on the privacy of subsampled mechanisms and develop approximation methods designed to remain numerically stable.

For subsampled Gaussian and Laplace mechanisms, the paper proves analytical Rényi privacy formulas that match the lower bound exactly. This establishes tightness for those mechanisms in the studied setting. Numerical results demonstrate an order-of-magnitude improvement in the privacy–utility tradeoff. The contribution combines sharper privacy accounting with practical numerical evaluation, showing how a precise treatment of the sampling scheme can materially improve the resulting privacy analysis.
summary.tldr: Analyzing Poisson subsampling yields tighter Rényi privacy bounds, stable approximations, and exact formulas for subsampled Gaussian and Laplace mechanisms.

title: Poission Subsampled Rényi Differential Privacy

abstract: In this paper, we study distributed algorithms for large-scale AUC maximization with a deep neural network as a predictive model. Although distributed learning techniques have been investigated extensively in deep learning, they are not directly applicable to stochastic AUC maximization with deep neural networks due to its striking differences from standard loss minimization problems (e.g., cross-entropy). Towards addressing this challenge, we propose and analyze a communication-efficient distributed optimization algorithm based on a \emph{non-convex concave} reformulation of the AUC maximization, in which the communication of both the primal variable and the dual variable between each worker and the parameter server only occurs after multiple steps of gradient-based updates in each worker. Compared with the naive parallel version of an existing algorithm that computes stochastic gradients at individual machines and averages them for updating the model parameter, our algorithm requires a much less number of communication rounds and still achieves linear speedup in theory. To the best of our knowledge, this is the \textbf{first} work that solves the \emph{non-convex concave min-max} problem for AUC maximization with deep neural networks in a communication-efficient distributed manner while still maintaining the linear speedup property in theory. Our experiments on several benchmark datasets show the effectiveness of our algorithm and also confirm our theory.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to train deep neural networks for AUC maximization across multiple workers. The optimization problem differs enough from standard loss minimization, such as cross-entropy training, that familiar distributed learning techniques do not transfer directly. The goal is to obtain the computational benefit of multiple workers while limiting communication with a central parameter server.

The method uses a reformulation with a nonconvex minimization side and a concave maximization side. Each worker performs multiple gradient-based updates locally before communicating the variables associated with both sides of the problem. Delaying these exchanges reduces the frequency of synchronization compared with a straightforward parallel method that averages gradients computed on individual machines.

The analysis establishes substantially fewer communication rounds while retaining a theoretical linear speedup property. Experiments on several benchmark datasets support the method's effectiveness and the theoretical findings. The central result is that less frequent communication can coexist with the stated speedup guarantee for this particular distributed AUC optimization formulation.
summary.tldr: A distributed AUC optimization method reduces communication through multiple local updates while preserving a theoretical linear speedup.

title: Communication-Efficient Distributed Stochastic AUC Maximization with Deep Neural Networks

abstract: This paper studies how to sketch element-wise functions of low-rank matrices. Formally, given low-rank matrix A = [Aij] and scalar non-linear function f, we aim for finding an approximated low-rank representation of the (possibly high-rank) matrix [f(Aij)]. To this end, we propose an efficient sketching-based algorithm whose complexity is significantly lower than the number of entries of A, i.e., it runs without accessing all entries of [f(Aij)] explicitly. The main idea underlying our method is to combine a polynomial approximation of f with the existing tensor sketch scheme for approximating monomials of entries of A. To balance the errors of the two approximation components in an optimal manner, we propose a novel regression formula to find polynomial coefficients given A and f. In particular, we utilize a coreset-based regression with a rigorous approximation guarantee. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability and superiority of the proposed scheme under various machine learning tasks.

paragraphs: Applying a nonlinear function separately to every entry of a low-rank matrix can produce a matrix with high rank. This paper asks how to approximate that transformed matrix with a compact low-rank representation. Its algorithm runs in time substantially below the number of entries in the original matrix, without explicitly accessing every transformed entry.

The approach combines two approximations. A polynomial approximates the nonlinear function, and tensor sketching approximates the monomial terms applied to matrix entries. Choosing a polynomial solely for function approximation would overlook the error introduced by sketching. The authors therefore develop a regression formula that chooses coefficients while balancing the two sources of approximation error.

A coreset-based regression procedure makes this coefficient selection efficient and comes with a rigorous approximation guarantee. Experiments across machine learning tasks demonstrate applicability and improvements over compared approaches. The contribution is a coordinated approximation scheme: it accounts for how polynomial fitting and randomized sketching interact when producing the final compact matrix representation.
summary.tldr: Polynomial approximation and tensor sketching jointly produce compact representations of nonlinear matrix transformations without explicitly processing every entry.

title: Polynomial Tensor Sketch for Element-wise Function of Low-Rank Matrix

abstract: In E-commerce, advertising is essential for merchants to reach their target users. The typical objective is to maximize the advertiser’s cumulative revenue over a period of time under a budget constraint. In real applications, an advertisement (ad) usually needs to be exposed to the same user multiple times until the user finally contributes revenue (e.g., places an order). However, existing advertising systems mainly focus on the immediate revenue with single ad exposures, ignoring the contribution of each exposure to the final conversion, thus usually falls into suboptimal solutions. In this paper, we formulate the sequential advertising strategy optimization as a dynamic knapsack problem. We propose a theoretically guaranteed bilevel optimization framework, which significantly reduces the solution space of the original optimization space while ensuring the solution quality. To improve the exploration efficiency of reinforcement learning, we also devise an effective action space reduction approach. Extensive offline and online experiments show the superior performance of our approaches over state-of-the-art baselines in terms of cumulative revenue.

paragraphs: An advertisement may contribute to a purchase even when the purchase happens only after several later exposures. Systems that optimize revenue from each exposure independently can miss those delayed contributions. This paper instead studies how to allocate a limited advertising budget across sequences of exposures to maximize cumulative revenue.

The authors formulate sequential advertising as a dynamic knapsack problem. They introduce a bilevel optimization framework with theoretical guarantees that reduces the original solution space while preserving solution quality. An additional action-space reduction method is designed to improve the exploration efficiency of reinforcement learning in this setting.

Offline and online experiments report higher cumulative revenue than the compared state-of-the-art baselines. The work connects a budget-allocation formulation to practical reductions in planning and learning complexity. Its central shift is to value exposures through their contribution to an eventual sequence outcome; the abstract does not provide the numerical revenue gains or the detailed assumptions behind the theoretical guarantees.
summary.tldr: Dynamic knapsack optimization accounts for repeated ad exposures and improves budgeted cumulative revenue in the reported experiments.

title: Dynamic Knapsack Optimization Towards Efficient Multi-Channel Sequential Advertising

abstract: Despite the power of deep neural networks for a wide range of tasks, an overconfident prediction issue has limited their practical use in many safety-critical applications. Many recent works have been proposed to mitigate this issue, but most of them require either additional computational costs in training and/or inference phases or customized architectures to output confidence estimates separately. In this paper, we propose a method of training deep neural networks with a novel loss function, named Correctness Ranking Loss, which regularizes class probabilities explicitly to be better confidence estimates in terms of ordinal ranking according to confidence. The proposed method is easy to implement and can be applied to the existing architectures without any modification. Also, it has almost the same computational costs for training as conventional deep classifiers and outputs reliable predictions by a single inference. Extensive experimental results on classification benchmark datasets indicate that the proposed method helps networks to produce well-ranked confidence estimates. We also demonstrate that it is effective for the tasks closely related to confidence estimation, out-of-distribution detection and active learning.

paragraphs: A neural classifier can make a prediction with high confidence even when it is wrong. This creates problems when confidence helps determine whether a prediction should be trusted. The paper addresses the issue through training, aiming to make the class probabilities already produced by a network more useful as confidence estimates.

The proposed Correctness Ranking Loss regularizes those probabilities so that confidence has a better ordinal relationship with correctness. The emphasis is on ordering predictions by confidence: predictions that deserve more trust should receive higher confidence scores. This ranking objective is the specific property studied, rather than a claim that every probability becomes an exact measure of correctness.

The method works with existing architectures without modification, has almost the training cost of conventional deep classifiers, and requires only one inference pass. Classification experiments indicate improved confidence rankings. The authors also demonstrate benefits for out-of-distribution detection and active learning, showing that better confidence ordering can help tasks that use uncertainty to guide decisions.
summary.tldr: Correctness Ranking Loss trains existing classifiers to produce better-ordered confidence estimates with little additional computational cost.

title: Confidence-Aware Learning for Deep Neural Networks

abstract: A longstanding goal in the theory of deep learning is to characterize the conditions under which a given neural network architecture will be trainable, and if so, how well it might generalize to unseen data. In this work, we provide such a characterization in the limit of very wide and very deep networks, for which the analysis simplifies considerably. For wide networks, the trajectory under gradient descent is governed by the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK), and for deep networks the NTK itself maintains only weak data dependence. By analyzing the spectrum of the NTK, we formulate necessary conditions for trainability and generalization across a range of architectures, including Fully Connected Networks (FCNs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). We identify large regions of hyperparameter space for which networks can memorize the training set but completely fail to generalize. We find that CNNs without global average pooling behave almost identically to FCNs, but that CNNs with pooling have markedly different and often better generalization performance. These theoretical results are corroborated experimentally on CIFAR10 for a variety of network architectures. We include a \href{https://colab.research.google.com/github/google/neural-tangents/blob/master/notebooks/disentangling_trainability_and_generalization.ipynb}{colab} notebook that reproduces the essential results of the paper.

paragraphs: A network's ability to fit training examples does not by itself establish that it will perform well on new data. This paper analyzes these two properties separately in the limit of very wide and very deep networks, where the mathematics becomes simpler. It studies both fully connected and convolutional architectures.

For wide networks, gradient-descent training is governed by the Neural Tangent Kernel, or NTK. At large depth, that kernel retains only weak dependence on the data. By examining its spectrum, the authors derive necessary conditions for trainability and generalization. These are requirements that successful behavior must satisfy, rather than sufficient guarantees of success.

The analysis identifies broad hyperparameter regions where networks can memorize training data yet fail to generalize. It also finds that convolutional networks without global average pooling behave much like fully connected networks, while pooling produces substantially different and often better generalization. CIFAR10 experiments corroborate the theory. The findings show why architectural choices must be assessed for both optimization and generalization within the studied regime.
summary.tldr: An NTK analysis of very wide, deep networks separates conditions for fitting training data from conditions for generalizing.

title: Disentangling Trainability and Generalization in Deep Neural Networks

abstract: This paper studies Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for data lying in hyperbolic spaces. Given directions, PCA relies on: (1) a parameterization of subspaces spanned by these directions, (2) a method of projection onto subspaces that preserves information in these directions, and (3) an objective to optimize, namely the variance explained by projections. We generalize each of these concepts to the hyperbolic space and propose HoroPCA, a method for hyperbolic dimensionality reduction. By focusing on the core problem of extracting principal directions, HoroPCA theoretically better preserves information in the original data such as distances, compared to previous generalizations of PCA. Empirically, we validate that HoroPCA outperforms existing dimensionality reduction methods, significantly reducing error in distance preservation. As a data whitening method, it improves downstream classification by up to 3.9% compared to methods that don’t use whitening. Finally, we show that HoroPCA can be used to visualize hyperbolic data in two dimensions.

paragraphs: HoroPCA adapts principal component analysis to data in hyperbolic space. The paper starts from three ingredients of PCA: defining subspaces from directions, projecting data while retaining information along those directions, and measuring the variance captured by a projection. Each ingredient must be reconsidered for the geometry in which the data lives.

The proposed method generalizes these ingredients while centering the problem on extracting principal directions. The authors establish that this approach better preserves original information, including distances, than previous PCA generalizations in their theoretical analysis. This matters because reducing dimensionality is useful only to the extent that the smaller representation retains relationships needed for subsequent analysis.

Experiments report substantially lower distance-preservation error than existing dimensionality reduction methods. Used for data whitening, HoroPCA improves downstream classification by up to 3.9% compared with methods without whitening. The authors also demonstrate two-dimensional visualization of hyperbolic data. These results connect the geometric formulation to practical uses in compression, preprocessing, and visual inspection.
summary.tldr: HoroPCA generalizes PCA to hyperbolic space, improving distance preservation and supporting whitening and visualization.

title: HoroPCA: Hyperbolic Dimensionality Reduction via Horospherical Projections

abstract: The maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) test could in principle detect any distributional discrepancy between two datasets. However, it has been shown that the MMD test is unaware of adversarial attacks–the MMD test failed to detect the discrepancy between natural data and adversarial data. Given this phenomenon, we raise a question: are natural and adversarial data really from different distributions? The answer is affirmative–the previous use of the MMD test on the purpose missed three key factors, and accordingly, we propose three components. Firstly, the Gaussian kernel has limited representation power, and we replace it with an effective deep kernel. Secondly, the test power of the MMD test was neglected, and we maximize it following asymptotic statistics. Finally, adversarial data may be non-independent, and we overcome this issue with the help of wild bootstrap. By taking care of the three factors, we verify that the MMD test is aware of adversarial attacks, which lights up a novel road for adversarial data detection based on two-sample tests.

paragraphs: Maximum mean discrepancy, or MMD, is a statistical tool for testing whether two datasets come from different distributions. Although it can in principle detect any distributional discrepancy, earlier applications failed to distinguish natural data from adversarial data. This paper investigates whether that failure reflects similarity between the distributions or shortcomings in the test’s application.

The authors identify three factors and modify the procedure accordingly. They replace the Gaussian kernel with a deep kernel to improve representation power, explicitly optimize statistical test power, and use a wild bootstrap to handle possible dependence among adversarial examples. These changes address how differences are represented, how sensitively they are detected, and how the test handles the structure of the data.

With all three factors addressed, the authors demonstrate that MMD can detect adversarial attacks and affirm a distributional difference between natural and adversarial data in their study. The finding changes the interpretation of the earlier negative result: failure to reject a distributional match did not establish that the datasets shared a distribution. It also supports further adversarial detection methods based on two-sample testing.
summary.tldr: Addressing kernel representation, test power, and possible sample dependence allows MMD tests to detect differences between natural and adversarial data.

title: Maximum Mean Discrepancy Test is Aware of Adversarial Attacks

abstract: We consider the problem of supervised learning with Bayesian Networks when the used dependency structure is incomplete due to missing edges or missing variable states. These modeling errors induce independence constraints on the learned model that may not hold in the true, data-generating distribution. We provide a unified treatment of these modeling errors as instances of state-space abstractions. We then identify a class of Bayesian Networks and queries which allow one to fully recover from such modeling errors if one can choose Conditional Probability Tables (CPTs) dynamically based on evidence. We show theoretically that the recently proposed Testing Bayesian Networks (TBNs), which can be trained by compiling them into Testing Arithmetic Circuits (TACs), provide a promising construct for emulating this CPT selection mechanism. Finally, we present empirical results that illustrate the promise of TBNs as a tool for recovering from certain modeling errors in the context of supervised learning.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of supervised learning with Bayesian Networks when the used dependency structure is incomplete due to missing edges or missing variable states. These modeling errors induce independence constraints on the learned model that may not hold in the true, data-generating distribution. We provide a unified treatment of these modeling errors as instances of state-space abstractions. We then identify a class of Bayesian Networks and queries which allow one to fully recover from such modeling errors if one can choose Conditional Probability Tables (CPTs) dynamically based on evidence. We show theoretically that the recently proposed Testing Bayesian Networks (TBNs), which can be trained by compiling them into Testing Arithmetic Circuits (TACs), provide a promising construct for emulating this CPT selection mechanism. Finally, we present empirical results that illustrate the promise of TBNs as a tool for recovering from certain modeling errors in the context of supervised learning.

paragraphs: A Bayesian network can misrepresent data when its dependency graph omits connections or its variables omit possible states. These modeling errors impose independence assumptions that may be false in the process generating the observations. The paper studies how supervised learning can recover from such errors without treating the two kinds of omission as unrelated problems.

The authors unify them through state-space abstractions. They then identify a class of networks and queries for which full recovery is possible if conditional probability tables can be selected dynamically based on the observed evidence. The key mechanism is therefore to let the evidence influence which probability tables are used.

Testing Bayesian Networks offer a promising way to emulate this selection mechanism, and they can be trained through compilation into Testing Arithmetic Circuits. The paper provides theoretical support for this connection and empirical illustrations of recovery in supervised learning. The full-recovery result is conditional on the identified network and query class and on the availability of dynamic table selection.
summary.tldr: Evidence-dependent probability tables can fully compensate for certain Bayesian-network modeling errors, with Testing Bayesian Networks offering a promising implementation.

title: On Recovering from Modeling Errors Using Testing Bayesian Networks

abstract: Recent efforts to unravel the mystery of implicit regularization in deep learning have led to a theoretical focus on matrix factorization — matrix completion via linear neural network. As a step further towards practical deep learning, we provide the first theoretical analysis of implicit regularization in tensor factorization — tensor completion via certain type of non-linear neural network. We circumvent the notorious difficulty of tensor problems by adopting a dynamical systems perspective, and characterizing the evolution induced by gradient descent. The characterization suggests a form of greedy low tensor rank search, which we rigorously prove under certain conditions, and empirically demonstrate under others. Motivated by tensor rank capturing the implicit regularization of a non-linear neural network, we empirically explore it as a measure of complexity, and find that it captures the essence of datasets on which neural networks generalize. This leads us to believe that tensor rank may pave way to explaining both implicit regularization in deep learning, and the properties of real-world data translating this implicit regularization to generalization.

This paper studies those preferences in tensor factorization, extending a theoretical line of work on matrix factorization. The tensor-completion setting corresponds to a certain type of nonlinear neural network, bringing the analysis closer to nonlinear learning.

The authors use a dynamical-systems perspective to characterize how gradient descent evolves the factorization. Their characterization suggests a greedy search toward low tensor rank. They prove this behavior under certain conditions and demonstrate it empirically under others. The distinction matters: the paper combines a conditional theoretical result with evidence beyond the conditions covered by that proof.

Motivated by this connection, the authors also investigate tensor rank as an empirical measure of complexity. They find that it captures important characteristics of datasets on which neural networks generalize. The work therefore proposes tensor rank as a promising route toward explaining training-induced preferences and their relationship to data properties, while presenting that broader explanatory role as a possibility for further development.
summary.tldr: Gradient-descent dynamics in tensor factorization suggest a greedy low-rank search, proved under certain conditions and supported empirically under others.

title: Implicit Regularization in Tensor Factorization

abstract: The lottery ticket hypothesis (LTH) reveals the existence of winning tickets (sparse but critical subnetworks) for dense networks, that can be trained in isolation from random initialization to match the latter’s accuracies. However, finding winning tickets requires burdensome computations in the train-prune-retrain process, especially on large-scale datasets (e.g., ImageNet), restricting their practical benefits. This paper explores a new perspective on finding lottery tickets more efficiently, by doing so only with a specially selected subset of data, called Pruning-Aware Critical set (PrAC set), rather than using the full training set. The concept of PrAC set was inspired by the recent observation, that deep networks have samples that are either hard to memorize during training, or easy to forget during pruning. A PrAC set is thus hypothesized to capture those most challenging and informative examples for the dense model. We observe that a high-quality winning ticket can be found with training and pruning the dense network on the very compact PrAC set, which can substantially save training iterations for the ticket finding process. Extensive experiments validate our proposal across diverse datasets and network architectures. Specifically, on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet, we locate effective PrAC sets at 35.32% 78.19% of their training set sizes. On top of them, we can obtain the same competitive winning tickets for the corresponding dense networks, yet saving up to 82.85% 92.77%, 63.54% 74.92%, and 76.14% 86.56% training iterations, respectively. Crucially, we show that a PrAC set found is reusable across different network architectures, which can amortize the extra cost of finding PrAC sets, yielding a practical regime for efficient lottery ticket finding.

Finding these subnetworks can be expensive because it involves repeated training, pruning, and retraining. This paper investigates whether the search can use a carefully chosen subset of training examples.

The authors introduce a Pruning-Aware Critical set, or PrAC set. Its motivation comes from examples that are difficult for a network to memorize during training or easy for it to forget during pruning. They hypothesize that these examples capture especially challenging and informative parts of the dataset, making them useful for discovering a strong sparse subnetwork.

Experiments across datasets and architectures show that training and pruning on compact PrAC sets can find competitive winning tickets while substantially reducing training iterations. The authors also demonstrate that a selected set can be reused across different network architectures. That reuse matters because the effort of identifying the subset can be shared across multiple searches.
summary.tldr: Carefully selected training subsets can reduce the work of finding competitive sparse subnetworks and can be reused across architectures.

title: Efficient Lottery Ticket Finding: Less Data is More

abstract: Federated learning allows clients to collaboratively learn statistical models while keeping their data local. Federated learning was originally used to train a unique global model to be served to all clients, but this approach might be sub-optimal when clients’ local data distributions are heterogeneous. In order to tackle this limitation, recent personalized federated learning methods train a separate model for each client while still leveraging the knowledge available at other clients. In this work, we exploit the ability of deep neural networks to extract high quality vectorial representations (embeddings) from non-tabular data, e.g., images and text, to propose a personalization mechanism based on local memorization. Personalization is obtained by interpolating a collectively trained global model with a local $k$-nearest neighbors (kNN) model based on the shared representation provided by the global model. We provide generalization bounds for the proposed approach in the case of binary classification, and we show on a suite of federated datasets that this approach achieves significantly higher accuracy and fairness than state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Federated learning allows clients to train collaboratively while retaining their data locally. A single shared model may nevertheless fit clients poorly when their data distributions differ. This paper proposes personalization through local memorization, using the shared model's learned representations to connect collective learning with each client's own examples.

The method combines predictions from a collectively trained global model and a local k-nearest-neighbors model. The local model uses embeddings supplied by the global network, taking advantage of neural networks' ability to extract useful vector representations from images and text. Personalization comes from interpolating these two sources of predictions: shared knowledge and similarity to locally stored data.

The authors derive generalization bounds for binary classification. Across a suite of federated datasets, the method achieves significantly higher accuracy and fairness than the state-of-the-art methods used for comparison. The theoretical result is specific to binary classification, while the empirical study evaluates the personalization mechanism on federated datasets. Together, they support local memorization as a way to make shared representations useful for heterogeneous clients.
summary.tldr: Combining a global federated model with local nearest-neighbor predictions improves reported personalization accuracy and fairness.

title: Personalized Federated Learning through Local Memorization

abstract: Federated learning is a machine learning training paradigm that enables clients to jointly train models without sharing their own localized data. However, the implementation of federated learning in practice still faces numerous challenges, such as the large communication overhead due to the repetitive server-client synchronization and the lack of adaptivity by SGD-based model updates. Despite that various methods have been proposed for reducing the communication cost by gradient compression or quantization, and the federated versions of adaptive optimizers such as FedAdam are proposed to add more adaptivity, the current federated learning framework still cannot solve the aforementioned challenges all at once. In this paper, we propose a novel communication-efficient adaptive federated learning method (FedCAMS) with theoretical convergence guarantees. We show that in the nonconvex stochastic optimization setting, our proposed FedCAMS achieves the same convergence rate of $O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{TKm}})$ as its non-compressed counterparts. Extensive experiments on various benchmarks verify our theoretical analysis.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients jointly train a model while keeping their local datasets to themselves. This arrangement still requires repeated communication with a server, which can become expensive. The paper also identifies limited adaptivity in updates based on stochastic gradient descent as a separate obstacle to effective training.

Existing approaches address these concerns through different mechanisms: compression or quantization reduces communication, while federated adaptive optimizers change how model updates are made. The authors propose FedCAMS to address both concerns within one method. Its contribution is a communication-efficient adaptive training approach accompanied by a theoretical convergence analysis.

For nonconvex stochastic optimization, the analysis establishes a convergence rate of O(1/√(TKm)), matching the rate of non-compressed counterparts. This means that, in the analyzed setting, introducing communication savings does not worsen the stated convergence order. Experiments across multiple benchmarks support the theoretical analysis, providing empirical evidence alongside the mathematical result for combining compression with adaptive federated learning.
summary.tldr: FedCAMS combines communication efficiency with adaptive federated optimization while matching its non-compressed counterparts’ theoretical convergence rate.

title: Communication-Efficient Adaptive Federated Learning

abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) of graph neural networks is emerging as a promising way of leveraging unlabeled data. Currently, most methods are based on contrastive learning adapted from the image domain, which requires view generation and a sufficient number of negative samples. In contrast, existing predictive models do not require negative sampling, but lack theoretical guidance on the design of pretext training tasks. In this work, we propose the LaGraph, a theoretically grounded predictive SSL framework based on latent graph prediction. Learning objectives of LaGraph are derived as self-supervised upper bounds to objectives for predicting unobserved latent graphs. In addition to its improved performance, LaGraph provides explanations for recent successes of predictive models that include invariance-based objectives. We provide theoretical analysis comparing LaGraph to related methods in different domains. Our experimental results demonstrate the superiority of LaGraph in performance and the robustness to decreasing of training sample size on both graph-level and node-level tasks.

paragraphs: Self-supervised graph learning aims to learn useful representations without labels. Many methods adapt contrastive learning, which requires generated views and enough negative examples. Predictive alternatives avoid negative sampling, but their training tasks have often lacked theoretical guidance. LaGraph addresses this design question by grounding predictive learning in the goal of recovering unobserved latent graphs.

The framework derives usable self-supervised objectives as upper bounds on objectives for latent-graph prediction. This gives the training task a connection to a stated prediction goal, even though the latent graphs themselves are unobserved. The analysis also explains recent successes of predictive methods using invariance-based objectives and compares LaGraph with related approaches from other domains.

Experiments report improved performance on both graph-level and node-level tasks, together with robustness as the number of training samples decreases. These findings support the usefulness of the derived objectives across two scales of graph prediction. The central contribution is a theoretical foundation for constructing predictive self-supervised tasks, accompanied by evidence that this foundation produces effective graph representations.
summary.tldr: LaGraph derives self-supervised objectives from latent-graph prediction, improving graph representations and showing robustness to smaller training sets in experiments.

title: Self-Supervised Representation Learning via Latent Graph Prediction

abstract: Bayesian persuasion studies how an informed sender should influence beliefs of rational receivers that take decisions through Bayesian updating of a common prior. We focus on the online Bayesian persuasion framework, in which the sender repeatedly faces one or more receivers with unknown and adversarially selected types. First, we show how to obtain a tight $\tilde O(T^{1/2})$ regret bound in the case in which the sender faces a single receiver and has bandit feedback, improving over the best previously known bound of $\tilde O(T^{4/5})$. Then, we provide the first no-regret guarantees for the multi-receiver setting under bandit feedback. Finally, we show how to design no-regret algorithms with polynomial per-iteration running time by exploiting type reporting, thereby circumventing known complexity results on online Bayesian persuasion. We provide efficient algorithms guaranteeing a $O(T^{1/2})$ regret upper bound both in the single- and multi-receiver scenario when type reporting is allowed.

paragraphs: Bayesian persuasion studies how an informed sender influences rational receivers who update a shared prior using the information they receive. This paper considers repeated interactions with receivers whose types are unknown and selected adversarially. It asks how effectively the sender can learn when feedback is limited and how efficiently the resulting algorithms can run.

For a single receiver under bandit feedback, the authors obtain a tight regret bound growing as the square root of the number of rounds, up to logarithmic factors. This improves the previous bound with a four-fifths exponent. They also establish the first no-regret guarantees for the multiple-receiver setting with bandit feedback, extending learning guarantees beyond one receiver.

The paper then introduces type reporting as a condition enabling computational efficiency. When reporting is allowed, it provides algorithms with polynomial running time per iteration and square-root regret bounds for both single and multiple receivers. These results distinguish two achievements: improved regret under limited feedback, and efficient implementation when additional type information is available. The latter guarantee specifically depends on allowing type reporting.
summary.tldr: The paper improves regret guarantees for online Bayesian persuasion and obtains efficient square-root-regret algorithms when type reporting is allowed.

title: Optimal Rates and Efficient Algorithms for Online Bayesian Persuasion

abstract: This paper investigates an interesting weakly supervised regression setting called regression with interval targets (RIT). Although some of the previous methods on relevant regression settings can be adapted to RIT, they are not statistically consistent, and thus their empirical performance is not guaranteed. In this paper, we provide a thorough study on RIT. First, we proposed a novel statistical model to describe the data generation process for RIT and demonstrate its validity. Second, we analyze a simple selecting method for RIT, which selects a particular value in the interval as the target value to train the model. Third, we propose a statistically consistent limiting method for RIT to train the model by limiting the predictions to the interval. We further derive an estimation error bound for our limiting method. Finally, extensive experiments on various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

paragraphs: Regression usually learns from exact numerical targets. In regression with interval targets, the supervision instead gives a range. This paper studies how to learn reliably from that weaker information, noting that adaptations of some related regression methods lack statistical consistency in this setting.

The authors first introduce a statistical model for the process that generates interval-target data and demonstrate its validity. They then analyze a simple selecting approach, which chooses one value from each interval and treats it as the training target. This makes explicit the consequences of converting a range into a single numerical label.

Their proposed limiting method trains by restricting predictions to the supplied intervals. They establish statistical consistency and derive an estimation-error bound, giving theoretical support under their formulation. Experiments across various datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The work therefore connects a model of how interval supervision arises with a learning objective that respects that supervision, providing both a theoretical foundation and empirical evidence for regression from ranges.
summary.tldr: A statistically consistent regression method learns from interval-valued supervision by limiting predictions to the supplied ranges.

title: Weakly Supervised Regression with Interval Targets

abstract: In this paper, we study representation learning in partially observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs), where the agent learns a decoder function that maps a series of high-dimensional raw observations to a compact representation and uses it for more efficient exploration and planning. We focus our attention on the sub-classes of $\gamma$-observable and decodable POMDPs , for which it has been shown that statistically tractable learning is possible, but there has not been any computationally efficient algorithm. We first present an algorithm for decodable PMMDPs that combines maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) and optimism in the face of uncertainty (OFU) to perform representation learning and achieve efficient sample complexity, while only calling supervised learning computational oracles. We then show how to adapt this algorithm to also work in the broader class of $\gamma$-observable POMDPs.

paragraphs: In a partially observable decision process, an agent must act using observations that do not directly reveal the full state. This paper studies learning a decoder that converts a sequence of high-dimensional observations into a compact representation. Such representations are intended to make exploration and planning more efficient.

The work focuses on decodable and gamma-observable subclasses of these processes. Earlier results had established that learning in these classes could be statistically tractable, but had not supplied a computationally efficient algorithm. The distinction matters: needing a manageable amount of data does not by itself make the required calculations manageable.

For the decodable setting, the authors combine maximum likelihood estimation with optimism in the face of uncertainty. Their algorithm achieves efficient sample complexity while relying only on supervised-learning computational oracles. They then adapt it to the broader gamma-observable class. The contribution connects representation learning, exploration, and tractable planning under these structural conditions, with the computational result explicitly expressed through access to the stated supervised-learning oracles.
summary.tldr: The paper develops sample-efficient representation learning and tractable planning for structured POMDP classes using supervised-learning oracles.

title: Provably Efficient Representation Learning with Tractable Planning in Low-Rank POMDP

abstract: The goal of this paper is open-vocabulary object detection (OVOD) — building a model that can detect objects beyond the set of categories seen at training, thus enabling the user to specify categories of interest at inference without the need for model retraining. We adopt a standard two- stage object detector architecture, and explore three ways for specifying novel categories: via language descriptions, via image exemplars, or via a combination of the two. We make three contributions: first, we prompt a large language model (LLM) to generate informative language descriptions for object classes, and construct powerful text-based classifiers; second, we employ a visual aggregator on image exemplars that can ingest any number of images as input, forming vision-based classifiers; and third, we provide a simple method to fuse information from language descriptions and image exemplars, yield- ing a multi-modal classifier. When evaluating on the challenging LVIS open-vocabulary bench- mark we demonstrate that: (i) our text-based classifiers outperform all previous OVOD works; (ii) our vision-based classifiers perform as well as text-based classifiers in prior work; (iii) using multi-modal classifiers perform better than either modality alone; and finally, (iv) our text-based and multi-modal classifiers yield better performance than a fully-supervised detector.
