paragraphs: Open-vocabulary object detection aims to detect categories beyond those seen during detector training. Users can specify categories at inference time without retraining the model. This paper explores three ways to supply that category information within a standard two-stage detector: language descriptions, example images, and a combination of both.

For language, the authors prompt a large language model to generate informative descriptions of object classes and use them to construct text-based classifiers. For images, a visual aggregator accepts any number of exemplars and forms a vision-based classifier. A simple fusion method then combines the descriptions and exemplars into a multimodal classifier.

On the LVIS open-vocabulary benchmark, the text classifiers outperform previous open-vocabulary detection work, while the visual classifiers match the performance of earlier text-based approaches. Combining modalities performs better than either alone. The reported text and multimodal classifiers also outperform a fully supervised detector. These comparisons support using richer category descriptions and complementary visual examples in the evaluated setting, especially when both forms of category information are available.
summary.tldr: Language-model descriptions and image exemplars form complementary classifiers for detecting object categories beyond detector training.

title: Multi-Modal Classifiers for Open-Vocabulary Object Detection

abstract: Domain adaptation aims to mitigate distribution shifts among different domains. However, traditional formulations are mostly limited to categorical domains, greatly simplifying nuanced domain relationships in the real world. In this work, we tackle a generalization with taxonomy-structured domains, which formalizes domains with nested, hierarchical similarity structures such as animal species and product catalogs. We build on the classic adversarial framework and introduce a novel taxonomist , which competes with the adversarial discriminator to preserve the taxonomy information. The equilibrium recovers the classic adversarial domain adaptation’s solution if given a non-informative domain taxonomy (e.g., a flat taxonomy where all leaf nodes connect to the root node) while yielding non-trivial results with other taxonomies. Empirically, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets with successful adaptation.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation helps models cope with differences between data domains. Treating domains as separate categories can overlook meaningful relationships among them. This paper studies domains arranged in a taxonomy, where nested groups express hierarchical similarities, as in animal species or product catalogs. The aim is to preserve this structure while adapting across distributions.

The method extends an adversarial adaptation framework with a component called a taxonomist. It competes with the adversarial discriminator to retain information about the domain hierarchy. This introduces an explicit role for relationships between domains, allowing adaptation to account for more than the identity of the domain that produced an example.

The equilibrium reduces to the classic adversarial adaptation solution when the taxonomy supplies no useful structure, such as a flat hierarchy connecting every leaf directly to the root. Other taxonomies yield nontrivial solutions. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on synthetic and real-world datasets, supporting the usefulness of representing hierarchical domain relationships within the adaptation process.
summary.tldr: A taxonomist component preserves hierarchical domain relationships within adversarial adaptation and improves performance on the evaluated datasets.

title: Taxonomy-Structured Domain Adaptation

abstract: Pre-trained diffusion models have been successfully used as priors in a variety of linear inverse problems, where the goal is to reconstruct a signal from noisy linear measurements. However, existing approaches require knowledge of the linear operator. In this paper, we propose GibbsDDRM, an extension of Denoising Diffusion Restoration Models (DDRM) to a blind setting in which the linear measurement operator is unknown. GibbsDDRM constructs a joint distribution of the data, measurements, and linear operator by using a pre-trained diffusion model for the data prior, and it solves the problem by posterior sampling with an efficient variant of a Gibbs sampler. The proposed method is problem-agnostic, meaning that a pre-trained diffusion model can be applied to various inverse problems without fine-tuning. In experiments, it achieved high performance on both blind image deblurring and vocal dereverberation tasks, despite the use of simple generic priors for the underlying linear operators.

In this paper, we propose GibbsDDRM, an extension of Denoising Diffusion Restoration Models (DDRM) to a blind setting in which the linear measurement operator is unknown. GibbsDDRM constructs a joint distribution of the data, measurements, and linear operator by using a pre-trained diffusion model for the data prior, and it solves the problem by posterior sampling with an efficient variant of a Gibbs sampler. The proposed method is problem-agnostic, meaning that a pre-trained diffusion model can be applied to various inverse problems without fine-tuning. In experiments, it achieved high performance on both blind image deblurring and vocal dereverberation tasks, despite the use of simple generic priors for the underlying linear operators.

paragraphs: A linear inverse problem asks for an underlying signal given noisy measurements produced by a linear transformation. Diffusion models can provide useful prior information about plausible signals, but existing approaches discussed here require that transformation to be known. GibbsDDRM extends diffusion-based restoration to the blind setting, where the measurement operator is also unknown.

The method builds a joint probability distribution over the signal, its measurements, and the unknown operator. A pretrained diffusion model supplies the signal prior. An efficient variant of Gibbs sampling then draws from the posterior, allowing uncertainty about the signal and the measurement process to be handled within the same inference procedure.

The framework can reuse a pretrained diffusion model across different inverse problems without fine-tuning it for each problem. Experiments on blind image deblurring and vocal dereverberation report high performance even with simple, generic priors for the operators. These findings support the usefulness of jointly inferring the signal and its corruption process while retaining the information already captured by a pretrained diffusion model.
summary.tldr: GibbsDDRM combines a pretrained diffusion prior with posterior sampling to restore signals when the linear measurement operator is unknown.

title: GibbsDDRM: A Partially Collapsed Gibbs Sampler for Solving Blind Inverse Problems with Denoising Diffusion Restoration

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) based methods have achieved impressive performance on node clustering task. However, they are designed on the homophilic assumption of graph and clustering on heterophilic graph is overlooked. Due to the lack of labels, it is impossible to first identify a graph as homophilic or heterophilic before a suitable GNN model can be found. Hence, clustering on real-world graph with various levels of homophily poses a new challenge to the graph research community. To fill this gap, we propose a novel graph clustering method, which contains three key components: graph reconstruction, a mixed filter, and dual graph clustering network. To be graph-agnostic, we empirically construct two graphs which are high homophily and heterophily from each data. The mixed filter based on the new graphs extracts both low-frequency and high-frequency information. To reduce the adverse coupling between node attribute and topological structure, we separately map them into two subspaces in dual graph clustering network. Extensive experiments on 11 benchmark graphs demonstrate our promising performance. In particular, our method dominates others on heterophilic graphs.

paragraphs: Many graph clustering methods assume that connected nodes tend to belong to similar groups, a property called homophily. Graphs with connections between unlike nodes challenge that assumption. In an unlabeled clustering problem, the authors argue that one cannot first identify the graph’s homophily type and then choose an appropriate model, motivating a method that accommodates different connection patterns.

Their method reconstructs two graphs from each dataset: one with high homophily and one with high heterophily. A mixed filter uses these structures to extract both low-frequency and high-frequency information, capturing different patterns of variation across nodes. A dual clustering network then maps node attributes and graph structure into separate subspaces to reduce harmful coupling between those information sources.

Experiments cover 11 benchmark graphs and report promising overall performance, with particularly strong results on heterophilic graphs. The approach matters because it builds multiple views of connectivity into the clustering process instead of relying on one homophily assumption. The findings support this reconstruction-and-filtering strategy across the tested graphs, especially where conventional similarity-based connections are a poor fit.
summary.tldr: Reconstructing complementary graph structures helps cluster nodes across different homophily levels, with especially strong reported results on heterophilic graphs.

title: Beyond Homophily: Reconstructing Structure for Graph-agnostic Clustering

abstract: Instruction-tuned LMs such as ChatGPT, FLAN, and InstructGPT are finetuned on datasets that contain user-submitted examples, e.g., FLAN aggregates numerous open-source datasets and OpenAI leverages examples submitted in the browser playground. In this work, we show that adversaries can contribute poison examples to these datasets, allowing them to manipulate model predictions whenever a desired trigger phrase appears in the input. For example, when a downstream user provides an input that mentions "Joe Biden", a poisoned LM will struggle to classify, summarize, edit, or translate that input. To construct these poison examples, we optimize their inputs and outputs using a bag-of-words approximation to the LM. We evaluate our method on open-source instruction-tuned LMs. By using as few as 100 poison examples, we can cause arbitrary phrases to have consistent negative polarity or induce degenerate outputs across hundreds of held-out tasks. Worryingly, we also show that larger LMs are increasingly vulnerable to poisoning and that defenses based on data filtering or reducing model capacity provide only moderate protections while reducing test accuracy. Notice: This paper contains tasks with obscene content.

This paper studies how adversarial contributions to those datasets can change a language model’s behavior. The targeted effect appears when a chosen trigger phrase occurs in a later input, potentially disrupting several kinds of tasks.

The authors construct poisoned examples by optimizing their inputs and outputs using a bag-of-words approximation to the language model. They evaluate the approach on open-source instruction-tuned models. With as few as 100 poisoned examples, the reported attacks make arbitrary phrases consistently negative or produce degenerate outputs across hundreds of held-out tasks.

The experiments also find increasing vulnerability in larger models. Defenses based on filtering training data or reducing model capacity provide only moderate protection while lowering test accuracy. These findings show that a small contribution to instruction-tuning data can have effects extending across many downstream tasks. They also identify a tradeoff in the evaluated defenses: reducing the attack’s impact comes with a loss in ordinary task performance.
summary.tldr: As few as 100 poisoned instruction-tuning examples cause trigger-dependent failures across many held-out tasks in the evaluated open-source language models.

title: Poisoning Language Models During Instruction Tuning

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a powerful approach for acquiring a good-performing policy. However, learning diverse skills is challenging in RL due to the commonly used Gaussian policy parameterization. We propose Diverse Skill Learning (Di-SkilL), an RL method for learning diverse skills using Mixture of Experts, where each expert formalizes a skill as a contextual motion primitive. Di-SkilL optimizes each expert and its associate context distribution to a maximum entropy objective that incentivizes learning diverse skills in similar contexts. The per-expert context distribution enables automatic curricula learning, allowing each expert to focus on its best-performing sub-region of the context space. To overcome hard discontinuities and multi-modalities without any prior knowledge of the environment’s unknown context probability space, we leverage energy-based models to represent the per-expert context distributions and demonstrate how we can efficiently train them using the standard policy gradient objective. We show on challenging robot simulation tasks that Di-SkilL can learn diverse and performant skills.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning policy can perform well without acquiring several distinct ways to act. This paper links that difficulty to the commonly used Gaussian policy representation and introduces Di-SkilL, a method that represents skills through a mixture of experts. Each expert describes a contextual motion primitive, connecting a particular skill to the circumstances in which it operates.

Di-SkilL jointly optimizes each expert and the distribution of contexts it encounters. A maximum entropy objective encourages diverse skills even in similar contexts. The separate context distributions also create automatic curricula: each expert can concentrate on the part of the context space where it performs best. Skill specialization and the selection of learning situations are therefore developed together.

The method uses energy-based models to represent context distributions with abrupt changes or multiple modes, without prior knowledge of the environment’s context probability space. The authors show how to train these distributions using a standard policy gradient objective. Results on challenging robot simulation tasks demonstrate that Di-SkilL can acquire skills that are both varied and effective.
summary.tldr: Di-SkilL combines expert policies with automatic curricula to learn diverse, effective skills in robot simulations.

title: Acquiring Diverse Skills using Curriculum Reinforcement Learning with Mixture of Experts

abstract: In this paper, we investigate the impact of test-time adversarial attacks on linear regression models and determine the optimal level of robustness that any model can reach while maintaining a given level of standard predictive performance (accuracy). Through quantitative estimates, we uncover fundamental tradeoffs between adversarial robustness and accuracy in different regimes. We obtain a precise characterization which distinguishes between regimes where robustness is achievable without hurting standard accuracy and regimes where a tradeoff might be unavoidable. Our findings are empirically confirmed with simple experiments that represent a variety of settings. This work covers feature covariance matrices and attack norms of any nature, extending previous works in this area.

We obtain a precise characterization which distinguishes between regimes where robustness is achievable without hurting standard accuracy and regimes where a tradeoff might be unavoidable. Our findings are empirically confirmed with simple experiments that represent a variety of settings. This work covers feature covariance matrices and attack norms of any nature, extending previous works in this area.

paragraphs: A regression model can predict accurately on ordinary inputs yet respond poorly when an adversary perturbs them at test time. This paper studies that tension in linear regression. It asks how much adversarial robustness is attainable while keeping standard predictive performance at a specified level, making the relationship between the two objectives quantitative.

The analysis distinguishes settings in which robustness can be obtained without sacrificing ordinary accuracy from settings in which a tradeoff might be unavoidable. That distinction matters because it avoids treating robustness as carrying the same accuracy cost in every problem. The conclusions instead depend on which regime the regression problem occupies.

The framework accommodates arbitrary feature covariance matrices and attack norms. These describe, respectively, relationships among input features and how allowed perturbations are measured. This broadens the coverage of earlier work. Simple experiments spanning several settings confirm the theoretical findings empirically. The contribution is therefore a more precise account of attainable robustness, including when preserving standard accuracy is compatible with it.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes achievable robustness in linear regression and separates regimes with no accuracy cost from those where a tradeoff may be unavoidable.

title: Precise Accuracy / Robustness Tradeoffs in Regression: Case of General Norms

abstract: The remarkable generalization ability of neural networks is usually attributed to the implicit bias of SGD, which often yields models with lower complexity using simpler (e.g. linear) and low-rank features. Recent works have provided empirical and theoretical evidence for the bias of particular variants of SGD (such as label noise SGD) toward flatter regions of the loss landscape. Despite the folklore intuition that flat solutions are ’simple’, the connection with the simplicity of the final trained model (e.g. low-rank) is not well understood. In this work, we take a step toward bridging this gap by studying the simplicity structure that arises from minimizers of the sharpness for a class of two-layer neural networks. We show that, for any high dimensional training data and certain activations, with small enough step size, label noise SGD always converges to a network that replicates a single linear feature across all neurons; thereby implying a simple rank one feature matrix. To obtain this result, our main technical contribution is to show that label noise SGD always minimizes the sharpness on the manifold of models with zero loss for two-layer networks. Along the way, we discover a novel property — a local geodesic convexity — of the trace of Hessian of the loss at approximate stationary points on the manifold of zero loss, which links sharpness to the geometry of the manifold. This tool may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Flat regions of a neural network's loss landscape are often associated with simple learned models, but the connection requires explanation. This paper studies that relationship for a class of two-layer networks. It asks how minimizing sharpness shapes the features learned by stochastic gradient descent with label noise.

For high-dimensional training data, certain activation functions, and a sufficiently small step size, the authors show that label-noise SGD converges to a network whose neurons repeat one linear feature. The resulting feature matrix has rank one. Under these stated conditions, simplicity is therefore expressed as a precise structural property of the learned representation.

The proof identifies a local geodesic convexity property of the loss Hessian's trace near approximate stationary points on that manifold. This connects sharpness to the geometry of zero-loss solutions and supplies a route from the training dynamics to the rank-one conclusion.
summary.tldr: For a specified class of two-layer networks and sufficiently small steps, label-noise SGD minimizes sharpness and converges to rank-one linear features.

title: Simplicity Bias via Global Convergence of Sharpness Minimization

abstract: Differentiable processes have proven an invaluable tool for machine learning (ML) in scientific and engineering settings, but most ML libraries are not primarily designed for such applications. We present $\Phi_\textrm{Flow}$, a Python toolkit that seamlessly integrates with PyTorch, TensorFlow, Jax and NumPy, simplifying the process of writing differentiable simulation code at every step. $\Phi_\textrm{Flow}$ provides many essential features that go beyond the capabilities of the base libraries, such as differential operators, boundary conditions, the ability to write dimensionality-agnostic code, floating-point precision management, fully differentiable preconditioned (sparse) linear solves, automatic matrix generation via function tracing, integration of SciPy optimizers, simulation vectorization, and visualization tools. At the same time, $\Phi_\textrm{Flow}$ inherits all important traits of the base ML libraries, such as GPU / TPU support, just-in-time compilation, and automatic differentiation. Put together, these features drastically simplify scientific code like PDE or ODE solvers on grids or unstructured meshes, and $\Phi_\textrm{Flow}$ even includes out-of-the-box support for fluid simulations. $\Phi_\textrm{Flow}$ has been used in various publications and as a ground-truth solver in multiple scientific data sets.

paragraphs: ΦFlow is a Python toolkit for writing simulations that support differentiation and integrate with PyTorch, TensorFlow, Jax, and NumPy. Its motivation is that scientific and engineering simulations need capabilities that general machine learning libraries do not primarily target. The toolkit supplies those capabilities while retaining the computational features of its underlying libraries.

Its tools include differential operators, boundary conditions, precision management, and code that works across different numbers of dimensions. It also provides differentiable preconditioned sparse linear solves, automatic matrix construction through function tracing, SciPy optimizer integration, simulation vectorization, and visualization. Together, these features address both the mathematical operations and the practical programming work involved in implementing simulations.

The resulting framework simplifies differential equation solvers on grids and unstructured meshes, with built-in support for fluid simulation. It retains automatic differentiation, just-in-time compilation, and GPU or TPU support through the base libraries. The abstract also reports use in research publications and as a ground-truth solver for scientific datasets, establishing applications beyond the toolkit's feature list.
summary.tldr: ΦFlow adds scientific simulation tools to major numerical and machine learning libraries while retaining differentiation and hardware acceleration.

title: $\bfΦ_\textrmFlow$: Differentiable Simulations for PyTorch, TensorFlow and Jax

abstract: This paper addresses the complex issue of resource-constrained scheduling, an NP-hard problem that spans critical areas including chip design and high-performance computing. Traditional scheduling methods often stumble over scalability and applicability challenges. We propose a novel approach using a differentiable combinatorial scheduling framework, utilizing Gumbel-Softmax differentiable sampling technique. This new technical allows for a fully differentiable formulation of linear programming (LP) based scheduling, extending its application to a broader range of LP formulations. To encode inequality constraints for scheduling tasks, we introduce constrained Gumbel Trick, which adeptly encodes arbitrary inequality constraints. Consequently, our method facilitates an efficient and scalable scheduling via gradient descent without the need for training data. Comparative evaluations on both synthetic and real-world benchmarks highlight our capability to significantly improve the optimization efficiency of scheduling, surpassing state-of-the-art solutions offered by commercial and open-source solvers such as CPLEX, Gurobi, and CP-SAT in the majority of the designs.

paragraphs: Resource-constrained scheduling must choose arrangements that respect limited resources while optimizing a scheduling objective. Such problems arise in chip design and high-performance computing and are NP-hard. This paper addresses the scalability and applicability difficulties of existing methods by making a combinatorial scheduling formulation accessible to gradient-based optimization.

A central addition is the constrained Gumbel Trick, which encodes arbitrary inequality constraints. Handling these constraints within the formulation broadens the range of scheduling problems to which the differentiable approach can be applied.

The resulting method optimizes schedules through gradient descent without requiring training data. This matters because the gradients serve the scheduling problem directly, rather than depending on a collection of previously solved examples. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world benchmarks report improved optimization efficiency over CPLEX, Gurobi, and CP-SAT in the majority of tested designs. The empirical claim concerns those comparisons, while the general contribution is a differentiable route to constrained scheduling.
summary.tldr: A constrained differentiable sampling framework enables gradient-based scheduling without training data.

title: Differentiable Combinatorial Scheduling at Scale

abstract: We develop two density ratio estimation (DRE) methods with robustness to outliers. These are based on the divergence with a weight function to weaken the adverse effects of outliers. One is based on the Unnormalized Kullback-Leibler divergence, called Weighted DRE, and its optimization is a convex problem. The other is based on the γ-divergence, called γ-DRE, which improves a normalizing term problem of Weighted DRE. Its optimization is a DC (Difference of Convex functions) problem and needs more computation than a convex problem. These methods have doubly strong robustness, which means robustness to the heavy contamination of both the reference and target distributions. Numerical experiments show that our proposals are more robust than the previous methods.

The other is based on the γ-divergence, called γ-DRE, which improves a normalizing term problem of Weighted DRE. paragraphs: Density ratio estimation measures how the probability of an observation differs between a reference distribution and a target distribution. Outliers can distort that comparison. This paper develops two estimators designed to remain robust even when both distributions contain heavy contamination, a property the authors call doubly strong robustness.

Both methods use divergences with a weighting function that reduces the adverse influence of outliers. The first, Weighted DRE, is based on unnormalized Kullback-Leibler divergence and leads to a convex optimization problem. The second, gamma-DRE, uses gamma-divergence to improve a problem involving Weighted DRE's normalizing term. Its optimization instead takes the form of a difference of convex functions and requires more computation.

The methods therefore offer different computational tradeoffs within the same robustness objective. Numerical experiments show greater robustness than previous approaches. The key finding concerns contamination on both sides of the ratio: the methods address settings where neither the reference data nor the target data can be treated as free of substantial outlier effects.
summary.tldr: Two weighted density ratio estimators improve robustness to heavy contamination in both reference and target distributions, with different computational costs.

title: Density Ratio Estimation with Doubly Strong Robustness

abstract: Imagine generating a city’s electricity demand pattern based on weather, the presence of an electric vehicle, and location, which could be used for capacity planning during a winter freeze. Such real-world time series are often enriched with paired heterogeneous contextual metadata (e.g., weather and location). Current approaches to time series generation often ignore this paired metadata. Additionally, the heterogeneity in metadata poses several practical challenges in adapting existing conditional generation approaches from the image, audio, and video domains to the time series domain. To address this gap, we introduce TIME WEAVER, a novel diffusion-based model that leverages the heterogeneous metadata in the form of categorical, continuous, and even time-variant variables to significantly improve time series generation. Additionally, we show that naive extensions of standard evaluation metrics from the image to the time series domain are insufficient. These metrics do not penalize conditional generation approaches for their poor specificity in reproducing the metadata-specific features in the generated time series. Thus, we innovate a novel evaluation metric that accurately captures the specificity of conditional generation and the realism of the generated time series. We show that TIME WEAVER outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks, such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), by up to 30% in downstream classification tasks on real-world energy, medical, air quality, and traffic datasets.

paragraphs: Time series often come with context that helps explain their patterns, such as location or changing weather. Generating useful synthetic sequences requires accounting for that context, but metadata can combine categories, numerical values, and variables that change over time. TIME WEAVER is a diffusion model designed to use this heterogeneous information.

The paper also addresses how conditional generation should be evaluated. A generated sequence may look realistic while failing to reflect the metadata it was given. The authors show that straightforward adaptations of image-generation metrics do not adequately penalize this failure. They introduce an evaluation metric that captures both realism and specificity to the conditioning information.

Experiments cover real-world energy, medical, air quality, and traffic datasets. TIME WEAVER outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks, including generative adversarial networks, by up to 30% in downstream classification tasks. That reported improvement concerns the evaluated downstream tasks. The broader contribution pairs a model for varied contextual inputs with an evaluation method that checks whether generated sequences actually express their requested context.
summary.tldr: TIME WEAVER generates time series from heterogeneous metadata and introduces an evaluation metric for realism and contextual specificity.

title: Time Weaver: A Conditional Time Series Generation Model

abstract: The usage of Rational Speech Acts (RSA) framework has been successful in building pragmatic program synthesizers that return programs which, in addition to being logically consistent with user-generated examples, account for the fact that a user chooses their examples informatively. We present a general method of amortizing the slow, exact RSA synthesizer. Our method first compiles a communication dataset of partially ranked programs by querying the exact RSA synthesizer. It then distills a global ranking – a single, total ordering of all programs, to approximate the partial rankings from this dataset. This global ranking is then used at inference time to rank multiple logically consistent candidate programs generated from a fast, non-pragmatic synthesizer. Experiments on two program synthesis domains using our ranking method resulted in orders of magnitudes of speed ups compared to the exact RSA synthesizer, while being more accurate than a non-pragmatic synthesizer. Finally, we prove that in the special case of synthesis from a single example, this approximation is exact.

paragraphs: Program synthesis from examples can leave several programs that all satisfy the examples provided. A pragmatic synthesizer also considers that a person may have chosen those examples to communicate something informative. The Rational Speech Acts framework supports this reasoning, but computing its exact answer is slow.

The authors transfer some of that expensive reasoning into a reusable ranking. They query the exact synthesizer to collect partial rankings of programs, then distill these into one total ordering. At inference time, a fast synthesizer generates logically consistent candidates, and the learned ordering decides which candidates to prefer. This shifts work from repeated exact reasoning into preparation that can be reused.

Experiments in two synthesis domains report orders-of-magnitude speedups over exact pragmatic synthesis and greater accuracy than a non-pragmatic synthesizer. The authors also prove that the approximation is exact when synthesis uses a single example. That special-case result gives a precise guarantee alongside the broader empirical evidence for the ranking approach.
summary.tldr: A reusable program ranking approximates pragmatic synthesis, delivering large empirical speedups and exactness in the single-example case.

title: Amortizing Pragmatic Program Synthesis with Rankings

abstract: We propose a method to improve the efficiency and accuracy of amortized Bayesian inference by leveraging universal symmetries in the joint probabilistic model of parameters and data. In a nutshell, we invert Bayes’ theorem and estimate the marginal likelihood based on approximate representations of the joint model. Upon perfect approximation, the marginal likelihood is constant across all parameter values by definition. However, errors in approximate inference lead to undesirable variance in the marginal likelihood estimates across different parameter values. We penalize violations of this symmetry with a self-consistency loss which significantly improves the quality of approximate inference in low data regimes and can be used to augment the training of popular neural density estimators. We apply our method to a number of synthetic problems and realistic scientific models, discovering notable advantages in the context of both neural posterior and likelihood approximation.

In a nutshell, we invert Bayes’ theorem and estimate the marginal likelihood based on approximate representations of the joint model. Upon perfect approximation, the marginal likelihood is constant across all parameter values by definition. However, errors in approximate inference lead to undesirable variance in the marginal likelihood estimates across different parameter values. We penalize violations of this symmetry with a self-consistency loss which significantly improves the quality of approximate inference in low data regimes and can be used to augment the training of popular neural density estimators. We apply our method to a number of synthetic problems and realistic scientific models, discovering notable advantages in the context of both neural posterior and likelihood approximation.

paragraphs: Amortized Bayesian inference uses learned approximations to make repeated inference more efficient. This paper improves those approximations by checking a consistency property of the joint model of parameters and observations. The property supplies an additional training signal, especially when data available for learning are limited.

The authors rearrange Bayes' theorem to estimate the marginal likelihood from approximate model components. For fixed observations, this quantity should be the same regardless of which parameter values are used in the calculation. Imperfect approximations can instead produce different estimates across parameter values. A self-consistency loss penalizes this unwanted variation.

The loss can augment training for popular neural density estimators. Across synthetic problems and realistic scientific models, the authors report advantages for both posterior and likelihood approximation, with significant improvements in low-data settings. The method's central benefit is to make learned probability models respect an identity they should already satisfy, turning an internal agreement requirement into a practical source of better inference.
summary.tldr: A Bayes-based self-consistency loss improves neural posterior and likelihood approximations, particularly when training data are scarce.

title: Leveraging Self-Consistency for Data-Efficient Amortized Bayesian Inference

abstract: Maximal ancestral graph (MAG) is a prevalent graphical model to characterize causal relations in the presence of latent variables including latent confounders and selection variables. Given observational data, only a Markov equivalence class (MEC) of MAGs is identifiable if without some additional assumptions. Due to this fact, MAG listing, listing all the MAGs in the MEC, is usually demanded in many downstream tasks. To the best of our knowledge, there are no relevant methods for MAG listing other than brute force in the literature. In this paper, we propose the first brute-force-free MAG listing method, by determining the local structures of each vertex recursively. We provide the graphical characterization for each valid local transformation of a vertex, and present sound and complete rules to incorporate the valid local transformation in the presence of latent confounders and selection variables. Based on these components, our method can efficiently output all the MAGs in the MEC with no redundance, that is, every intermediate graph in the recursive process is necessary for the MAG listing task. The empirical analysis demonstrates the superiority of our proposed method on efficiency and effectiveness.

paragraphs: Maximal ancestral graphs represent causal relationships when hidden confounders and selection variables may be present. Observational data alone generally identify a Markov equivalence class rather than a single graph unless additional assumptions are made. Downstream analysis can therefore require listing all graphs in that class, preserving the causal possibilities that the observations do not distinguish.

The proposed algorithm constructs this list by recursively determining the local structure around each vertex. The authors characterize which local transformations are valid and provide sound and complete rules for incorporating them. These rules explicitly accommodate latent confounders and selection variables, so the construction respects the setting that makes maximal ancestral graphs useful.

The method outputs every graph in the equivalence class without redundancy. The authors further state that every intermediate graph generated by the recursive procedure is necessary for the listing task. This avoids the brute-force approach they identify as the previous available option. Empirical analysis supports improvements in efficiency and effectiveness, making systematic exploration of observationally indistinguishable causal graphs more practical.
summary.tldr: A recursive algorithm lists all maximal ancestral graphs in a Markov equivalence class without brute-force enumeration or redundant intermediate graphs.

title: An Efficient Maximal Ancestral Graph Listing Algorithm

abstract: Selecting high-quality pre-training data is important for creating capable language models, but existing methods rely on simple heuristics. We introduce QuRating, a method for selecting pre-training data that can capture human intuitions about data quality. In this paper, we investigate four qualities - writing style, required expertise, facts & trivia, and educational value - and find that LLMs are able to discern these qualities, especially when making pairwise judgments of texts. We train a QuRater model to learn scalar ratings from pairwise judgments, and use it to annotate a 260B training corpus with quality ratings for each of the four criteria. In our experiments, we select 30B tokens according to the different quality ratings and train 1.3B-parameter language models on the selected data. We find that it is important to balance quality and diversity. When we sample using quality ratings as logits over documents, our models obtain lower perplexity and stronger in-context learning performance than baselines. Our best model is based on educational value and performs similarly to a model trained with uniform sampling for 50% more steps. Beyond data selection, we use the quality ratings to construct a training curriculum which improves performance without changing the training dataset. We extensively analyze the quality ratings and discuss their characteristics, biases, and wider implications.

paragraphs: QuRating investigates how to select language-model pretraining data using judgments that reflect human ideas of quality. These results show two uses for quality judgments: deciding which documents to sample and shaping training over a fixed collection. The paper additionally examines the ratings’ characteristics, biases, and implications.
summary.tldr: QuRating turns pairwise quality judgments into document ratings that improve data sampling and training curricula while balancing quality with diversity.

title: QuRating: Selecting High-Quality Data for Training Language Models

abstract: Graph transformers extend global self-attention to graph-structured data, achieving notable success in graph learning. Recently, Relative Random Walk Probabilities (RRWP) has been found to further enhance their predictive power by encoding both structural and positional information into the edge representation. However, RRWP cannot always distinguish between edges that belong to different local graph patterns, which reduces its ability to capture the full structural complexity of graphs. This work introduces Simple Path Structural Encoding (SPSE), a novel method that utilizes simple path counts for edge encoding. We show theoretically and experimentally that SPSE overcomes the limitations of RRWP, providing a richer representation of graph structures, particularly in capturing local cyclic patterns. To make SPSE computationally tractable, we propose an efficient approximate algorithm for simple path counting. SPSE demonstrates significant performance improvements over RRWP on various benchmarks, including molecular and long-range graph datasets, achieving statistically significant gains in discriminative tasks. These results pose SPSE as a powerful edge encoding alternative for enhancing the expressivity of graph transformers.

paragraphs: Graph transformers need structural information alongside attention to distinguish different graph patterns. Relative Random Walk Probabilities, or RRWP, provide such information through edge representations. However, the authors identify cases where RRWP cannot distinguish edges belonging to different local structures, limiting how much graph detail those representations communicate.

The proposed Simple Path Structural Encoding, or SPSE, instead encodes edges using counts of simple paths, which do not revisit nodes. The authors show theoretically and experimentally that this captures structural distinctions missed by RRWP, particularly local cyclic patterns. Because counting simple paths can be computationally demanding, they also develop an efficient approximation algorithm to make the encoding practical.

SPSE improves performance over RRWP on several benchmarks, including molecular graphs and datasets requiring long-range graph reasoning. The paper reports statistically significant gains in discriminative tasks. These results indicate that changing the structural information supplied to a graph transformer can improve its predictive ability: a richer edge encoding helps expose patterns that the previous representation could leave indistinguishable.
summary.tldr: SPSE uses approximate simple-path counts to give graph transformers richer structural information and improve performance over random-walk edge encodings.

title: Simple Path Structural Encoding for Graph Transformers

abstract: Simulation modeling offers a flexible approach to constructing high-fidelity synthetic representations of complex real-world systems. However, the increased complexity of such models introduces additional complications, for example when carrying out statistical inference procedures. This has motivated a large and growing literature on likelihood-free or simulation-based inference methods, which approximate (e.g., Bayesian) inference without assuming access to the simulator’s intractable likelihood function. A hitherto neglected problem in the simulation-based Bayesian inference literature is the challenge of constructing minimally informative reference priors for complex simulation models. Such priors maximise an expected Kullback-Leibler distance from the prior to the posterior, thereby influencing posterior inferences minimally and enabling an “objective” approach to Bayesian inference that does not necessitate the incorporation of strong subjective prior beliefs. In this paper, we propose and test a selection of likelihood-free methods for learning reference priors for simulation models, using variational approximations to these priors and a variety of mutual information estimators. Our experiments demonstrate that good approximations to reference priors for simulation models are in this way attainable, providing a first step towards the development of likelihood-free objective Bayesian inference procedures.

paragraphs: Complex simulators can generate realistic synthetic observations even when the probability of a particular observation cannot be evaluated directly. Simulation-based inference addresses this difficulty, but Bayesian inference still requires a prior. This paper studies how to construct reference priors when the simulator's likelihood is unavailable.

Reference priors are designed to be minimally informative in a specific statistical sense. They maximize an expected Kullback–Leibler separation between prior and posterior, supporting inference without requiring strong subjective prior beliefs. The authors propose several likelihood-free learning methods that represent these priors through variational approximations and use different mutual information estimators to guide their construction.

Experiments show that the proposed methods can obtain good approximations to reference priors for simulation models. The contribution extends simulation-based inference to a prior-selection problem that has received comparatively little attention. The authors frame it as an initial step toward likelihood-free objective Bayesian procedures: the evidence supports the feasibility of learning these priors, rather than a completed solution for every complex simulator.
summary.tldr: The paper learns approximate reference priors for simulators using variational representations and mutual information estimation without evaluating likelihoods.

title: Learning Likelihood-Free Reference Priors

abstract: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection (UAD) plays a crucial role in identifying abnormal patterns within data without labeled examples, holding significant practical implications across various domains. Although the individual contributions of representation learning and clustering to anomaly detection are well-established, their interdependencies remain under-explored due to the absence of a unified theoretical framework. Consequently, their collective potential to enhance anomaly detection performance remains largely untapped. To bridge this gap, in this paper, we propose a novel probabilistic mixture model for anomaly detection to establish a theoretical connection among representation learning, clustering, and anomaly detection. By maximizing a novel anomaly-aware data likelihood, representation learning and clustering can effectively reduce the adverse impact of anomalous data and collaboratively benefit anomaly detection. Meanwhile, a theoretically substantiated anomaly score is naturally derived from this framework. Lastly, drawing inspiration from gravitational analysis in physics, we have devised an improved anomaly score that more effectively harnesses the combined power of representation learning and clustering. Extensive experiments, involving 17 baseline methods across 30 diverse datasets, validate the effectiveness and generalization capability of the proposed method, surpassing state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Unsupervised anomaly detection identifies unusual data without labeled examples of abnormalities. Representation learning and clustering both help, but their interaction is less clearly understood. This paper introduces a probabilistic mixture model that connects them with anomaly detection in one theoretical framework, making their joint contribution an explicit part of the model.

The training objective maximizes an anomaly-aware likelihood. Its purpose is to reduce the disruptive effect of anomalous observations while allowing representation learning and clustering to improve detection together. The framework also yields a theoretically supported anomaly score, connecting the way the model is trained with the way it judges whether a point is unusual.

The authors additionally develop an improved score inspired by gravitational analysis in physics to make better use of the learned representations and clusters. Experiments compare against 17 baseline methods across 30 datasets and report performance above state-of-the-art approaches. The results support both effectiveness and generalization across the tested datasets, showing practical value in treating representation learning, clustering, and scoring as connected parts of the detection problem.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic mixture framework jointly connects representation learning, clustering, and anomaly scoring, improving detection across 30 evaluated datasets.

title: Towards a Unified Framework of Clustering-based Anomaly Detection

abstract: Graph Transformers (GTs) have demonstrated remarkable performance in graph representation learning over popular graph neural networks (GNNs). However, self-attention, the core module of GTs, preserves only low-frequency signals in graph features, leading to ineffectiveness in capturing other important signals like high-frequency ones. Some recent GT models help alleviate this issue, but their flexibility and expressiveness are still limited since the filters they learn are fixed on predefined graph spectrum or spectral order. To tackle this challenge, we propose a Graph Fourier Kolmogorov-Arnold Transformer (GrokFormer), a novel GT model that learns highly expressive spectral filters with adaptive graph spectrum and spectral order through a Fourier series modeling over learnable activation functions. We demonstrate theoretically and empirically that the proposed GrokFormer filter offers better expressiveness than other spectral methods. Comprehensive experiments on 10 real-world node classification datasets across various domains, scales, and graph properties, as well as 5 graph classification datasets, show that GrokFormer outperforms state-of-the-art GTs and GNNs. Our code is available at https://github.com/GGA23/GrokFormer.

paragraphs: Graph transformers use attention to learn from relationships among graph elements. The paper identifies a spectral limitation: their attention preserves low-frequency feature signals while failing to capture other important signals, including high-frequency ones. Recent approaches partly address this issue, but their filters remain constrained by a predefined graph spectrum or spectral order.

GrokFormer introduces spectral filters whose graph spectrum and order can adapt during learning. It builds these filters through Fourier-series modeling over learnable activation functions. The purpose is to give the model a more expressive way to select and combine graph signals, rather than restricting its filters to a fixed spectral design.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical evidence that these filters are more expressive than other spectral methods. Evaluations cover ten real-world node-classification datasets and five graph-classification datasets, with reported improvements over state-of-the-art graph transformers and graph neural networks. The range of domains, scales, and graph properties makes the experiments relevant to whether this added spectral flexibility helps across varied graph-learning settings.
summary.tldr: GrokFormer learns adaptive spectral filters to capture graph signals that conventional graph-transformer attention can miss.

title: GrokFormer: Graph Fourier Kolmogorov-Arnold Transformers

abstract: High-dimensional imaging of neural activity, such as widefield calcium and functional ultrasound imaging, provide a rich source of information for understanding the relationship between brain activity and behavior. Accurately modeling neural dynamics in these modalities is crucial for understanding this relationship but is hindered by the high-dimensionality, complex spatiotemporal dependencies, and prevalent behaviorally irrelevant dynamics in these modalities. Existing dynamical models often employ preprocessing steps to obtain low-dimensional representations from neural image modalities. However, this process can discard behaviorally relevant information and miss spatiotemporal structure. We propose SBIND, a novel data-driven deep learning framework to model spatiotemporal dependencies in neural images and disentangle their behaviorally relevant dynamics from other neural dynamics. We validate SBIND on widefield imaging datasets, and show its extension to functional ultrasound imaging, a recent modality whose dynamical modeling has largely remained unexplored. We find that our model effectively identifies both local and long-range spatial dependencies across the brain while also dissociating behaviorally relevant neural dynamics. Doing so, SBIND outperforms existing models in neural-behavioral prediction. Overall, SBIND provides a versatile tool for investigating the neural mechanisms underlying behavior using imaging modalities.

paragraphs: Neural imaging records activity across many locations and times, but only some of those patterns relate to the behavior being studied. Modeling these recordings is difficult because spatial relationships, temporal changes, and behaviorally irrelevant activity are intertwined. Compressing images into smaller representations before modeling can simplify the task, yet it can also discard useful information and obscure spatial and temporal structure.

The paper introduces SBIND, a deep learning framework that models dependencies within neural images while separating behaviorally relevant dynamics from other activity. Its central aim is to make this separation part of dynamical modeling, so that a representation of changing brain activity also retains the patterns needed to explain or predict behavior.

The authors validate SBIND on widefield imaging and demonstrate an extension to functional ultrasound imaging. They report that it captures both nearby and long-range spatial dependencies, distinguishes behavior-related dynamics, and improves neural-behavioral prediction over existing models. These findings support its use as a tool for investigating how distributed patterns of neural activity relate to behavior.
summary.tldr: SBIND models neural images over space and time while separating behavior-related activity, improving neural-behavioral prediction.

title: Dynamical Modeling of Behaviorally Relevant Spatiotemporal Patterns in Neural Imaging Data

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in generation tasks, yet their causal attention mechanisms limit performance in embedding tasks. While bidirectional modeling may enhance embeddings, naively fine-tuning unidirectional models bidirectionally severely degrades generative performance. To investigate this trade-off, we analyze attention weights as dependence indicators and find that bidirectional fine-tuning increases subsequent dependence, impairing unidirectional generation. Through systematic Transformer module evaluations, we discover the FFN layer is least affected by such dependence. Leveraging this discovery, we propose UBMoE-LLM, a novel Uni-Bi-directional Mixture-of-Experts LLM, which integrates the original unidirectional FFN with a bidirectionally fine-tuned FFN via unsupervised contrastive learning. This MoE-based approach enhances embedding performance while preserving robust generation. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets and model scales validate our attention dependence metric and demonstrate UBMoE-LLM’s superior generative quality and reduced hallucination. Code is available at: https://github.com/heiyonghua/ubmoe_llm.

paragraphs: Language generation and embedding tasks benefit from different attention patterns. Causal models only use preceding context, while bidirectional processing can strengthen embeddings by using context on both sides. This paper investigates why directly fine-tuning a causal model bidirectionally can severely damage its ability to generate text.

Using attention weights as indicators of dependence, the authors find that bidirectional fine-tuning increases reliance on subsequent context. That reliance impairs generation in the unidirectional setting. Evaluating Transformer components reveals that the feedforward network layer is least affected by this dependence, motivating a design centered on combining feedforward components.

UBMoE-LLM integrates the original unidirectional feedforward network with a bidirectionally fine-tuned one through unsupervised contrastive learning. The resulting mixture-of-experts model improves embeddings while preserving robust generation. Experiments across datasets and model scales support the attention-dependence metric and show superior generative quality with reduced hallucination. The work connects a diagnosis of incompatible context dependence to an architecture intended to retain benefits from both processing directions.
summary.tldr: UBMoE-LLM combines unidirectional and bidirectionally fine-tuned feedforward experts to improve embeddings while preserving generation quality.

title: What Limits Bidirectional Model’s Generative Capabilities? A Uni-Bi-Directional Mixture-of-Expert Method For Bidirectional Fine-tuning

abstract: Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) has emerged as a promising approach for NP-hard problems. However, prevailing RL-based methods suffer from low sample efficiency due to sparse rewards and underused solutions. We propose Best-anchored and Objective-guided Preference Optimization (BOPO), a training paradigm that leverages solution preferences via objective values. It introduces: (1) a best-anchored preference pair construction for better explore and exploit solutions, and (2) an objective-guided pairwise loss function that adaptively scales gradients via objective differences, removing reliance on reward models or reference policies. Experiments on Job-shop Scheduling Problem (JSP), Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), and Flexible Job-shop Scheduling Problem (FJSP) show BOPO outperforms state-of-the-art neural methods, reducing optimality gaps impressively with efficient inference. BOPO is architecture-agnostic, enabling seamless integration with existing NCO models, and establishes preference optimization as a principled framework for combinatorial optimization.

paragraphs: Neural combinatorial optimization trains models to solve difficult discrete problems such as routing and scheduling. Reinforcement-learning approaches can use training samples inefficiently because rewards are sparse and available solutions are not fully exploited. BOPO turns differences in solution quality into preference comparisons that provide another source of training guidance.

Its best-anchored construction organizes preference pairs around the best solution to support exploration and exploitation. An objective-guided pairwise loss then adjusts gradient strength according to differences in objective values. This makes the learning signal sensitive to how much better one solution is, while avoiding a separate reward model or reference policy.

The authors evaluate BOPO on job-shop scheduling, traveling-salesman, and flexible job-shop scheduling problems. They report smaller optimality gaps than state-of-the-art neural methods, together with efficient inference. Because the training approach is architecture-agnostic, it can be integrated with existing neural optimization models. The stated findings support preference optimization as a useful way to extract more learning value from candidate solutions and their objective scores.
summary.tldr: BOPO trains neural combinatorial solvers using solution preferences whose learning strength reflects differences in objective values.

title: BOPO: Neural Combinatorial Optimization via Best-anchored and Objective-guided Preference Optimization

abstract: Prompt learning is a cutting-edge parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique for pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs). Instead of learning a single text prompt, recent works have revealed that learning diverse text prompts can effectively boost the performances on downstream tasks, as the diverse prompted text features can comprehensively depict the visual concepts from different perspectives. However, diverse prompt learning demands enormous computational resources. This efficiency issue still remains unexplored. To achieve efficient and diverse prompt learning, this paper proposes a novel Surrogate Prompt Learning (SurPL) framework. Instead of learning diverse text prompts, SurPL directly generates the desired prompted text features via a lightweight Surrogate Feature Generator (SFG), thereby avoiding the complex gradient computation procedure of conventional diverse prompt learning. Concretely, based on a basic prompted text feature, SFG can directly and efficiently generate diverse prompted features according to different pre-defined conditional signals. Extensive experiments indicate the effectiveness of the surrogate prompted text features, and show compelling performances and efficiency of SurPL on various benchmarks.

However, diverse prompt learning demands enormous computational resources. This efficiency issue still remains unexplored. To achieve efficient and diverse prompt learning, this paper proposes a novel Surrogate Prompt Learning (SurPL) framework. Instead of learning diverse text prompts, SurPL directly generates the desired prompted text features via a lightweight Surrogate Feature Generator (SFG), thereby avoiding the complex gradient computation procedure of conventional diverse prompt learning. Concretely, based on a basic prompted text feature, SFG can directly and efficiently generate diverse prompted features according to different pre-defined conditional signals. paragraphs: Prompt learning adapts a pretrained vision-language model by learning prompts with relatively few trainable parameters. Using several diverse prompts can describe visual concepts from different perspectives and improve downstream performance. However, learning that diversity can require substantial computation, creating an efficiency problem even within a parameter-efficient adaptation strategy.

Surrogate Prompt Learning changes what the framework generates. Instead of learning many text prompts, it uses a lightweight Surrogate Feature Generator to produce the corresponding prompted text features directly. Starting from a basic prompted feature, the generator receives different predefined conditional signals and produces diverse representations. This avoids the complex gradient computation associated with conventional diverse prompt learning.

Experiments across several benchmarks report effective surrogate features together with strong performance and efficiency. The result supports obtaining useful representational diversity through a smaller feature-generating component. The key distinction is between creating multiple prompts and creating the features those prompts are meant to supply: SurPL focuses computation on the latter while retaining the intended diversity.
summary.tldr: SurPL efficiently produces diverse prompted text features with a lightweight generator instead of learning many separate text prompts.

title: Surrogate Prompt Learning: Towards Efficient and Diverse Prompt Learning for Vision-Language Models

abstract: Online Continual Learning (OCL) models continuously adapt to nonstationary data streams, usually without task information. These settings are complex and many traditional CL methods fail, while online methods (mainly replay-based) suffer from instabilities after the task shift. To address this issue, we formalize replay-based OCL as a second-order online joint optimization with explicit KL-divergence constraints on replay data. We propose Online Curvature-Aware Replay (OCAR) to solve the problem: a method that leverages second-order information of the loss using a K-FAC approximation of the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) to precondition the gradient. The FIM acts as a stabilizer to prevent forgetting while also accelerating the optimization in non-interfering directions. We show how to adapt the estimation of the FIM to a continual setting, stabilizing second-order optimization for non-iid data, uncovering the role of the Tikhonov damping in the stability-plasticity tradeoff. Empirical results show that OCAR outperforms state-of-the-art methods in continual metrics, achieving higher average accuracy throughout the training process in three different benchmarks.

paragraphs: Online continual learning requires a model to adapt as the data stream changes, usually without being told where tasks begin or end. Replay methods revisit stored data to help retain earlier knowledge, but they can become unstable after a task shift. This paper develops a second-order optimization account of that instability.

The authors formulate replay learning as joint online optimization with explicit KL-divergence constraints on replay data. Their method, Online Curvature-Aware Replay, uses a K-FAC approximation of the Fisher Information Matrix to precondition gradients. The curvature information stabilizes updates that could cause forgetting while allowing faster optimization along directions that do not interfere with retained knowledge.

The work also adapts Fisher estimation to changing, non-independent data and explains how Tikhonov damping affects the balance between stability and adaptation. On three benchmarks, OCAR outperforms state-of-the-art methods on continual-learning metrics and achieves higher average accuracy throughout training. The results support using curvature to shape updates as the stream changes, alongside the protection supplied by replay.
summary.tldr: OCAR uses approximate Fisher curvature to stabilize replay-based continual learning and improve average training accuracy on three benchmarks.

title: Online Curvature-Aware Replay: Leveraging $\mathbf2^nd$ Order Information for Online Continual Learning

abstract: Finding a minimum spanning tree (MST) for $n$ points in an arbitrary metric space is a fundamental primitive for hierarchical clustering and many other ML tasks, but this takes $\Omega(n^2)$ time to even approximate. We introduce a framework for metric MSTs that first (1) finds a forest of trees using practical heuristics, and then (2) finds a small weight set of edges to connect disjoint components in the forest into a spanning tree. We prove that optimally solving step (2) still takes $\Omega(n^2)$ time, but we provide a subquadratic 2.62-approximation algorithm. In the spirit of learning-augmented algorithms, we then show that if the heuristic forest found in step (1) overlaps with an optimal MST, we can approximate the original MST problem in subquadratic time, where the approximation factor depends on a measure of overlap. In practice, we find nearly optimal spanning trees for a wide range of metrics, while being orders of magnitude faster than exact algorithms.

paragraphs: A minimum spanning tree connects a collection of points with the smallest possible total edge weight. It is useful for hierarchical clustering, but even approximating it in an arbitrary metric space requires quadratic time in the number of points. This paper investigates how a useful initial collection of connections can change that computational picture.

The proposed framework first uses practical heuristics to build a forest: several separate trees. It then connects those trees using a low-weight set of additional edges. The authors prove that finding the optimal completion still requires quadratic time, but give a subquadratic algorithm with a 2.62 approximation factor for this completion problem.

The guarantee for the original spanning-tree problem depends on how much the initial forest overlaps with an optimal tree. Sufficiently useful heuristic information therefore supports faster approximation, with quality tied to that overlap. In experiments across many metrics, the framework produces nearly optimal trees while running orders of magnitude faster than exact algorithms.
summary.tldr: A two-stage spanning-tree framework uses heuristic forests to enable subquadratic approximation, with guarantees depending on overlap with an optimal tree.

title: Approximate Forest Completion and Learning-Augmented Algorithms for Metric Minimum Spanning Trees

abstract: Effectively utilizing extensive unlabeled high-density EEG data to improve performance in scenarios with limited labeled low-density EEG data presents a significant challenge. In this paper, we address this challenge by formulating it as a graph transfer learning and knowledge distillation problem. We propose a Unified Pre-trained Graph Contrastive Masked Autoencoder Distiller, named EEG-DisGCMAE, to bridge the gap between unlabeled and labeled as well as high- and low-density EEG data. Our approach introduces a novel unified graph self-supervised pre-training paradigm, which seamlessly integrates the graph contrastive pre-training with the graph masked autoencoder pre-training. Furthermore, we propose a graph topology distillation loss function, allowing a lightweight student model trained on low-density data to learn from a teacher model trained on high-density data during pre-training and fine-tuning. This method effectively handles missing electrodes through contrastive distillation. We validate the effectiveness of EEG-DisGCMAE across four classification tasks using two clinical EEG datasets with abundant data.

paragraphs: EEG learning faces a mismatch between abundant unlabeled recordings with many electrodes and practical settings with fewer electrodes and limited labeled data. EEG-DisGCMAE addresses this by treating the transfer between these settings as both a graph-learning problem and a knowledge-distillation problem.

The method combines graph contrastive learning with graph masked-autoencoder learning in one self-supervised pretraining framework. It also introduces a graph topology distillation loss, allowing a lightweight student using low-density recordings to learn from a teacher trained on high-density recordings. This transfer occurs during both pretraining and fine-tuning, linking the two stages rather than restricting knowledge sharing to one.

Contrastive distillation helps the method handle missing electrodes. Evaluation covers four classification tasks across two clinical EEG datasets with abundant data and supports the approach's effectiveness. The contribution is a unified route for transferring information across both label availability and electrode density. It uses the richer recordings to inform a smaller student designed for the lower-density setting, directly addressing the gap between available training resources and the data used by that student.
summary.tldr: EEG-DisGCMAE transfers knowledge from unlabeled, high-density EEG to lightweight models learning from limited labeled, low-density recordings.

title: Pre-Training Graph Contrastive Masked Autoencoders are Strong Distillers for EEG

abstract: Process Reward Models (PRMs) have proven effective at enhancing mathematical reasoning for Large Language Models (LLMs) by leveraging increased inference-time computation. However, they are predominantly trained on mathematical data and their generalizability to non-mathematical domains has not been rigorously studied. In response, this work first shows that current PRMs have poor performance in other domains. To address this limitation, we introduce VersaPRM, a multi-domain PRM trained on synthetic reasoning data generated using our novel data generation and annotation method. VersaPRM achieves consistent performance gains across diverse domains. For instance, in the MMLU-Pro category of Law, VersaPRM via weighted majority voting, achieves a 7.9% performance gain over the majority voting baseline–surpassing Qwen2.5-Math-PRM’s gain of 1.3%. We further contribute to the community by open-sourcing all data, code and models for VersaPRM.

paragraphs: Process reward models assess reasoning processes and can help language models benefit from additional computation when answering questions. Their training has largely centered on mathematics. This paper first examines transfer beyond that area and finds that current process reward models perform poorly in other domains, motivating broader training data.

VersaPRM is trained on synthetic reasoning data spanning multiple domains, produced through a new generation and annotation method. The contribution links the construction of that data to a process reward model intended for more varied reasoning tasks. The reported evaluations show consistent gains across diverse domains.

One example comes from the Law category of MMLU-Pro. With weighted majority voting, VersaPRM achieves a 7.9% performance gain over ordinary majority voting, compared with a 1.3% gain from Qwen2.5-Math-PRM. This comparison illustrates how a model trained for broader reasoning can provide more useful weighting outside mathematics in the tested setting. The authors also release the data, code, and models, making the synthetic-data approach available for further use.
summary.tldr: VersaPRM uses synthetic reasoning data from multiple domains to improve process-based answer evaluation beyond mathematics.

title: VersaPRM: Multi-Domain Process Reward Model via Synthetic Reasoning Data

abstract: Mathematical diagrams have a distinctive structure. Standard feature transforms designed for natural images (e.g., CLIP) fail to process them effectively, limiting their utility in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Current efforts to improve MLLMs have primarily focused on scaling mathematical visual instruction datasets and strengthening LLM backbones, yet fine-grained visual recognition errors remain unaddressed. Our systematic evaluation on the visual grounding capabilities of state-of-the-art MLLMs highlights that fine-grained visual understanding remains a crucial bottleneck in visual mathematical reasoning (GPT-4o exhibits a 70% grounding error rate, and correcting these errors improves reasoning accuracy by 12%). We thus propose a novel approach featuring a geometrically-grounded vision encoder and a feature router that dynamically selects between hierarchical visual feature maps. Our model accurately recognizes visual primitives and generates precise visual prompts aligned with the language model’s reasoning needs. In experiments, PRIMITIVE-Qwen2.5-7B outperforms other 7B models by 12% on MathVerse and is on par with GPT-4V on MathVista. Our findings highlight the need for better fine-grained visual integration in MLLMs. Code is available at github.com/AI4Math-ShanZhang/SVE-Math.

The findings connect improved fine-grained visual processing with stronger diagram-based mathematical performance. They support investing in how diagram structure is encoded and passed to the language model as an important part of improving multimodal mathematical reasoning.
summary.tldr: Primitive Vision improves mathematical diagram understanding through geometry-aware visual encoding and dynamic selection of features for language-model reasoning.

title: Primitive Vision: Improving Diagram Understanding in MLLMs

abstract: With the increase in the number of parameters in large language models, the training process increasingly demands larger volumes of GPU memory. A significant portion of this memory is typically consumed by the optimizer state. To overcome this challenge, recent approaches such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA), low-rank gradient projection (GaLore), and blockwise optimization (BAdam) have been proposed. However, in all these algorithms, the effective rank of the weight updates remains low-rank, which can lead to a substantial loss of information from the gradient. This loss can be critically important, especially during the pre-training stage. In this paper, we introduce FRUGAL (Full-Rank Updates with GrAdient spLitting), a new memory-efficient optimization framework. FRUGAL leverages gradient splitting to perform low-dimensional updates using advanced algorithms (such as Adam), while updates along the remaining directions are executed via state-free methods like SGD or signSGD. Our framework can be integrated with various low-rank update selection techniques, including GaLore and BAdam. We provide theoretical convergence guarantees for our framework when using SGDM for low-dimensional updates and SGD for state-free updates. Additionally, our method consistently outperforms concurrent approaches, achieving state-of-the-art results in pre-training and fine-tuning tasks while balancing memory efficiency and performance metrics.
