paragraphs: MAMBO-G accelerates text-to-image and text-to-video generation by adjusting classifier-free guidance during sampling. Guidance helps steer generation toward the prompt, but the paper observes that standard schedules apply excessively large updates early in the process. Those updates can slow convergence, making high-quality generation require more computation.

The method tracks the ratio between the magnitude of a guidance update and the magnitude of the model’s prediction. It uses that ratio to change the guidance scale dynamically, stabilizing the sampling trajectory and enabling faster convergence. Because this intervention operates during sampling, it requires no additional training and can be integrated into existing generation pipelines.

The reported speedups reach up to three times on Stable Diffusion v3.5 and four times on Lumina. For the 14-billion-parameter Wan2.1 video model, the authors report a twofold speedup while maintaining visual fidelity. These results make the approach especially relevant to expensive video synthesis, where reducing sampling computation can materially change the cost of using a large model.
summary.tldr: MAMBO-G accelerates diffusion generation without training by dynamically scaling guidance to avoid disproportionately large updates.

title: MAMBO-G: Magnitude-Aware Mitigation for Boosted Guidance

abstract: AI advancements have been significantly driven by a combination of foundation models and curiosity-driven learning aimed at increasing capability and adaptability. Within this landscape, open-endedness, where AI agents autonomously and indefinitely generate novel behaviors, representations, or solutions, has gained increasing interest. This has become relevant in the context of self-evolving agents and long-horizon discovery. This position paper argues that the defining properties of open-ended AI systems introduce a distinct and underexplored class of safety challenges, including loss of predictability, emergent misalignment, and difficulties in maintaining effective control as systems evolve beyond their initial design assumptions, that must be addressed preemptively. These challenges differ qualitatively from those associated with task-bounded or static models and are unlikely to be addressed by existing safety frameworks alone, which is why these risks must be examined proactively, before large-scale deployment. The paper proposes a taxonomy for key challenges, discusses research opportunities, and calls for coordinated action to support the safe and responsible development of open-ended AI.

paragraphs: Open-ended AI agents can keep generating new behaviors, representations, or solutions autonomously and indefinitely. This paper argues that these defining properties create safety challenges requiring attention before large-scale deployment. The concern becomes especially relevant for agents that evolve themselves or pursue discovery over long periods, where continued adaptation is part of the intended capability.

The authors identify declining predictability, emerging misalignment, and difficulty maintaining control as systems move beyond their original design assumptions. They argue that these challenges differ qualitatively from those of static models or agents restricted to bounded tasks. A safety approach designed around fixed behavior may therefore be insufficient for systems whose behavior continues to develop.

The paper proposes a taxonomy of key challenges, discusses research opportunities, and calls for coordinated action. Its contribution is to organize a distinct safety agenda around open-endedness itself. The claim about existing frameworks is qualified: they are unlikely to address these risks on their own. The proposed response is proactive research and preparation, so safety work develops before deployment creates extensive exposure to evolving systems.
summary.tldr: Agents that continually invent new behaviors need proactive safety research addressing evolving predictability, alignment, and control.

abstract: A sensible use of classifiers must be based on the estimated reliability of their predictions. A cautious classifier would delegate the difficult or uncertain predictions to other, possibly more specialised, classifiers. In this paper we analyse and develop this idea of delegating classifiers in a systematic way. First, we design a two-step scenario where a first classifier chooses which examples to classify and delegates the difficult examples to train a second classifier. Secondly, we present an iterated scenario involving an arbitrary number of chained classifiers. We compare these scenarios to classical ensemble methods, such as bagging and boosting. We show experimentally that our approach is not far behind these methods in terms of accuracy, but with several advantages: (i) improved efficiency, since each classifier learns from fewer examples than the previous one; (ii) improved comprehensibility, since each classification derives from a single classifier; and (iii) the possibility to simplify the overall multiclassifier by removing the parts that lead to delegation.

paragraphs: The paper studies classifiers that use estimated prediction reliability to decide which examples to handle themselves. Difficult or uncertain examples are delegated to another classifier, which may become more specialized. This makes the decision to pass an example onward an explicit part of the classification process.

The authors first develop a two-stage setup: one classifier selects the examples it will classify, and the difficult examples are used to train a second classifier. They then extend the idea to chains containing an arbitrary number of classifiers. Each successive classifier learns from fewer examples, concentrating training on the cases delegated by earlier stages.

Experiments compare these arrangements with bagging and boosting. Accuracy is reported as not far behind those methods, alongside advantages in efficiency and comprehensibility. Each final classification comes from a single classifier, making its origin easier to identify. The authors also describe the possibility of simplifying the overall system by removing parts that lead to delegation, adding a route to a smaller multiclassifier.
summary.tldr: Chains of classifiers delegate uncertain examples, approaching bagging and boosting accuracy while offering efficiency and interpretability advantages.

title: Delegating classifiers

Traditionally, thistask is considered under the assumption that examplesare independent and identically distributed. However,it turns out that many results of pattern recognition theory carry over undera much weaker assumption. Namely, under the assumptionof conditional independence and identical distribution of objects only,while the only condition on the distribution of labels is that therate of occurrence of each label should be above some positive threshold.We find a broad class of learning algorithms for which estimations ofthe probability of a classification error achieved under the classical i.i.d.assumption canbe generalised to the similar estimates for the case of conditionally i.i.d.distributed examples.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much independence online classification theory really needs. In the task considered, a learner predicts a sequence of labels using each presented object and the labeled examples seen so far. Traditional analysis assumes that complete object-label examples are independent and identically distributed, a restriction the authors seek to weaken.

The alternative assumption requires conditional independence and identical distribution of the objects. The label distribution is constrained only by requiring each label's occurrence rate to remain above a positive threshold. This allows the analysis to move beyond the usual assumption on whole examples while retaining a specific structure for objects and a frequency requirement for labels.

The authors identify a broad class of learning algorithms whose classification-error probability estimates under the classical assumption can be generalized to similar estimates in this conditional setting. The contribution is theoretical: it extends the applicability of existing learning guarantees. Its scope depends on the stated conditional distribution and label-frequency assumptions, rather than permitting completely unrestricted sequences of data.
summary.tldr: Error guarantees for a broad class of online classifiers extend to conditionally independent objects with a positive occurrence-rate requirement for every label.

title: Online learning of conditionally I.I.D. data

abstract: We propose statistical predicate invention as a key problem for statistical relational learning. SPI is the problem of discovering new concepts, properties and relations in structured data, and generalizes hidden variable discovery in statistical models and predicate invention in ILP. We propose an initial model for SPI based on second-order Markov logic, in which predicates as well as arguments can be variables, and the domain of discourse is not fully known in advance. Our approach iteratively refines clusters of symbols based on the clusters of symbols they appear in atoms with (e.g., it clusters relations by the clusters of the objects they relate). Since different clusterings are better for predicting different subsets of the atoms, we allow multiple cross-cutting clusterings. We show that this approach outperforms Markov logic structure learning and the recently introduced infinite relational model on a number of relational datasets.

paragraphs: The paper introduces statistical predicate invention as the task of discovering new concepts, properties, and relations in structured data. It brings together hidden-variable discovery in statistical modeling and predicate invention in inductive logic programming. The goal is to learn useful relational concepts rather than rely entirely on a vocabulary supplied beforehand.

The proposed initial model uses second-order Markov logic, allowing both predicates and their arguments to be variables while leaving the domain incompletely specified in advance. Its learning procedure repeatedly refines clusters of symbols using the clusters of symbols with which they occur. For example, relations can be grouped according to the groups of objects they connect.

The model permits multiple overlapping ways of clustering because different groupings may better predict different subsets of relational statements. This gives concept discovery flexibility beyond a single partition of the symbols. On several relational datasets, the approach outperforms Markov logic structure learning and the infinite relational model, supporting the usefulness of the proposed discovery mechanism in those evaluations.
summary.tldr: A second-order Markov logic approach discovers relational concepts through multiple interacting clusterings and outperforms two established approaches on several datasets.
